(Wismar) Am 9. Oktober 2026 lud das noch junge, fakultätsübergreifende Institut für Immobilienmanagement (IFIM) erstmals zum Norddeutschen Tag des Immobilienmanagements ein.
Im Mittelpunkt der neuen Fachtagung mit Perspektiven aus Wissenschaft, Wohnungswirtschaft und Praxis stand die Revitalisierung als zentrale Frage der Bauwende. Fachbeiträge zeigten, wie sich Ressourcen schonen, Flächenverbrauch reduzieren und CO₂-Emissionen minimieren lassen, indem Bestehendes neu gedacht wird. Diskussion, Master-Thesen und Case Studies boten Raum für Austausch. Die Bündelung von Fachkompetenzen aus drei Fakultäten im IFIM schafft beste Voraussetzungen für weitere zukunftsweisende Themen.
Weltweite Entwicklungen und Anforderungen im Immobilienmanagement
Prof. Dr.-Ing. Marcus Hackel ordnete die Revitalisierung in die weltweiten Entwicklungen und Anforderungen des Immobilienmanagements ein. Megatrends wie Digitalisierung, neue Mobilitätsformen, Gesundheit und Wohlbefinden der Nutzer, das Internet der Dinge, 3D-Drucktechnologien sowie demografische Veränderungen beeinflussen zunehmend Nutzungskonzepte und Standorte von Immobilien. Daraus ergeben sich neue Forschungsfelder und Anforderungen an die strategische Ausrichtung von Immobilienbeständen sowie an zukunftsfähige Corporate-Real-Estate-Strategien. Diese reichen von der Optimierung des Immobilienportfolios über die Unterstützung von Marketing und Vertrieb bis zur Förderung von Innovation, Mitarbeiterzufriedenheit und Produktivität. Vor diesem Hintergrund gewinnt die Revitalisierung als Beitrag zu Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, Nachhaltigkeit und ESG an Bedeutung, insbesondere durch Green Branding und die adaptive Weiternutzung des Bestandes. Professor Hackels seit 2009 an der Fakultät Gestaltung der Hochschule Wismar bestehende Lehr- und Forschungstätigkeit für das Fachgebiet "Baudurchführung und Entwerfen" ist dabei sowohl international und interkulturell als auch auf das Marketing für nachhaltige Stadtentwicklung und Architektur ausgerichtet.
Revitalisierung im genossenschaftlichen Wohnungsbau Hamburgs
Marko Lohmann stellte als Vorsitzender des VNW-Landesverband Hamburg e.V. und Vorstand der Bergedorf-Bille eG Immobilien in der Freien und Hansestadt in den Mittelpunkt seines Vortrags. Er betonte: „Zukunftsorientierter Neubau mit Augenmaß ein wichtiger Bestandteil des Erfolgs der Bergedorf-Bille“, die kontinuierlich in Bestand und Neubau investiert. Dabei stehen nachhaltige, altersgerechte und sozial ausgewogene Wohnangebote sowie eine vielfältige Nutzerstruktur im Mittelpunkt. So befinden sich aktuell rund 400 neue Wohnungen in unterschiedlichen Planungs- und Realisierungsphasen. Ein Beispiel für die Verbindung von Bestandsentwicklung und Neubau ist die Quartiersentwicklung Bergedorf-West, eine Großwohnsiedlung aus den Jahren 1967 bis 1970. Sie ist seit 2019 offizielles Fördergebiet im hamburgischen Rahmenprogramm Integrierte Stadtteilentwicklung (RISE). Die Planungen reagieren auf veränderte Bedürfnisse mit altersgerechten und generationenübergreifenden Wohnangeboten, mehr Barrierearmut, einer Stärkung der sozialen Mischung und zusätzlichem bezahlbarem Wohnraum. Gleichzeitig sollen Verkehr und Freiräume neu geordnet, nachhaltige Mobilität gestärkt und Flächen sparsamer genutzt werden. Serielles und modulares Bauen soll dabei einen zügigen Baufortschritt und mehr Kostensicherheit ermöglichen, sodass die Nutzungsentgelte für die Mitglieder der Baugenossenschaft langfristig bezahlbar bleiben.
Revitalisierung am Beispiel WoBau Wismar
Katharina Franzke stellte am Praxisbeispiel Wismar-Wendorf die Revitalisierung baugleicher, dreigeschossiger Mehrfamilienhäuser aus den 1950er Jahren vor. Die Geschäftsführerin der Wohnungsbaugesellschaft mbH der Hansestadt Wismar betonte, dass dabei Barrierefreiheit, Inklusion und zeitgemäße Wohnstandards im Mittelpunkt gestanden haben. Ursprünglich diskutierte Abriss- und Neubaupläne wurden angepasst, um die bestehende Bausubstanz und damit die darin gebundene graue Energie zu erhalten. Sie ging auf neue Wohnmodelle und die Nutzung von Leerständen als Zwischenlösung für umziehende Mieter ein. In der anschließenden Diskussionsrunde wurden auch Gespräche mit sozialen Trägern thematisiert.
Graue Energie bezeichnet die Energiemenge, die für Herstellung, Transport, Lagerung, Verkauf und Entsorgung eines Gebäudes aufgewendet wird und damit in der bestehenden Bausubstanz gebunden ist. „Wenn wir unsere alten Häuser nicht abreißen, sondern modernisieren und aufpeppen, sparen wir die „graue Energie“ für neue Häuser – ein guter Schritt zu mehr Nachhaltigkeit!“, so Franzke.
IFIM – das interdisziplinäre Institut
Das Institut für Immobilienmanagement IFIM stärkt die Immobilienwirtschaftliche Kompetenz an der Hochschule Wismar und arbeitet dabei auch mit der hochschuleigenen WINGS GmbH zusammen. Ziel ist es, das Fachgebiet in Forschung, Lehre und regionaler Vernetzung sichtbar auszubauen sowie die Hochschule als starken Partner der Branche zu positionieren. Im Mittelpunkt der Institutstätigkeit stehen praxisnahe Kooperationen mit Unternehmen und Verbänden, anwendungsorientierte Forschungs- und Transferprojekte sowie eine enge Begleitung der Studierenden durch Mentoring und Unterstützung studentischer Projekte sowie Initiativen. Durch Formate wie den jährlich stattfindenden „Norddeutschen Tag des Immobilienmanagements“ trägt das Institut dazu bei, Wissen sichtbar zu machen und aktuelle Entwicklungen der Immobilienwirtschaft breit zugänglich zu machen.

Forschen in Architektur, Stadt und Kunst: Internationales Bauhaus-Kolloquium feiert 50. Jubiläum

1. Bauhaus-Kolloquium 1976 in Weimar.
| Copyright:

Download
1976 trafen sich Forschende erstmals in Weimar, dem Gründungsort des Staatlichen Bauhauses, um sich über drängende Fragen der Architektur, Stadt und Gestaltung auszutauschen. Seitdem findet die Tagung regelmäßig an der Universität statt und verhandelt aktuelle Themen im Spannungsfeld zwischen dem historischen Bauhaus und gegenwärtigen gesellschaftlichen Entwicklungen. Vom 4. bis 7. November 2026 versammelt die 15. Ausgabe unter dem Titel »Politics of Research« an der Bauhaus-Universität Weimar internationale Forschende aus Architektur, Urbanistik, Kunst und Theorie. Das 50-jährige Bestehen wird am 5. November, 18 Uhr, gefeiert, begleitet von einer studentischen Ausstellung zu Archivfunden.
Das 1919 von Walter Gropius in Weimar gegründete Bauhaus musste die Stadt 1925 unter politischem Druck verlassen und wurde 1933 von den Nationalsozialisten endgültig geschlossen. Während seine Ideen in den USA und Westdeutschland weiterentwickelt und umgeschrieben wurden, blieb seine Geschichte in der DDR lange Zeit kaum erforscht. Erst in den frühen 1970er Jahren etablierte sich die Geschichte des Staatlichen Bauhauses als Forschungsfeld und sein bauliches Erbe rückte wieder in den Blick. Ein wichtiger Anlass war die Rekonstruktion des Bauhaus-Gebäudes in Dessau – eine Initiative, die maßgeblich an der Hochschule für Architektur und Bauwesen in Weimar vorbereitet und wissenschaftlich begleitet wurde.
Die wissenschaftliche Wiederaneignung des Bauhauses an der Hochschule für Architektur und Bauwesen Weimar bildete zugleich den Ausgangspunkt für das erste Kolloquium 1976. In diesem staatlich gewährten und überwachten Rahmen tauschten sich Forschende, Theoretiker*innen, Künstler*innen, Architekt*innen und frühere Mitglieder des Bauhauses aus und teilten ihr Wissen über den Verbleib der Objekte und Personen des Bauhauses sowie über Sammlungs- und Denkmalschutzinitiativen. Stück für Stück entstand daraus ein vollständigeres Bild der Bauhaus-Geschichte, deren materielles Erbe 1996 mit der Aufnahme der Bauhaus-Stätten in Weimar und Dessau in die UNESCO-Welterbeliste internationale Anerkennung fand.
Über die folgenden Jahrzehnte hinweg wurden die Kolloquien in Weimar mit zunehmender internationaler Resonanz fortgesetzt. In diesem Jahr begeht das wissenschaftliche Format seinen 50. Geburtstag unter dem Titel »Politics of Research«. Damit nimmt das Kolloquium einerseits die eigenen Entstehungsbedingungen in den Fokus, andererseits fragt es in Zeiten politischer Polarisierung nach den politischen Dimensionen von Forschung, ihren vielfältigen Voraussetzungen, ihrem Verhältnis zu gesellschaftlichen Konflikten und den ökonomischen Logiken, von denen sie abhängt.
Am Abend des 5. November 2026 findet ein Empfang anlässlich des Jubiläums statt, bei dem Prof. Dr. Daniela Spiegel und Prof. Dr. Max Welch Guerra Vorträge zur Geschichte des Kolloquiums halten. Anschließend besteht die Möglichkeit zum Austausch mit Akteuren aus der Geschichte des Kolloquiums, mit den Teilnehmenden der diesjährigen Konferenz und mit den Mitwirkenden der Bauhaus-Universität Weimar. Darüber hinaus gibt es die Gelegenheit, eine studentische Ausstellung zu Archivfunden aus 50 Jahren des Internationalen Bauhaus-Kolloquiums zu besuchen sowie weitere künstlerische Arbeiten, die das XV. Internationale Bauhaus-Kolloquium eingeladen hat. Der Abend klingt bei Gesprächen und Musik aus.
Politische Bedingungen der Wissensproduktion
Das XV. Internationale Bauhaus-Kolloquium wird von der Deutschen Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), der Ernst-Abbe-Stiftung und der Wüstenrot Stiftung gefördert. Die englischsprachige Konferenz bringt rund 100 internationale Forschende aus Architektur und Stadtplanung, Kunst und Gestaltung sowie Medien- und Kulturwissenschaften zusammen, um über die politischen, institutionellen und gesellschaftlichen Bedingungen von Forschung zu diskutieren.
Das Programm umfasst vier parallele Panels mit Vorträgen, Diskussionen und Performances. Künstlerische Arbeiten und partizipative Workshopformate erproben alternative Erkenntnisformen. Internationale Abendvorträge von Samia Henni, Matteo Pasquinelli sowie eine Filmpräsentation mit anschließender Diskussion von Hito Steyerl und Oleksiy Radynski eröffnen Perspektiven auf Architektur, Medien, Technologie und die politischen Dimensionen von Raum- und Wissensproduktion.

title: Abschluss der VDI Student Challenge: Studierende der TH Aschaffenburg präsentieren innovative Prototypen

Abschluss der VDI Student Challenge: Studierende der TH Aschaffenburg präsentieren innovative Prototypen

Teilnehmende der VDI-Student-Challenge 2026 an der TH Aschaffenburg
| Quelle:
Laura Fee Pache
Download
Von intelligenter Espressozubereitung bis zur essbaren Batterie: Studierende zeigen die Vielfalt praxisnaher Ingenieurwissenschaften. Die drei besten Projekte der VDI-Student-Challenge wurden mit einem Geldpreis prämiert.
Die Ergebnisse ihrer sechsmonatigen Projektarbeit stellten sechs studentische Teams der Fakultät Ingenieurwissenschaften und Informatik (IWIN) der Technischen Hochschule Aschaffenburg am Donnerstag, 15. Oktober 2026, bei der Abschlussveranstaltung der VDI Student Challenge 2026 vor. Eine Fachjury und das Publikum bewerteten die entwickelten Prototypen. Den ersten Platz belegten Pascal Köhnlein, Daniel Levin, Yannick Naß und Leon Schuck mit ihrem Projekt „Intelligente Espressozubereitung durch automatisierte Mahlgradverstellung“.
Organisiert wurde der Wettbewerb gemeinsam von der Fakultät IWIN und dem VDI Bezirksverein Aschaffenburg. Für die Umsetzung ihrer ingenieur- oder informatikbezogenen Ideen erhielten die Teams jeweils 600 Euro für Materialkosten. Zusätzlich stellte der VDI Preisgelder für die drei bestplatzierten Ideen bereit: 750 Euro für den ersten, 500 Euro für den zweiten und 350 Euro für den dritten Platz.
Der perfekte Espresso als ingenieurwissenschaftliche Herausforderung
Die Idee für ihr Gewinnerprojekt entstand aus der eigenen Vorliebe der vier Studenten für guten Kaffee. Sie entwickelten eine drahtlos vernetzte Einheit aus Kaffeemühle und Siebträgermaschine, die den Mahlgrad automatisch an die jeweiligen Zubereitungsparameter anpassen soll.
Dafür erfasst und analysiert der Prototyp die Parameter der Espressozubereitung und ermöglicht eine dynamische Mahlgradeinstellung. Mit kostengünstigen elektrotechnischen Komponenten erweiterten die Studierenden die Funktionalität handelsüblicher Geräte. Ziel ist es, die professionelle Espressozubereitung zu vereinfachen und künftig weitere Funktionen softwarebasiert ergänzen zu können.
Die vier Studenten haben sich für die Entwicklung innovativer Technologien im Bereich der Antriebstechnik im Labor elektrische Maschinen an der TH Aschaffenburg im Studienschwerpunkt „Antriebstechnik und Robotik“ entschieden.
Sechs Projekte, vielfältige Ideen
Auch die fünf weiteren Teams zeigten ihre Prototypen an eigenen Ständen mit Postern und Anschauungsmaterialien und kamen mit Besuchenden und Fachjury ins Gespräch:
• Il Pulito – Pizzaschaufel mit Absaugfunktion: Eine Konstruktion, die Mehl, Asche und Rauch reduzieren soll.
• Entwicklung einer essbaren Batterie: Ein biologisch abbaubarer Energiespeicher aus lebensmittelbasierten Materialien.
• JUPITER – Modulares Lichtpult für intelligente Assistenzsysteme: Eine offene Plattform für intelligente Unterstützung in der professionellen Lichttechnik.
• Test-Dummy zur Bewertung mittelalterlicher Rüstung: Eine Untersuchung der Kräfte, die bei der Einwirkung mittelalterlicher Waffen auf Rüstungen auftreten.
• Launch O’Clock – Die Countdown-Anzeige: Ein digitaler Wecker, der die verbleibende Zeit bis zum nächsten Raketenstart anzeigt.
Nach der Präsentation der Prototypen bewerteten die Fachjury sowie das Publikum die Projekte. Den zweiten Platz erreichte die Gruppe mit der „Entwicklung einer essbaren Batterie“. Auf Platz drei landete das Projekt „JUPITER – Modulares Lichtpult für intelligente Assistenzsysteme“.
Erfolgreicher Abschluss der Challenge
Eröffnet wurde die Abschlussveranstaltung von TH-Präsidentin Prof. Dr. Eva Beck-Meuth und Markus Grundmann vom VDI. Nach den Grußworten stellte Prof. Dr.-Ing. Johannes Teigelkötter die Challenge vor und würdigte den großen Einsatz der Studierenden. Alle sechs Teams hätten ihre Projekte konsequent weiterverfolgt, Budget- und Terminverantwortung übernommen und vorzeigbare Ergebnisse geschaffen. Insofern haben alle Teams bei dem Wettbewerb neue Fähigkeiten gewonnen.
Neben den technischen Ergebnissen hob er insbesondere den Wert der Zusammenarbeit hervor:
„Das schweißt zusammen im Team. Man lernt voneinander und das ist ja das Wichtige, dass wir hier keine Einzelkämpfer ausbilden, sondern Leute, die in der Gesellschaft klarkommen.“ (Prof. Dr.-Ing. Johannes Teigelkötter)
Mit der Prämierung als Höhepunkt hat die VDI Student Challenge 2026 gezeigt, wie Studierende theoretisches Wissen in konkrete Lösungen überführen können. Gleichzeitig verdeutlichen die Projekte, wie vielfältig ingenieurwissenschaftliche Ideen sein können – von der Weiterentwicklung bestehender Technik bis hin zu neuen Lösungsansätzen für unterschiedliche Anwendungsbereiche.
Eine Wiederholung der Challenge ist für 2027 geplant. Ende Oktober wird ein neuer Aufruf zur Einreichung von Ideen veröffentlicht.

title: Fraunhofer-Bessel-Preisträger Professor Daniel Gianola von der University of California forscht am Fraunhofer IWM
content:
Fraunhofer-Bessel-Preisträger Professor Daniel Gianola von der University of California forscht am Fraunhofer IWM
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Das Bildmaterial darf nur in Zusammenhang mit dem Inhalt dieser Pressemitteilung verwendet werden. Professor Dan Gianola neben einem Transmissionselektronenmikroskop.
| Quelle:
Lilli Walker
| Copyright:
Download
Die Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung verleiht Professor Daniel S. Gianola von der University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) den Fraunhofer-Bessel-Forschungspreis. Der mit 45.000 Euro dotierte Preis würdigt seine herausragenden Beiträge zur Erforschung der mechanischen Eigenschaften von Strukturwerkstoffen und zur Entwicklung innovativer In-situ-Charakterisierungsmethoden. Von November 2026 bis Juli 2027 wird der Materialwissenschaftler einen Forschungsaufenthalt am Fraunhofer-Institut für Werkstoffmechanik IWM in Freiburg und am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie KIT absolvieren.
Professor Daniel Gianola ist ein international anerkannter Experte für das mechanische Verhalten von Werkstoffen an den Grenzen ihrer Belastbarkeit. Seine Forschung verbindet fortschrittliche Materialcharakterisierung mit der Untersuchung von Mikrostruktur-Eigenschafts-Beziehungen und hat zu wegweisenden Erkenntnissen über Defektmechanismen in kristallinen und amorphen Materialien geführt.
Besonders hervorzuheben ist seine Pionierarbeit bei der Verbesserung der Untersuchung von Funktionsmaterialien wie Halbleitern oder Batteriewerkstoffen im Rasterelektronenmikroskop. Mit dem Einsatz direkter Elektronendetektoren für Elektronenbeugung und -bildgebung, konnte er die Charakterisierung und Aufklärung von Strukturwerkstoffen um Größenordnungen beschleunigen.
Dass Dan Gianola 2026 mit der Brimacombe-Medaille der amerikanischen Minerals, Metals & Materials Society (TMS) geehrt wurde, unterstreicht seine wissenschaftliche Exzellenz. Mit der Auszeichnung, die die TMS an herausragende Mitglieder der materialwissenschaftlichen Community verleiht, wurden Gianolas »Innovationen in der In-situ-Elektronenmikroskopie und der Mikromechanik von Kristalldefekten sowie sein Engagement für die TMS« gewürdigt.
»Wir freuen uns sehr darauf, Professor Gianola an unserem Institut begrüßen zu dürfen«, sagt Professor Peter Gumbsch, Institutsleiter des Fraunhofer IWM. »Seine Expertise in der In-situ-Mikromechanik und der beschleunigten Materialcharakterisierung ergänzt unsere Kompetenzen in der Materialdatenanalyse und im maschinellen Lernen hervorragend. Gemeinsam wollen wir KI-gestützte Analysemethoden entwickeln, um aus den enormen Datenströmen moderner Elektronendetektoren automatisiert Informationen über Materialstruktur, Chemie und Defekte zu gewinnen.«
Während seines Forschungsaufenthalts wird Professor Gianola am Fraunhofer IWM gemeinsam mit Professor Peter Gumbsch und Professor Chris Eberl an neuen mikromechanischen Charakterisierungstechniken arbeiten, die durch maschinelles Lernen und künstliche Intelligenz unterstützt werden. Ziel ist die Entwicklung von Workflows zum Materialdatenmanagement, mit denen die enormen Datenmengen, die durch direkte Elektronendetektoren erzeugt werden, vollautomatisch analysiert werden können. Zudem wird er sich in die nationale Forschungsdateninfrastruktur NFDI-MatWerk einbringen, die vom Fraunhofer IWM koordiniert wird.
Am KIT sind Kooperationen mit Professor Christoph Kirchlechner (Institut für Angewandte Materialien) zu neuartigen In-situ-Prüfverfahren sowie mit Professorin Yolita Eggeler (Fakultät für Physik) zur fortgeschrittenen Elektronenmikroskopie und Beugung geplant. Dabei stehen die Beobachtung von Versetzungsbewegungen und das Verständnis von Verformungsmechanismen in Hochtemperatur-Strukturwerkstoffen im Fokus.
Zum Preisträger
Daniel S. Gianola ist Professor im Materials Department der University of California, Santa Barbara. Nach seiner Promotion an der Johns Hopkins University war er als Alexander von Humboldt-Stipendiat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie tätig, bevor er zunächst an der University of Pennsylvania und dann an der UCSB seine Forschungsgruppe aufbaute. Für seine Arbeiten wurde er unter anderem mit den renommiertesten Nachwuchspreisen der USA ausgezeichnet, darunter Förderungen der National Science Foundation (NSF) und des Department of Energy (DOE) sowie das Early Career Faculty Fellowship der Minerals, Metals and Materials Society (TMS). Seine Forschungsschwerpunkte umfassen die Mechanik von Nanostrukturen, die Entwicklung hochfester Legierungen für extreme Umgebungen und die datengetriebene Materialentdeckung.
Der Fraunhofer-Bessel-Forschungspreis wird von der Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung und der Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft gemeinsam an international herausragende Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler aus dem Ausland vergeben, die anwendungsnahe Forschung betreiben. Die Auszeichnung ermöglicht einen Forschungsaufenthalt an einem Fraunhofer-Institut in Deutschland und fördert die langfristige wissenschaftliche Zusammenarbeit.

title: Kinder- und Jugendmedienschutz: Weizenbaum-Institut betont die Notwendigkeit konsequenter Plattformverantwortung
content:
Kinder- und Jugendmedienschutz: Weizenbaum-Institut betont die Notwendigkeit konsequenter Plattformverantwortung
Die Bundesregierung hat die Eckpunkte zum Kinder- und Jugendmedienschutz beschlossen. Das Weizenbaum-Institut betont: Maßnahmen können Kinder und Jugendliche nur dann wirksam schützen, wenn Plattformbetreibende stärker in die Verantwortung genommen werden.
Die Bundesregierung hat die von Bundesministerin Karin Prien vorgelegten Eckpunkte zum Kinder- und Jugendmedienschutz beschlossen. Das Weizenbaum-Institut begrüßt grundsätzlich diese Eckpunkte, die die Grundlage für die Ausarbeitung konkreter Maßnahmen bieten sollen. Wissenschaftler:innen des Weizenbaum-Instituts betonen jedoch: Maßnahmen und Regelungen können Kinder und Jugendliche nur dann wirksam schützen, wenn Plattformbetreibende stärker in die Verantwortung genommen und bestehende Regulierungslücken geschlossen werden.
Die beschlossenen Eckpunkte bauen unmittelbar auf den Empfehlungen einer unabhängigen Sachverständigenkommission auf, die die Bundesregierung im Vorfeld beraten hat. Teil dieses Gremiums war auch Dr. Annika Baumann, Digitalexpertin und Forschungsgruppenleiterin am Weizenbaum-Institut:
„Die verabschiedeten Eckpunkte sind ein sinnvoller erster Schritt hin zu einem umfassenderen Kinder- und Jugendmedienschutz. Altersgrenzen und Medienbildung können dabei wichtige Bausteine sein. Sie reichen jedoch nicht aus, wenn Risiken durch die Gestaltung digitaler Angebote mitverursacht werden“, erklärt Dr. Annika Baumann anlässlich der Veröffentlichung des Papiers. „Die Eckpunkte benennen klar die Hauptverantwortung der Plattformen. Nun kommt es darauf an, bestehende Pflichten konsequent durchzusetzen und angekündigte Anforderungen konkret auszugestalten. Zugleich braucht es Prävention sowie niedrigschwellige Hilfe- und Meldewege, etwa die geplante Kinder-Onlinewache.“
Interdisziplinäre Forschung für ein sichereres Netz
Das Weizenbaum-Institut begleitet und prägt die Debatte um den Schutz von Kindern und Jugendlichen im Internet seit Jahren mit fundierten wissenschaftlichen Analysen. In verschiedenen Forschungsgruppen an der Schnittstelle von Digitalisierung, Recht und Gesellschaft untersuchen die Wissenschaftler:innen, wie Algorithmen, Suchtmechanismen (wie „Dark Patterns“) und Geschäftsmodelle digitaler Konzerne das Wohlbefinden junger Nutzer:innen beeinflussen.
Im Zentrum der Weizenbaum-Forschung steht dabei der von der Expert:innenkommission benannte Ansatz „Safety by Design“: Digitale Angebote sollen von Grund auf so gestaltet sein, dass Risiken wie Cybermobbing, Desinformation oder algorithmische Manipulation minimiert werden.
Wissenschaft und Praxis: Impulse für die Medienbildung
Effektiver Jugendschutz braucht zudem eine starke demokratische und medienpädagogische Praxis. Einen zentralen Baustein dieses Wissenstransfers bietet auch die gemeinsame Publikationsreihe des Weizenbaum-Instituts mit der Landeszentrale für politische Bildung: In dieser Reihe werden komplexe wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse über die Dynamiken des digitalen Raums speziell für die pädagogische Praxis, Schulen und die politische Bildung aufbereitet. Die Veröffentlichungen bieten konkrete Handlungsempfehlungen zu Themen wie algorithmischer Meinungsbildung, digitaler Resilienz und dem Umgang mit Desinformation.

Sigrun Gunnhildarottir, CPO at AGR. Credit: AGR
The statistics at a glance:
34.7% of UK businesses were using AI in June 2026.
However, only 26.9% of manufacturing businesses and 28.4% of wholesale and retail businesses were using AI: below the national business adoption rate.
Around 47% of AI-using businesses in manufacturing, wholesale and retail reported operational improvements, compared with around 59% nationally.
Six in ten respondents reported being concerned about supply chain costs over the following year.
Only 2.7% of wholesale and retail businesses used AI for data processing, compared with 7.6% across UK businesses overall.
UK manufacturing and retail trail on AI
In 2026, supply chain leaders are operating in a challenging environment. Natural disasters, component shortages and geopolitical events have produced a series of disruptions to supply, making inventory management increasingly difficult to navigate.
Companies are under pressure to reduce expenditure as disruptions impact order times and stock. As businesses aim to future-proof their operations, scaling AI presents a potential route to protecting value.
According to RELEX’s 2026 global State of Supply Chain report, 71% of supply chain leaders plan to invest in AI over the next three to five years.
However, AGR’s UK analysis indicates
a lag in actual AI implementation
among manufacturers and retailers, with adoption rates sitting at 7.8% and 6.3% the national average respectively.
The gap also extends to reported business benefits. While close to 59% of UK businesses using AI said it was improving their operations, the proportion fell to approximately 47% across manufacturing, wholesale and retail.
While AGR’s findings cover a UK footprint, global research retains the pattern. A September 2025 survey by the
Boston Consulting Group
found that 60% of organisations reported low return on investment from their AI implementation.
AGR’s analysis suggests that adoption alone does not demonstrate progress towards better supply chain decisions.
"These businesses want AI, and they're under pressure on costs. But they don't just want more AI,” says Sigrun.
“They want tools that understand their operational data, show them how recommendations are reached and leave them in control of the final decision.”
When AI investment misses operational bottlenecks
Beyond adoption rates, AGR’s findings raise questions about which AI applications businesses should prioritise.
"When our clients tell us what they want from AI, forecasting comes first,” says Sigrun. “They want earlier warning on demand shifts, anomalies and the effect of promotions, so they can plan replenishment around it.”
Figures for June 2026 show that text generation and visual content creation are more widely adopted than data processing across UK businesses. Nationally, 17.1% used AI for text generation and 14.4% for visual content, compared with 7.6% using AI for data processing.
In wholesale and retail, only 2.7% of businesses reported using AI for data processing. Manufacturing recorded 6.1%.
Companies are under pressure to reduce expenditure as supply-chain disruptions impact order times and stock. Credit: Unsplash / Russ Murray
While general-purpose tools can support administrative and content-related tasks, forecasting and inventory optimisation require data-processing technology. AGR’s results reflect that businesses’ desire for AI forecasting is failing to reach the implementation stage.
“Businesses need to be able to see what data an AI recommendation is based on, rather than simply being given an answer," Sigrun says. “Without that context, they can’t support a replenishment decision.”
These results are supported by a wider research scope. Examining the UK’s manufacturing sector,
Make UK’s
June 2026 report found that just 7% of organisations used AI to enhance their supply chain operations, despite 83% recording back-office AI use.
The focus on automating administrative work neglects core business functions, where
larger cost-saving opportunities
could lie.
For supply chain decision-making, this includes inventory management, wherein inaccuracy can drive up costs though emergency stock purchasing and lost revenue.
Priorities for supply chain leaders
For supply chain leaders, connecting AI investment to specific, high-priority operational requirements could be the key to producing measurable outcomes.
Research demonstrates that to secure valuable outcomes from AI, businesses must avoid viewing the technology as an automation tool.
Identifying key bottlenecks – like inaccurate forecasting – can provide a foundation. From there, organisations can scale AI systems to process and connect their data, producing insights that inform the business functions where greater value lies.
Key companies
Advantage Business Systems
Advantage Business Systems is a UK business software specialist who works in partnership with AGR. The partnership extends AGR’s demand forecasting and inventory optimisation solutions to Microsoft Dynamics users, connecting businesses with stock planning and replenishment tools.
Braintree Technologies
A partner of Microsoft, South African technology company Braintree Technologies works with AGR to specifically connect AGR’s intelligence software with supply-chain businesses across South Africa.
UK technology provider TVT is another distributor of AGR’s forecasting capabilities. With 25 years of experience as an ERP specialist, the company unifies businesses’ finances and data in the cloud.

title: Korean Operator Completes Northern Sea Route Trial
content:
Korean Operator Completes Northern Sea Route Trial
Prioritise Us
on Google
South Korean ship operator Panstar completed a round trip journey between Busan and ports in northwest Europe in October 2026. Credit: Panstar
Panstar Group Chairman Kim Hyun-gyeom says Panstar Line’s Northern Sea Route trial supports future Korea-Europe Arctic shipping
Panstar Line has completed South Korea’s first round-trip container-ship trial through Russia’s Northern Sea Route. The 2,758 TEU Panstar Acro departed Busan on 22 August 2026, sailed through Arctic waters to Felixstowe, Rotterdam and Gdansk, and returned to Busan on 11 October after a 50-day voyage.
The operation was intended to assess whether operating commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route between East Asia and northern Europe could shorten the journey time by 10 days to 20 days, compared with journey times of almost 30 days for East Asia-Northern Europe shipments via the Suez Canal.
Commenting on X on the successful trial, the President of South Korea, Lee Jae-Myung, writes “We will continue to prepare for an Arctic shipping era, and this test trip would create new opportunities for businesses.”
After the pilot project was announced, a Chinese-owned Singapore-based ship operator, Sea Legend Shipping,
announced
that it was launching a scheduled Northern Sea Route connecting Qingdao, Shanghai and Ningbo in China with Felixstowe, Rotterdam, Hamburg and Gdansk. The first and only scheduled sailing of the service in 2026 departed Qingdao on 22 September, using a 4,890 TEU container vessel, Istanbul Bridge. The service offers an 18-day transit time.
The Inauguration Ceremony of the 21th President of Republic of Korea Lee Jae-Myung. Credit: Korea.net / Korean Culture and Information Service
South Korean Northern Sea Route Pilot Project
The Panstar round trip was part of a South Korean government-led pilot project on the Arctic route promoted by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, Korea Ocean Business Corporation, and Korea Shipping Association.
In May, Panstar was selected as a pilot shipping company through a public contest, becoming the first South Korean ship operator to accumulate experience and data on operating container ships on commercial Arctic routes.
Kim Hyun-gyeom, Chairman of Panstar Group, comments, "As this is Korea's first container ship pilot operation, we are prioritising safety above all else. Once the operation is successfully completed, we will lay the foundation for establishing regular services on the Asia-Europe Arctic route based on our operational experience and the data we have secured."
The trial intended to demonstrate that travelling between Busan and Rotterdam route via the NSR would shorten the operating distance by about 35% and the operating period by approximately 10 days compared to the existing Suez Canal route. The trial’s projected efficiencies did not take into account the greater fuel efficiency of larger capacity container carriers per TEU compared with small capacity vessels. Supply Chain Digital notes.
Singapore-based shipping operator Sea Legend completed a first shipment to Felixstowe, UK via the Northern Sea Route in October 2025. Credit: Peter Fass
Commercial Viability Faces Cost and Seasonal Constraints
Despite the successful conclusion of the trial, there remain a number of constraints before ship operators in South Korea consider adding routes via the Northern Sea Route to their schedules.
Beyond practical considerations such as the need for vessel modifications, the window for container vessels to traverse the NSR is likely to be limited to late summer and early autumn.
There also remain operational challenges for international ship operators to comply with sanctions that restrict commercial activities with Russian entities.
While the pace of climate change has coincided with reduced seasonal sea-ice coverage, which has increased navigability in some periods, the Northern Sea Route remains seasonal and operationally demanding.
Until 2020, the
was on demonstrating the feasibility of LNG shipments using ice-class LNG carriers along the NSR between LNG projects in Russia’s High North and customers in East Asia. However, Russian attempts to promote the development of the Northern Sea Route have slowed since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The longer term focus of the South Korean project is understood to be in preparation for further climatic changes, which may potentially lead to reductions in Arctic seasonal sea-ice coverage from the mid 2030s.
Operating vessels along the Northern Sea Route entails overcoming significant challenges.
Key facts about Panstar Northern Sea Route trial
Vessel: Panstar Acro is a 2,758 TEU container vessel operated by Panstar Line.
Departure: The vessel left Busan on 22 August 2026.
Route: The trial used the Northern Sea Route and included calls at Felixstowe, Rotterdam and Gdansk.
Return: Panstar Acro returned to Busan on 11 October after a 50-day round trip.
Cargo: The vessel carried 837 TEUs, including chemical products, used cars, auto parts and empty containers.
Project: The voyage was part of a South Korean government-led Arctic shipping pilot.
Potential benefit: Project planners expected the Northern Sea Route to reduce distance and transit time compared with the Suez Canal route.
Limitation: Seasonal ice, insurance, vessel modifications, operating costs and uncertain cargo volumes remain barriers to regular services.
Meet the partner
Panstar Line is a South Korean shipping operator and part of Panstar Group. The company operated the Panstar Acro during South Korea’s first government-supported round-trip container trial through the Northern Sea Route. The voyage was conducted with support from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, Korea Ocean Business Corporation and Korea Shipping Association to gather operational data for possible future Arctic services.

title: Green Science Alliance opens Swiss battery recycling lab - electrive.com
content:
The Japanese chemical and greentech firm has opened a battery recycling laboratory at the Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne (SIPBB) in the canton of Bern. In collaboration with the Swiss Battery Technology Center, the company aims to recover cathode material from used lithium-ion batteries, which can be directly reused in new cells. The detour via individual metals is to be eliminated.
Image: Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne AG
The lab was inaugurated on Monday, attended by GSA CEO Ryohei Mori and SBTC Director Christian Ochsenbein. Headquartered in Kawanishi, Japan, GSA specialises in areas such as quantum dots, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and deep eutectic solvents. Biel is set to serve as the company’s gateway to the European market. SBTC, for its part, covers material analysis, electrode manufacturing, battery cell development and testing, as well as recycling.
Black mass as a raw material
The focus is on so-called black mass. When end-of-life batteries are shredded and mechanically processed, a dark powder remains. This contains the active materials that store and release energy within the cell. In conventional recycling, individual metals such as lithium, nickel or cobalt are extracted using acids or alkalis. Several additional processing steps are then required to produce cathode material again. The variability of black mass – depending on cell chemistry, battery age and processing method – is being examined in the SHERLOCK research project, which aims to
develop quality standards for black mass
GSA aims to shorten this chain. Instead of breaking down the cathode material from the black mass into its constituent elements, the company reprocesses the material and reuses it directly. Experts refer to this as direct recycling. This approach is intended to save processing steps and resources. If successful, the production of new batteries would require fewer newly mined raw materials. However, the partners have not disclosed the exact details of the process.
Initial results are already available: batteries with regenerated cathode material from GSA achieved over 90 per cent of the initial capacity of comparable batteries with commercial-grade material. While this sounds promising, it is a laboratory figure provided by the participants. Details on the number of charge cycles, cell format or independent measurements are lacking. The technology is being developed for nickel-manganese-cobalt and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. For LFP cells in particular, a cost-effective method is crucial, as they contain neither nickel nor cobalt, making the recovery of individual metals far less economically viable.
A feasibility study
The division of labour in Biel is clearly defined: GSA contributes its recycling technology, while SBTC – one of four applied research centres of SIPBB – provides expertise, infrastructure and laboratory space. Together, the partners will examine the processed materials, build electrodes and cells from them, and conduct tests. The ultimate goal is to assess whether the process can be scaled up industrially.
Public funding remains modest so far. The first phase is being financed through an Innovation Cheque from the Swiss funding agency Innosuisse. This covers the costs of a Swiss research partner up to 15,000 Swiss francs (approximately €16,200 euros) and is intended for feasibility studies that must be completed within six months. The partners themselves describe it as the first step towards joint research.
Europe needs recycled materials
The demand is clear. The
EU Battery Regulation
mandates higher recovery rates for lithium, nickel and cobalt and, from August 2031, minimum proportions of recycled materials in new vehicle batteries. However, recycling remains economically challenging: according to the EU’s Safeloop study, losses currently amount to around €1.90 euros per kilogram of battery pack. Processes with fewer steps could provide a solution. The partners argue that, on a large scale, their method would also reduce dependence on newly mined raw materials and make European battery supply chains more resilient.
Research institutions are also seeking partners across borders. For example, the Fraunhofer FFB in Münster signed
letters of intent with South Korean partners
in early October, covering topics such as recycling and the implementation of the EU Battery Regulation. GSA intends to use SIPBB’s network to transition its technology from the lab to industry. Whether the 90 per cent performance can also be achieved with larger quantities remains to be seen.

title: Hydrovolt to recycle Iceland’s EV batteries in Future - electrive.com
content:
Norwegian battery recycler Hydrovolt has signed a cooperation agreement with the Icelandic Recycling Fund (IRF). Under this agreement, Hydrovolt will collect end-of-life batteries from electric vehicles and industrial applications in Iceland, transport them to Norway, and recycle them at its own facility in Fredrikstad. The company classifies this step as part of its Nordic strategy: no battery in the region should remain unused.
Image: Hydrovolt
The IRF (Icelandic Recycling Fund) implements extended producer responsibility in Iceland. The principle is simple: anyone who places products such as batteries on the market is also responsible for ensuring they are properly collected and recycled at the end of their life cycle. The fund manages the applicable recycling fees in accordance with Icelandic law and distributes them accordingly. Traction batteries from electric vehicles are explicitly included.
Demand is growing. According to a press release, 17 per cent of Iceland’s passenger car fleet now consists of battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. For new cars, Hydrovolt reports an electrified share of nearly 80 per cent – though this figure includes hybrids. Data from the Icelandic Automobile Club (FÍB) – as cited by
Iceland Review
in September 2025 – showed that around one-third of new cars were pure electric vehicles, 21 per cent were plug-in hybrids, and 24 per cent were hybrids at the time of reporting. In the future, end-of-life batteries will be recycled in Norway. “As battery volumes continue to grow, it is important that appropriate recycling solutions are in place,” said Íris Gunnarsdóttir, who is responsible for e-waste and batteries at the IRF. In collaboration with Hydrovolt, the aim is to establish an efficient and responsible system for end-of-life batteries and recover valuable raw materials.
Hydrovolt offers battery importers a complete package: assessing whether a battery can have a second life, collection, transport, and recycling. For Iceland, this means that end-of-life batteries will be transported across the North Atlantic to Fredrikstad, south of Oslo. “Through our logistics network and recycling process, we will ensure the recovery of critical raw materials from the batteries at high recovery rates,” said Hans Bjerkaas, Chief Commercial and Development Officer at Hydrovolt.
The Fredrikstad plant has been operational since May 2022 and, according to the company, is the largest battery recycling facility in the Nordic region. It is designed to process 12,000 tonnes of battery packs per year, equivalent to the batteries from 25,000 to 30,000 cars.
Hydrovolt uses a mechanical and dry process: the packs are discharged, disassembled, and shredded. Aluminium, copper, and plastics can be separated directly. What remains is the so-called black mass, a fine powder containing lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese. These metals are extracted in a second, chemical step. For this, Hydrovolt works with partners. In 2024, for example, the company agreed on a
collaboration with Fortum
, which further processes the black mass at its hydrometallurgical plant in Harjavalta, Finland. Hydrovolt states that the overall recycling rate is nearly 100 per cent.
Beyond Northvolt
Hydrovolt is authorised as a treatment facility in Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, supporting manufacturers and importers in fulfilling their extended producer responsibility obligations. The two neighbouring markets are still new: Hydrovolt entered Sweden in February 2026 and, together with partner KABoB, Denmark in September of the same year. Iceland is the next step. As early as 2024, the company expanded its plans beyond Scandinavia, deciding on an
expansion to Hordain in northern France
, initially as a collection and dismantling site.
Hydrovolt was founded in 2020 as a joint venture between aluminium producer Norsk Hydro and Swedish cell manufacturer Northvolt. Northvolt withdrew from financing in November 2024; since the second half of 2024, Hydro has been the sole owner of the recycling company. In January 2025, both parties agreed that Hydro would acquire the remaining shares for 78 million Norwegian kroner (approx. €6.7 million euros), increasing its stake from 72 to 100 per cent. The completion was planned for the end of the first quarter of 2025 and, among other things, depended on court approval in Northvolt’s US bankruptcy proceedings.
Northvolt
itself filed for bankruptcy in Sweden in March 2025.

title: Google Cloud outage in London knocks multiple UK services offline
content: A major Google Cloud outage disrupted banking apps, websites, and public services across the UK on Tuesday, October 20, after a power-related incident affected one of the company’s London availability zones. The disruption hit systems used for payments, money transfers, deliveries, property searches, and remote court hearings, exposing how a failure in one cloud region can ripple across much of the digital economy.Google said the incident affected multiple services in its europe-west2 region, which serves customers from London. Although engineers began restoring services during the day, the outage lasted nearly eight hours before Google marked the incident as closed.What caused the Google Cloud outage?Google attributed the disruption to a “power event” in its europe-west2-b availability zone, one of three zones in its London cloud region. The incident began at approximately 6:08 a.m. UTC (7:08 a.m. British Summer Time) on October 20.According to Google’s official Cloud Service Health dashboard, the incident affected 38 cloud products, including AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, Apigee, BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine. The company initially reported elevated errors and service disruptions while its engineering teams investigated.The Register reported that Google prioritized restoring existing workloads, warning that customers might not be able to create new ones immediately. The company later reported recovery across affected services and closed the incident after seven hours and 52 minutes. Google has not yet published a full technical explanation of the underlying power event.Revolut, banks, and public services affectedThe outage quickly spread beyond cloud infrastructure. Reuters reported that British digital bank Revolut experienced a related service disruption, affecting functions including card payments and ATM withdrawals. Revolut said customers’ money and data remained safe.Customers also reported difficulties accessing services from Lloyds, HSBC, and Halifax. Meanwhile, the disruption affected the video system used for remote court hearings across England and Wales, potentially delaying proceedings involving defendants appearing remotely.Other services reporting or experiencing disruption included property platform Rightmove, parcel delivery companies DPD and Royal Mail, telecommunications provider BT, and retailer Screwfix. The precise impact varied between organizations, and not every reported service problem was independently confirmed as a direct consequence of the cloud incident.The Guardian reported that the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) was engaging with Google and affected firms to understand the incident’s impact.The outage highlights the risks of cloud dependenceThe incident shows how a regional infrastructure failure can affect organizations that appear unrelated. Banks, retailers, delivery companies, and public services may all depend on the same cloud provider for parts of their digital operations, meaning a disruption can spread across multiple industries.Cloud providers operate multiple availability zones to help customers build resilient systems. However, simply using a major cloud provider does not guarantee uninterrupted service. Organizations must also design applications to tolerate infrastructure failures, distribute critical workloads where appropriate, and test backup and recovery procedures.The outage also comes as UK regulators pay closer attention to the concentration of critical financial services among a small number of technology providers. Reuters reported that UK regulators have brought Google Cloud and other major cloud companies under direct oversight as critical third-party suppliers to the financial sector. Google’s dashboard now lists the incident as closed. The company is expected to provide further technical details through its incident analysis.

title: Seven longest reported sniper shots across the world’s battlefields
content: A sniper’s place in history can come down to a distance. But behind that number is a battlefield engagement, a target barely visible across the landscape, and a shot whose details may remain classified or disputed for years.The longest reported sniper shots stretch beyond two kilometers, with the most recent claims reaching four. They span wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Ukraine, involving both named soldiers and operators whose identities remain undisclosed.However, not all do these achievements carry the same evidence. Some have military confirmation, while others remain wartime claims. Here are seven of the longest reported lethal sniper shots in combat history, ranked by distance.1. Ukrainian Pryvyd sniper (13,123 feet)The longest shot on this list emerged from Ukraine in August 2025. According to an account shared by Ukrainian journalist Yuriy Butusov, a sniper from the Pryvyd, or “Ghost,” unit struck Russian troops from 4,000 meters (13,123 feet) near the Pokrovsk–Myrnohrad front.The account identified the weapon as a 14.5 mm Alligator rifle and claimed that one bullet killed two soldiers on August 14. That would place the engagement above previously reported distances. However, the distance and double-kill account should remain attributed claims, rather than being presented as an independently verified world record.2. Viacheslav Kovalskyi (12,467 feet)In November 2023, Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, announced that one of its snipers had hit a Russian soldier from 3,800 meters (12,467 feet).The shooter was subsequently identified as Viacheslav Kovalskyi, whose reported achievement exceeded the Canadian military’s 2017 mark by 260 meters (853 feet).The rifle was identified in reporting as the Ukrainian-made Horizon’s Lord. Ukraine released footage associated with the engagement, and Kovalskyi later discussed the shot publicly. Nevertheless, the appropriate description is a claim by a Ukrainian security service. Footage and subsequent accounts do not establish independent verification of every detail.3. Canadian JTF2 sniper (11,614 feet)An unidentified member of Canada’s Joint Task Force 2 achieved one of the best-documented entries on this list during a 2017 operation in Iraq. Canadian Special Operations Command confirmed that the sniper had hit a target from 3,540 meters (11,614 feet).The achievement became public in June, with reports identifying the rifle as a McMillan TAC-50. Guinness World Records lists the engagement as its longest confirmed sniper-kill entry.While many operational details remain undisclosed, the military’s confirmation of the hit and distance distinguishes this shot from several longer claims.4. Australian commandos (9,236 feet)Two Australian commandos were involved in a reported 2,815-meter (9,236 feet) engagement in Afghanistan in 2012. Journalist Chris Masters described the pair firing Barrett M82A1 rifles simultaneously at a Taliban commander, with one bullet reportedly killing the target.There is an important complication. The account did not establish which shooter fired the fatal round. Masters also wrote that the Australian Defense Force declined to help confirm the story.The engagement belongs in a list of reported long-distance shots, but attributing an officially verified individual record to either unnamed commando would overstate what is publicly established.5. Ukrainian sniper (8,891 feet)Ukraine’s military released footage in November 2022 that it said showed a special forces sniper killing a Russian soldier from 2,710 meters (8,891 feet). The video circulated widely as another example of an exceptionally long battlefield engagement.Contemporary reporting, however, noted that no one had independently verified the shot. The shooter’s identity was not disclosed, and the available evidence did not firmly establish the rifle model.Those gaps matter. The distance can be reported as Ukraine’s claim without adding equipment details that remain uncertain.6. Craig Harrison (8,120 feet)British Army sniper Craig Harrison killed two Taliban machine gunners at a reported distance of 2,475 meters (8,120 feet) in Afghanistan’s Helmand province in November 2009. He used an Accuracy International L115A3 rifle during the engagement.The two men were struck in separate shots. Accounts also describe ranging shots before the successful hits, making this more involved than the frequently repeated image of two immediate, consecutive kills.7. Rob Furlong (7,972 feet)Canadian sniper Rob Furlong recorded a 2,430-meter (7,972 feet) kill during Operation Anaconda in Afghanistan in March 2002, using a McMillan TAC-50.His achievement surpassed fellow Canadian Arron Perry’s 2,310-meter shot from the same operation. Reporting describes Furlong hitting his target on the third shot, rather than the first.A record measured beyond distanceThese engagements show how far reported battlefield marksmanship has stretched, from Furlong’s 2002 achievement to Ukraine’s four-kilometer claim.Yet distance tells only part of the story. For a historical record to endure, the evidence behind the number matters just as much as the number itself.Until newer claims receive clearer verification, these shots remain a mix of established records and reported achievements.

title: Chinese cancer trial reports 84% disease control with iron-based injection
content: An iron-based injection inspired by wastewater treatment has shown early signs of activity against advanced cancer in a small clinical trial in China. The experimental therapy controlled disease in 16 of 19 patients, including two whose tumors shrank.The Phase I study tested the injection directly inside tumors in patients whose cancers had progressed despite previous treatment. Its 84.2 percent disease control rate includes both stable disease and tumor shrinkage. The objective response rate, which measures shrinkage, was 10.5 percent.Published on October 1 in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, the study was conducted at three hospitals in Sichuan, Hubei and Shandong provinces. A Phase II trial involving 52 patients is now underway across 10 Chinese hospitals to further assess safety and efficacy.The wastewater chemistryThe approach draws on a chemical reaction used to treat industrial wastewater. Iron reacts with hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals, highly reactive molecules that can break down organic pollutants.Researchers adapted that principle to attack malignant cells. They combined a clinically approved nanocrystalline carbon injection with ferrous sulfate to produce a formulation called CNSI-Fe.The treatment is designed to induce ferroptosis, a form of cell death involving iron-dependent damage to cell membranes. Normal cells have antioxidant defenses, including glutathione, that help protect against this damage.Previous animal experiments showed that CNSI-Fe inhibited tumour growth in six tumour models, including colorectal, breast and pancreatic cancer. The clinical trial examined whether that approach could translate into treatment for people with refractory solid tumors.What the trial found in patientsThe 19 participants had several cancer types, including sarcoma, head and neck cancer, pancreatic cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, ovarian cancer, breast cancer and vulval cancer.Sixteen had stage IV metastatic disease. All had received at least two previous lines of systemic therapy.Physicians administered different doses directly into tumor sites and assessed responses in both injected tumors and lesions elsewhere in the body. The injected target lesions responded better than the overall collection of lesions assessed throughout the body.The formulation remained stable for six hours after preparation, while serum iron levels peaked within half an hour of administration.“Overall, CNSI-Fe demonstrated a favorable safety profile and promising antitumor activity,” wrote Professor Wang Yongsheng, the trial’s lead principal investigator at West China Hospital.Side effects and the next testing stageInjection pain was the most common adverse reaction, affecting 89.5 percent of participants, followed by hypertension in 52.6 percent. One patient withdrew because of a hypersensitivity reaction.The researchers reported no severe hematological toxicity or liver and kidney toxicity. However, the small, single-arm study had no comparison group, limiting what its findings can establish about treatment effectiveness.“CNSI-Fe administered by intratumoral injection is effective for treating ferroptosis-sensitive solid tumors, but this single-arm study has limitations and requires further evaluation through randomized Phase II/III trials,” Wang added.The ongoing Phase II study expands testing, but larger, controlled trials remain necessary to determine whether these early findings translate into a reliable benefit for patients.

title: Underwater volcano generates 2 kW of electricity in 8.7 seconds
content: A Seattle-based energy startup, Endurance Energy, announced the world’s first successful attempt to generate electricity from geothermal heat on the ocean floor. They demonstrated the first end-to-end operation of an underwater geothermal power plant, comprising the entire process from drilling to electricity generation.The startup also showed that operators in Seattle could control the system from an offshore location, remotely starting and stopping the equipment, monitoring temperatures and pressures, and collecting data without being underwater.​The company said the newly installed underwater test plant, named Adelie, generated a net power of 2 kilowatts for nearly 9 seconds. The electricity produced exceeded than the system needed to operate, the startup claimed, founded just over a year ago in January 2025.​In the latest trial, completed on September 27, the company moved beyond testing single components to make geothermal energy from the seabed a reality. ​The process included drilling a well, landing and operating a power plant on the seafloor, converting geothermal heat into electricity, and communicating with the system from shore in real time, all in nearly three weeks.​”On Sept. 27, we put a power plant on an active underwater volcano and made power,” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy. “This historic milestone is also our first end-to-end test. We now know, firsthand, what works at depth, what needs to be improved, and how to build the next system for sustained commercial generation.”​From drilling hole to turning turbineEngineers at the company tapped the heat energy of a nearby active volcano to produce the clean electricity from the ocean floor. They began deploying a power plant at Axial Seamount volcano, located 300 miles off the Oregon coast at a depth of nearly a mile in the Pacific Ocean.​Using a robotic drilling machine resting on the seabed, they first began drilling to locate a geothermal well at the bottom of the ocean. Imagine drilling for oil—but instead of looking for oil, you’re drilling into hot rock and hot water.​Inside the crater (caldera) of an underwater volcano, roughly 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) below the ocean’s surface, the team completed drilling of an offshore geothermal well.​The machine bored two closely spaced holes, and both reached hydrothermal fluid, superheated water that occurs naturally underground. The team then inserted a steel pipe inside the hole, a process called casing, while also filling the gap around the pipe with cement.Following this, they installed a valve that allows engineers to control the flow of hot fluid. The finished well extended 52 feet (16 meters) below the seabed and produced water at 500°F (260°C), hot enough to generate electricity.​After the drilling operation, the team accurately placed the 3-ton power plant from a ship to the seabed instead of relying only on the drilled well, connecting the system to an existing hydrothermal vent. The vent naturally discharged water at 281°C, spinning the turbine at 26,000 rpm (over 430 revolutions per second). This turbine movement generated 2kW of net-positive electricity for only 8.7 seconds.​”The main question we had is can the system generate more power than it uses,” said Redd. “Adélie did. Goddard’s first liquid-fueled rocket flew for two and a half seconds. Our first net-positive run lasted about nine. Our approach is to make it exist, then make it good.”Remote operation controls​The startup also showed that operators in Seattle could control the system from an offshore location, remotely starting and stopping the equipment, monitoring temperatures and pressures, and collecting data without being underwater. The commands and data traveled through the Regional Cabled Array, undersea fiber-optic cables owned by the National Science Foundation.Meanwhile, the latest trial looks promising for operating a geothermal system on the deep-ocean floor; however, the company cautioned that the current system is not a commercial-scale power plant. It said the plant faces challenges, including sudden shutdowns due to battery overload, mineral buildup, and heat-transfer issues, that must be addressed before commercial use.​It added that once commercialized, the deep-sea geothermal systems would offer a continuous, weather-independent clean electricity by converting heat beneath the ocean floors. The energy generated could power coastal grids, industrial sites, and data centers around the Pacific and worldwide.

title: US Navy advances nuclear cruise missile system for Virginia-class subs
content: The US Navy is advancing plans to equip its future Virginia-class submarines with a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile. The program involves developing systems to integrate the weapon into the submarines and support its operation. General Dynamics Mission Systems has secured additional funding to continue work on a fire control subsystem for the planned missile. The effort forms part of a broader push to strengthen the Navy’s sea-based strategic deterrence capabilities, with development work scheduled to continue over the next two years as the service moves forward with the SLCM-N program.Submarine fire controlThe US Navy is developing a new fire control subsystem to support the integration of its planned nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile, known as SLCM-N, aboard Virginia-class submarines. The system will support the weapon’s integration with the submarine platform, with engineering work focused on developing and testing the required fire control capabilities. General Dynamics Mission Systems has received a $194 million contract modification to continue this work through September 2028.The contract modification covers engineering and technical services for the subsystem, which is intended to support the Navy’s future sea-based nuclear deterrence capability. Work began in April 2026 under an undefinitized contract action, a contracting arrangement in which work can begin before all contractual terms, including the final price, have been established.The fire control subsystem is a key part of the interface between the submarine and the weapon it carries. In general, submarine fire control systems support weapon employment by processing relevant information, preparing launch-related data, and coordinating the functions required to use a weapon from the platform.For SLCM-N, the subsystem must be developed and integrated to meet the requirements of the Virginia-class submarine. The available contract information does not specify its hardware architecture, software design, or the precise functions it will perform.Nuclear cruise missileThe Virginia-class is the Navy’s nuclear-powered attack submarine platform, designed for missions that include anti-submarine warfare, intelligence gathering, and land-attack operations. Integrating a new weapon onto an existing submarine class requires the relevant systems to work together within the platform’s operational and technical constraints.According to General Dynamics, fire control development and testing are therefore important steps in preparing the submarines to accommodate SLCM-N. However, the contract announcement does not identify a specific submarine variant or provide a schedule for completing weapon integration.The additional funding will also expand the company’s engineering and manufacturing workforce. General Dynamics Mission Systems expects the work to create about 200 positions, primarily in engineering and manufacturing, at its Pittsfield, Massachusetts, and Manassas, Virginia, facilities. Around 75 percent of the contract work will take place in Pittsfield, with the remaining 25 percent assigned to Manassas.The company is also investing $1.3 million to modify the two facilities for the program. The changes are intended to accommodate the SLCM-N effort and expand its fire control engineering and testing capacity. These investments will support the technical work required to develop and evaluate the subsystem as it progresses toward integration with the submarine platform.General Dynamics Mission Systems already serves as the prime integrator for the Trident II Fire Control System, which supports the US Navy’s submarine-launched ballistic missile capability. The company said it would draw on its experience in weapon control, mission planning, platform integration and system testing for the new program. The Trident II system and SLCM-N represent different weapon programs, however, and the contract announcement does not establish that they will share the same fire control architecture.The Navy’s SLCM-N program is intended to add a nuclear-armed cruise missile capability to its sea-based deterrence options. But the announcement does not provide a missile deployment date or confirm when Virginia-class submarines will become operational with the weapon.

title: YouTuber makes refrigerator that uses fire and salt for cooling
content: A fire is usually the last thing you would reach for when trying to keep something cold. But a new DIY refrigeration system built by Greenhill Forge flips that logic on its head, using heat, water, and road salt to cool without a conventional electric compressor.The experimental setup, shown in a YouTube video, cooled the section to around 5°C (41°F) while the surroundings were about 16°C (61°F). That is a substantial temperature drop for a system powered mainly by a fire, although it is still a prototype rather than a proven replacement for a household refrigerator.The project explores an old engineering idea with a potential modern use. Refrigeration that can operate in places where electricity is scarce or unreliable.How fire and salt produce coolingThe system uses a technique called absorption refrigeration, a process that has been around for more than a century. Instead of relying on an electrically driven compressor to circulate refrigerant, it uses heat to drive a chemical process that enables cooling.Greenhill Forge’s design has two main sections: a generator and an absorber. The generator contains a calcium chloride solution and distilled water. When a fire heats the mixture, water vapor separates from the solution and travels through a pipe to a condenser, where it cools and returns to liquid form.The liquid water then passes through a small adjustable valve into an evaporator operating under a strong vacuum. At the system’s very low pressure, about six millibars, water can evaporate at temperatures far below its usual boiling point. That evaporation absorbs heat from the surrounding area, creating the cooling effect.But there is a catch. As water vapor accumulates, the pressure would rise and eventually limit further evaporation. To prevent this, the system sprays concentrated calcium chloride solution into the absorber. The solution absorbs the vapor, helping maintain the low pressure needed for cooling. In effect, the fire supplies the heat that drives the cycle, while the salt solution helps sustain the conditions that allow water to evaporate at low temperatures.An Arduino keeps watch over the systemThe device is also a substantial metalworking project. Greenhill Forge fabricated much of it from stainless-steel sheet metal and tubing, welded the enclosures, and silver-brazed smaller pipe connections. The builder formed the cooling coil by filling a tube with water, freezing it, and bending it around the frozen core to prevent the tube from collapsing.Before filling the system, the builder tested it for leaks and evacuated it with a vacuum pump. Maintaining the vacuum is crucial because even small leaks can interfere with the low-pressure evaporation process.An Arduino-based controller monitors temperatures and pressures, adjusts pump speeds, and triggers safety alarms. The setup still needs electricity for its circulation pumps and cooling fans. The pumps alone consume about 30–50 watts.That means the refrigerator is not entirely electricity-free. However, a small solar panel or battery could potentially supply its modest electrical needs while a fire provides most of the thermal energy.Could fire-powered refrigeration work off-grid?The first test results are promising, but the temperature figures need context. The system reached about 5°C (41°F) with an ambient temperature near 16°C (61°F), according to Hackaday’s report. That demonstrates a cooling effect, but it doesn’t show how well the prototype would perform in hotter conditions, how much food it could keep cold, or how consistently it could maintain safe storage temperatures.The technology itself is not new. People have long used absorption refrigerators in settings where conventional electrical compressors are impractical. Greenhill Forge’s project instead explores a DIY implementation using accessible materials and a heat source such as firewood.With further development, similar systems could be useful in remote workshops, cabins, or other locations where fuel is easier to obtain than reliable grid power.

title: From THAAD to SeaRAM: US defense systems that protect against missile attacks
content: Stopping a missile starts long before an interceptor leaves its launcher. Radars and other sensors must detect the threat, track its flight, and provide the information needed to engage it.The challenge changes depending on whether that missile approaches through space or flies low through the atmosphere.The United States uses several air and missile defense systems to address these different threats. Some protect the homeland against long-range ballistic missiles. Others defend troops, infrastructure, or warships against closer-range attacks.From THAAD’s high-altitude interceptions to SeaRAM’s shipboard defenses, these six systems show how different weapons contribute to US missile protection.1. THAADTerminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, targets ballistic missiles during their terminal phase, when they descend toward their targets. It can intercept them inside or outside Earth’s atmosphere, giving it a distinctive role in regional missile defense.The truck-mounted system combines launchers, interceptor missiles, an AN/TPY-2 radar, and fire-control equipment. Its interceptor uses hit-to-kill technology, destroying the target through direct impact. THAAD addresses ballistic missile threats; its mission should not be confused with defending against low-flying cruise missiles. Its ability to engage at high altitudes complements lower-tier defenses such as Patriot. 2. Aegis Ballistic Missile DefenseAegis Ballistic Missile Defense gives equipped US Navy warships a role in intercepting ballistic missiles. It combines the Aegis weapon system with specialized interceptors, including the Standard Missile-3, or SM-3, and Standard Missile-6, or SM-6.These interceptors perform different missions. SM-3 engages ballistic missile threats ranging from short to intermediate range. SM-6 provides terminal defense against short-range ballistic missiles. Land-based Aegis Ashore installations also contribute to ballistic missile defense. Identifying the interceptor matters: Aegis is a weapon system with multiple capabilities, rather than a single missile with one engagement profile. 3. Patriot PAC-3Patriot’s PAC-3 interceptor family is designed to counter tactical ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft. PAC-3 stands for Patriot Advanced Capability-3, while the newer MSE designation means Missile Segment Enhancement.These are interceptor missiles used within the wider Patriot air defense system, which includes radar, launchers, and engagement-control equipment. PAC-3 uses direct impact to destroy incoming threats. Its terminal ballistic missile defense role overlaps with THAAD’s, allowing the systems to provide complementary protection. That distinction explains why both appear in US defenses. They contribute different engagement capabilities rather than simply duplicating each other. 4. Ground-Based Midcourse DefenseGround-Based Midcourse Defense, or GMD, addresses a different mission: defending the US homeland against limited long-range ballistic missile attacks. Its ground-based interceptors are deployed in Alaska and California.An interceptor carries an Exoatmospheric Kill Vehicle, which separates from its booster and engages the incoming warhead in space during midcourse. Destruction relies on collision rather than an explosive warhead. GMD’s mission distinguishes it from regional systems protecting individual bases or deployed forces. Its stated purpose also requires careful wording: protection against a limited ballistic missile attack does not mean guaranteed protection against every possible missile strike. 5. NASAMSThe National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, or NASAMS, brings cruise missile defense into the list. Developed by Norway’s Kongsberg and US company Raytheon, it is a short- to medium-range ground-based system that also counters aircraft, helicopters, and drones.NASAMS connects radars, a Fire Distribution Center, and dispersed launchers. Its baseline interceptor is the AMRAAM, a missile also carried by fighter aircraft. According to Kongsberg, NASAMS has protected Washington, DC, since 2005. Its role here concerns cruise missiles and other air-breathing threats, rather than the interception of intercontinental ballistic missile warheads in space. 6. SeaRAMSeaRAM provides warships with close-range defense against anti-ship cruise missiles. It combines the search-and-track radar and electro-optical sensor of the Phalanx Block 1B close-in weapon system with an 11-round Rolling Airframe Missile launcher.The distinction between RAM and SeaRAM is straightforward; RAM is the missile, while SeaRAM combines those missiles with sensors and engagement equipment on a single mount. The Navy describes SeaRAM as a self-contained detect-to-engage capability. Its task is ship self-defense, adding point protection alongside other naval defenses rather than performing the wide-area ballistic missile mission associated with Aegis BMD. ConclusionThese systems tackle different parts of the missile threat. Their roles span homeland defense, regional protection, and shipboard self-defense. Understanding those differences reveals what a simple ranking misses: missile protection depends on matching the defense to the threat.
