title: US Air Force seeks engine using continuous blasts to power missiles
content: The U.S. Air Force is seeking proposals to develop and flight-test a combined-cycle rotating detonation rocket engine designed for future high-speed weapons. The program aims to advance the technology from an early proof-of-concept stage to a prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment over 36 to 48 months.The engine uses rotating detonations, in which combustion occurs through a continuous series of shockwave-driven explosions, as part of its propulsion process. The effort supports the development of High-Speed Affordable Mass Munitions (HAMM), with initial proposals due November 16, 2026.Air Force explores detonationThe U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) is seeking industry proposals to develop and flight-test a combined-cycle rotating detonation rocket engine designed for future high-speed weapons.The technology uses continuously propagating detonation waves to burn fuel and could offer an alternative to conventional rocket propulsion. The program aims to advance the engine from laboratory proof of concept to a prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment over 36 to 48 months.The effort is being managed by AFRL’s Rocket Propulsion Division at Edwards Air Force Base in California under the HERMES Broad Agency Announcement. Initial white papers are due November 16, 2026, and the program targets a flight demonstration the support HAMM development.Conventional rocket engines typically burn fuel continuously inside a combustion chamber to generate hot gases that produce thrust. Rotating detonation engines (RDEs) use a different combustion process, generating a detonation wave that travels around a ring-shaped chamber at supersonic speed.As the wave moves through the chamber, it ignites the incoming fuel and oxidizer mixture, sustaining a repeating series of detonations. This process uses the pressure generated by detonation rather than relying solely on conventional deflagration-based combustion.Researchers are investigating the technology because it could improve propulsion efficiency while reducing engine size and complexity. The rotating detonation process may also reduce the need for some conventional engine components, potentially allowing more compact propulsion systems. However, the practical benefits depend on the engine design and its operating conditions.Rotating rocket enginesThe AFRL program focuses on a combined-cycle configuration, designated the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine-Combined Cycle (RDRE-CC). The design combines rocket propulsion with air-breathing operation, allowing the engine to use atmospheric oxygen during part of its flight rather than carrying all the required oxidizer onboard.This approach could help address the demands of high-speed flight, where propulsion systems must operate across different conditions. A combined-cycle engine must integrate the two operating modes while maintaining stable combustion and delivering the required performance throughout the flight profile.The planned development effort covers engine design, testing, and integration with a flight vehicle. Ground evaluations will include direct-connect tests, which examine engine operation using a connected test setup, and freejet tests that expose the propulsion system to simulated high-speed airflow.These tests are intended to assess the engine under conditions relevant to its intended flight environment before a demonstration vehicle is launched. The program is expected to conclude with a flight test in which a ground-launched sounding rocket boosts the engine-powered vehicle to the conditions needed to demonstrate its operation.AFRL intends to advance the technology from Technology Readiness Level 3, representing an early proof of concept, to Level 6, where a prototype has been demonstrated in a relevant environment.The solicitation requires participating companies to submit a proposed design, testing approach, schedule, and preliminary cost estimate. Selected applicants may then be invited to provide full technical and cost proposals, subject to funding availability.The program builds on ongoing U.S. military research into detonation-based propulsion. RTX’s Pratt & Whitney conducted rotating detonation engine tests in 2025 under DARPA’s Gambit program, which is pursuing air-breathing propulsion for future long-range weapons. AFRL researchers at Edwards have also tested rotating detonation rocket engines on ground-based test stands.

title: US Army plans to adopt Shahed-derived drones to breach enemy defenses
content: A warship does not have to sink to lose its ability to fight. Damage to its radar, communications equipment, or other critical systems can reduce its effectiveness and create an opening for an opposing force.That possibility is part of the U.S. Army’s emerging vision for long-range attack drones such as the Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System, or LUCAS.Army commanders outlined how these weapons could support operations against maritime and land threats during the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual symposium in October.The concept extends from the Pacific to Europe: use relatively inexpensive weapons in large numbers to disrupt enemy defenses, while preserving more sophisticated munitions for targets that require them.What is the LUCAS attack drone?LUCAS is a long-range, one-way attack drone reverse-engineered from Iran’s Shahed-136. The US military announced its initial fielding in December 2025, and the weapon made its combat debut during operations against Iran earlier in 2026.It uses a combustion engine and a rear-mounted propeller. A small rocket booster helps launch it from a static launcher, which can be positioned on land or installed aboard a ship.Its appeal centers on combining range with relatively low cost. Weapons in this category can provide commanders with more opportunities to strike distant targets without relying entirely on expensive cruise missiles.The Army has also begun incorporating long-range, one-way attack operations into training at its Bayonet Academy at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington. This includes maintaining the weapons, employing them, and coordinating their use to achieve a specific effect.How could drones disable enemy warships?In the Pacific, Army planning includes examining how these drones could help penetrate parts of an adversary’s anti-access and area-denial network. Such networks combine capabilities intended to prevent opposing forces from entering or operating within an area.One approach involves damaging selected systems aboard a warship rather than attempting to sink the vessel.Known as a mission kill, this could involve disabling radar or communications equipment. The ship might remain afloat, but its reduced combat effectiveness could leave it more vulnerable to subsequent attacks.That disruption could create a temporary opportunity for a carrier strike group or bomber force to operate.Army modeling has examined combining long-range attack drones with unmanned surface vessels and other launched systems. Coordinating these capabilities could help concentrate enough force to produce the required effect.Where do land targets and swarming fit?In Europe, commanders see long-range attack systems as a way to disrupt enemy defenses and counter missile forces. Potential targets include road-mobile launchers associated with Russia’s Iskander-M and the older Tochka ballistic missile systems.Large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones can also force defenders to expend valuable interceptors, pressuring their air-defense inventories.LUCAS is slated to gain swarming capabilities through Shield AI’s Hivemind autonomy software. The planned upgrade is intended to let multiple drones coordinate tasks and maneuver cooperatively.However, the Army’s approach remains under development. Decisions about wider fielding, personnel training, and the formations needed to operate these weapons are still taking shape.

title: China launches 200kV electron microscope to challenge US and Japan
content: American and Japanese companies controlled the market for advanced microscopes. Now, China is offering an alternative. China has officially launched the mass-market production of its own high-performance 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope.Reports suggest that Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK unveiled the microscope at the 2026 National Conference on Electron Microscopy in Nanjing. The TEM-F200 delivers advanced imaging capabilities with a point resolution of 0.25 nanometers. It also has a 0.1-nanometer resolution limit, allowing researchers to capture structural details at the atomic level.Scientists and engineers use electron microscopes to analyze molecular structures, study biological viruses, and inspect microscopic defects in semiconductor microchips.Atomic-scale precisionIt is a microscopic leap with massive geopolitical consequences.For a long time, global research labs and semiconductor foundries depended almost entirely on a tiny cartel of American and Japanese instrument giants. China bought them by the thousands. Without them, domestic chipmakers couldn’t inspect microscopic circuit defects, and biopharma firms couldn’t map molecular structures.The TEM-F200 could eventually help China take charge. An electron microscope is an advanced imaging tool that uses a focused beam of electrons, rather than light, to illuminate and magnify extremely small specimens.At an accelerating voltage of 200kV, the microscope delivers optimal performance, capturing ultra-fine atomic detail while preserving sensitive specimens.According to the South China Morning Post, CIQTEK Chairman He Yu confirmed that the microscope has moved beyond R&D into full factory “mass production and delivery”. The new device is already capable of supporting defect analysis for next-generation semiconductors and advanced materials.The timing is important. Beijing has deliberately accelerated efforts to address supply-chain issues in advanced scientific tools and semiconductor manufacturing. Advanced electron microscopes depend on volatile raw materials, including rare earth elements, tungsten, platinum, and specialized semiconductor components. Plus, these atomic-resolution devices are also classified as dual-use technologies with major military and industrial applications, making them frequent targets of international trade sanctions and export restrictions. With a small group of nations, including the U.S., Japan, Germany, and the Netherlands, dominating these supply chains, domestic production has become important for national security and technical independence.China’s rapid progressChina achieved self-reliance in microscopy in a remarkably short timeframe. The nation debuted its first commercial 120kV field-emission TEM in 2024, and Bozhon Instrument Technology unveiled the first 200kV prototype in 2025. Technical progress expanded in May 2026 when the Chinese Academy of Sciences introduced the AI-driven Aeye-1 system. Domestic capabilities reached full commercial scale in October 2026 with the mass production of both the TEM-F200 and the TEM-F120 models.Overall, the field has a long and interesting history worth mentioning. The development of light microscopes in the 17th century first expanded human vision beyond its natural limits. Of course, the technology was limited then, with a resolution of about 200 to 250 nanometers. This barrier prevented from viewing viruses and genetic structures until German researchers built the first working electron microscopes in the early 1930s. Rather than using light, electron microscopes direct focused beams of electrons at or through samples to capture atomic-level images on digital displays.Wu Aihua, secretary-general of the analytical instruments branch at the China Instrument and Control Society, said this development could boost national self-sufficiency in analytical testing.

title: Siemens uses digital twin technology to modernize traditional oil extraction in the Amazon
content: A traditional oil extraction process in Brazil’s Amazon is getting a digital upgrade as Siemens engineers work with Natura and local communities to bring simulation and automation into a rural agroindustry. The Moiru project in Santo Antônio do Tauá, Pará, is using digital twin technology to study how steam moves through plant material during essential oil extraction.The Campo Limpo Cooperative has grown aromatic plants for Natura since 2003 and began distilling them in 2024. The project brings this established process together with Siemens digital technologies, creating a digital twin of the extraction vat and adding automation to monitor and control key operating conditions.The work shows how digital twin and automation technologies can extend beyond conventional factories by combining the real and digital worlds. In this case, the technology is being shaped around local conditions, community knowledge, and the practical requirements of an Amazonian production site.Turning a physical vat into a digital modelSteam distillation has been used for generations. Plant material is placed in a vat, where steam passes through the biomass and vaporizes essential oil. The vapor then condenses and separates from water.The quality of the extraction depends heavily on how steam moves through the biomass, along with stable pressure and temperature during the process. Traditionally, many of these variables have depended on operator experience.For the Moiru project, Siemens engineers worked directly with Natura and community members to understand how the process operates in its local environment. The project sits within Siemens’ Tech4Amazonia initiative and emphasizes active listening and collaboration with people who already have extensive knowledge of the process.That work led to a digital twin of the extraction vat using computational fluid dynamics in Simcenter STAR-CCM+. The physical vessel could then be represented as a digital model, allowing the team to study what was happening inside it.Simulation reveals what happens insideThe digital model opened a view into parts of the process that are difficult to observe directly. Engineers and researchers could examine steam channels, pressure drops, and heat distribution through the plant material.The simulation also produced an important finding. It suggested that the extraction process could operate at pressures up to 50 percent lower than those previously being used. This provided a potential path toward improving the process while reducing the resources required to run it.Siemens then added an automation layer around the physical equipment. A pressure sensor was installed upstream of the extractor, while a proportional valve was added to the steam line. Mass-flow and temperature sensors were also introduced to capture important process data from each batch.The system is controlled and monitored through one PLC and one HMI and supervisory controls. An operator can set a target steam flow, while the automated system works to maintain that target during operation and assuring replicability of the receipt for each different plant.Digital tools built for remote conditionsConnectivity cannot always be assumed at a rural Amazonian site. The project therefore uses Industrial Edge to record each batch locally. This keeps production data available on site even when network connectivity is limited.The automation and simulation work is expected to bring practical operational benefits. More efficient boiler operation can reduce energy use, while improved control can lower biomass and water consumption. The project also points toward reduced operating costs and a smaller carbon footprint.More consistent temperature distribution can help produce more consistent volatilization during extraction. That can support greater consistency in the resulting essential oil across different batches and plant species.Building local expertise for what comes nextTechnology is only one part of the Moiru project. Training cooperative members in basic automation, instrumentation, and process monitoring is intended to give the local workforce greater autonomy over the system.That can also create opportunities for skilled technical work within the community, reducing the need for people to leave the area to find similar roles elsewhere.The proof of concept has now been completed, demonstrating how traditional knowledge, research, and digital engineering can work together around a real production process. The project also provides a foundation for future AI-driven optimization and potential scaling across Amazonian agroindustries.For Siemens, the Moiru project demonstrates a broader role for digital twins and industrial technologies. Their value can extend far beyond conventional manufacturing, provided the technology is developed around the people, processes, and conditions it is meant to serve.

title: Scientists find quantum link in how fast systems reach thermal balance
content: Physicists at the Austrian Academy of Sciences, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, and the University of Geneva have proven at a quantum level what others had long suspected – that quantum mechanics imposes a speed limit on how fast a system with a temperature difference among its components reaches thermal equilibrium. This speed limit is universal, and nothing one does to the system can actually change it. Thermal equilibrium might sound like a tough concept, but hundreds of systems reach them around us on a daily basis. A hot cup of coffee will eventually cool down to room temperature, or a glass of cola will also become warm to reach about the same temperature, even if they are not kept in close proximity to each other. How quickly this occurs can depend on external factors like the temperature of the room or how big a glass of drink you have poured, etc. But physicists have long suspected that at a subatomic level, there is a something that inherently controls how fast these changes can occur.A team of researchers from some of the top institutes in Spain, Austria and Switzerland have now arrived at mathematical proof that shows that there is indeed a quantum-level speed limit that determines how quickly systems reach their thermal equilibrium. Arriving at the proofEven though we may not have noticed this in our cooling cup of coffee, physicists have long noticed the likelihood of a speed limit when working with superconductors and other quantum systems. To demonstrate that it really exists, scientists need a mathematical proof, which is exactly what the European researchers set out to do. Using a universal mathematical framework, the researchers treated thermalization as a process that can bring different quantum systems into their corresponding thermal states. Using quantum information theory, they also determined how quickly this could be achieved based on quantum-mechanical principles. They then applied their equations to a theoretical model of quantum particles and attempted to analyze their behavior mathematically. The analysis showed that quantum mechanics does indeed put a speed limit on how quickly different quantum systems can reach a thermal equilibrium. A universal limitThe researchers found that the limit is not only determined by the temperature of the system but also by two constants – the reduced Planck’s constant and the Boltzmann constant, which relates the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas to the thermodynamic temperature of the system. This means that even when system components may be at higher temperatures and seem to reach equilibrium quickly, they still cannot go faster than the speed limit imposed by quantum mechanics. This confirms that the speed limit depends on the temperature and quantum mechanics and not the complexity of the environment it is operating in. Interestingly, though, when system components have very little temperature difference, the rate of thermal equilibrium is not the same as when the temperature differences are on the higher side. Instead, this is determined by the two lowest-energy states in the system. The findings open up new research avenues in quantum technologies such as computing and sensing. The research findings were published in the journal Nature Physics.

title: Humanoid robot shoves 77-pound load, lifts 44 pounds in new demo
content: Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology (KAIST) have demonstrated an updated version of their humanoid robot, showing its ability to handle heavy objects using visual feedback.The Humanoid v0.9 robot can push objects weighing up to 77.2 pounds (35 kg) and lift loads of up to 44.1 pounds (20 kg), according to a demonstration released on October 19. The demonstration highlights the team’s efforts to improve humanoid manipulation through learning-based control methods and visual feedback during physical interactions with objects.Recently, KAIST researchers showcased a humanoid robot capable of advanced lower-body movements, including high-speed running and Michael Jackson’s iconic Moonwalk.Humanoid masters manipulationKAIST’s Humanoid v0.9 combines whole-body movement with object manipulation, demonstrating the ability to push objects weighing up to 77.2 pounds (35 kg) and lift loads of up to 44.1 pounds (20 kg). The demonstration shows the robot using onboard visual feedback to arrange objects into the letters “KAIST.”Developed by KAIST’s Dynamic Robot Control & Design Laboratory (DRCD Lab) in collaboration with RAILAB, which developed its arms, the platform integrates locomotion, manipulation, and learning-based control.The new video, titled Whole-Body Locomanipulation with KAIST Humanoid v0.9, focuses on how the robot coordinates its body and arms while interacting with objects. Rather than treating walking and manipulation as separate tasks, the approach brings them together so the robot can move its body while applying force through its arms.According to the team, the coordination is important because pushing or lifting an object changes the forces acting on a humanoid’s body. Pushing a heavy load requires the robot to maintain balance while applying force, whereas lifting requires it to support the object’s weight and control its posture throughout the movement.The robot’s onboard visual feedback provides information about the objects and their positions during these interactions. In the demonstration, it uses this feedback while arranging objects to spell “KAIST.” The task combines visual perception with physical interaction, requiring the robot to adjust its movements as it handles the objects.The pushing and lifting capabilities represent two distinct aspects of its manipulation performance. During pushing, the force required to move an object depends on factors such as friction and the surface on which it rests. Lifting, by contrast, requires the robot to support the object’s weight directly.These figures therefore should not be treated as interchangeable measures of payload capacity. The demonstration establishes the loads handled in the showcased tasks, but does not provide enough information to determine the robot’s maximum sustained lifting capacity or performance under different operating conditions.Learning-based controlKAIST says the robot’s interaction skills were developed using deep reinforcement learning and learning from human demonstrations. These methods provide different approaches to developing robot behavior, allowing researchers to train control policies through experience and use demonstrations to guide how tasks are performed.Deep reinforcement learning trains a control policy through repeated interactions with an environment and performance feedback. In humanoid robotics, this approach can help develop coordinated movements that account for the robot’s body dynamics and interactions with external objects.Learning from human demonstrations offers another way to develop skills by using examples of how a task should be performed. The KAIST update combines these learning approaches with onboard visual feedback to support object manipulation.However, the available demonstration does not specify the training setup, how responsibilities the divided between the learning methods, or the precise control architecture used during execution. It also does not show whether the robot can reliably perform the same tasks across different objects, surfaces, and environmental conditions.The latest update builds on KAIST’s earlier Humanoid v0.7 platform, which highlighted high-speed locomotion and movements such as Michael Jackson’s Moonwalk. The v0.9 demonstration shifts the focus toward physical interaction, showing how the platform can combine movement with the application of force to external objects.

title: US Navy controls MQ-25A refueling drone from over 2,100 miles away
content: The US Navy has remotely connected to and controlled an MQ-25A Stingray unmanned refueling aircraft from an aircraft carrier more than 2,100 miles away, marking a new milestone in its effort to integrate drones into carrier operations.The test took place aboard the USS Ronald Reagan, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier operating in the Pacific Ocean. The MQ-25A test aircraft was at Boeing’s facility in Mascoutah, Illinois.During preliminary sea trials, operators aboard the carrier used the ship’s Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC) to establish a beyond-line-of-sight connection with the aircraft through a satellite network.The Navy described the event as its first successful connection between an underway aircraft carrier’s control station and an MQ-25A aircraft. The demonstration tested the communications and command systems needed for future carrier-based drone operations.Satellites bridge operational distanceThe connection used a proliferated low Earth orbit (pLEO) satellite network, which relies on satellites operating relatively close to Earth to support communications over long distances.The carrier’s UAWC used an MD-5C Ground Control Station to establish the link. The system combines the Navy’s command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence network with hardware and software developed by Lockheed Martin and other government-produced equipment.The MD-5C is designed to provide command and control for the MQ-25A and potentially other unmanned aircraft that could operate from US Navy carriers.The demonstration was part of a series of tests intended to validate the procedures, networks, and interfaces required to operate the Stingray from a carrier.Earlier testing included evaluations while ships were docked and at sea. The work involved the Navy’s Unmanned Carrier Aviation Program Office and an integrated test team comprising personnel from the Navy, Boeing and Lockheed Martin.“This first-ever underway connection between a carrier-based UAWC and an MQ-25A aircraft proves that the Carrier Air Wing of tomorrow is a reality today,” said Capt. Daniel Fucito, program manager for the Navy’s Unmanned Carrier Aviation Program Office.Although the test demonstrated remote connectivity and control over a considerable distance, the Navy did not report an autonomous flight, aerial refueling operation, or carrier landing as part of this event.Extending carrier aircraft reachBoeing’s MQ-25A Stingray is being developed to refuel US Navy aircraft in flight, reducing the need to assign crewed combat aircraft to tanker duties.The Navy expects the drone to support F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, allowing them to remain airborne longer and operate farther from their carrier.Using dedicated unmanned refueling aircraft could also free more Super Hornets for combat missions instead of requiring them to carry additional fuel for other aircraft.The MQ-25A is intended to become the Navy’s first operational carrier-based unmanned aerial refueling aircraft and establish a foundation for integrating additional unmanned aircraft into future carrier air wings.The latest demonstration validates an important part of that plan: the ability to maintain a command connection between a moving aircraft carrier and a remotely located aircraft.Further testing will be needed to establish how the system performs during routine flight operations and carrier-based missions.

title: 368-ton ex-US Navy vessel showcases autonomous mission control
content: HD Hyundai and Anduril have demonstrated an unmanned surface vessel operating autonomously off California, showcasing technology that could support future US Navy missions. The October 19 exercise tested how the vessel handled changing mission requirements and simulated machinery failures without onboard crew intervention.The demonstration took place off the Port of Long Beach. It brought together roughly 40 representatives from the United States and South Korea, including officials from the US Navy and Coast Guard. Representatives from the Republic of Korea Navy and South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration also attended.Testing autonomy at seaThe three-and-a-half-hour exercise used a modified 368-ton unmanned surface vessel previously operated by the US Navy. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering (HD KSOE) equipped the vessel with its VAone autonomy suite. Anduril supplied its Lattice mission autonomy platform.Together, the systems demonstrated how an unmanned vessel could navigate maritime environments and adjust its behavior as mission conditions changed. The trials included formation sailing and emergency responses to simulated machinery failures.Operators and observers followed the exercise remotely through a shore-based control station. A live feed allowed attendees to monitor the vessel’s actions and assess its ability to execute assigned missions without continuous onboard intervention.The scenarios tested more than autonomous navigation. They also examined how the vessel could respond to mechanical problems and potential damage while maintaining operational control.Two systems, one vesselHD KSOE developed VAone as an integrated autonomy solution for unmanned vessels. Its foundation is HiNAS Prime, an autonomous navigation system developed by Avikus, HD Hyundai’s autonomous navigation subsidiary.VAone also incorporates autonomous machinery management. The system monitors equipment conditions, identifies abnormalities, and can initiate automated responses. Its damage-control component detects vessel damage and takes corrective action.Anduril’s Lattice platform adds mission-level autonomy. HD Hyundai said the integration demonstrated unmanned operations spanning navigation, machinery management, damage control, and weapons autonomy.The distinction matters because operating an unmanned vessel requires more than plotting a route. The onboard systems must interpret changing conditions and coordinate responses when equipment malfunctions or mission requirements shift.During the exercise, the vessel made successive autonomous decisions as it encountered different scenarios. HD Hyundai said the results demonstrated its ability to handle situations representative of real-world maritime operations.Pursuing US defense programsThe demonstration could help both Anduril and HD Hyundai pursue American unmanned surface vessel programs. They also plan to target the wider international market as demand for uncrewed maritime platforms grows.For US defense planners, autonomous surface vessels offer a potential way to conduct selected maritime missions without placing sailors aboard every platform. Their usefulness will depend on reliable navigation, robust fault responses and effective coordination between onboard systems.The exercise provided a practical demonstration of how shipbuilding expertise and mission autonomy software can work together. However, the companies have not announced a specific US Navy procurement award arising from the trial.Jang Kwang-pil, executive vice president and head of the Future Technology Research Institute at HD KSOE, said the exercise confirmed the vessel’s ability to handle complex missions after leaving port. HD Hyundai plans to refine its autonomy technologies as it seeks a stronger position in the emerging unmanned surface vessel market.

title: New 30-lb truck trailer device slashes diesel waste on US highways
content: A US company has just presented a redesigned aerodynamic system that has the potential to reduce fuel consumption by up to three gallons for every 1,000 miles on the road.Dubbed the Trailer AeroSlider, the system was made by Texas-based engineering and manufacturing company FlowBelow Aero. The firm develops aerodynamic solutions for Class 8 semi-trucks and trailers.The new device was revealed at the American Trucking Associations’ Management Conference & Exhibition. Running from October 17 to 20 in the city of Charlotte, North Carolina, the event focuses on commercial vehicles and trucking tech. According to company representatives, the system can slash air resistance around the trailer wheels and suspension components. Additionally, it weighs less than 30 lbs, can be installed in under an hour (roughly 45 minutes), and requires no driver involvement once fitted. The system could cover its initial cost within a year.Reducing fuel consumptionAt highway speeds, trucks experience significant air resistance, also referred to as aerodynamic drag, due to their large, boxy shapes. This resistance increases fuel consumption, particularly at speeds above 31 miles per hour (50 kilometers per hour). Aerodynamic improvements mostly focus on trailer fronts and sides. Wheels and suspension parts, however, also generate turbulence. The AeroSlider was hence developed to address this issue, improve airflow around the trailer’s tandem axle assembly.Instead of blocking the airflow, the fairings redirect it outward and backward as it passes the wheels. This reduces the turbulence around the suspension and in the trailer’s wake, and lowers the aerodynamic drag.The AeroSlider targets the wheels, suspension, and underbody surrounding the trailer tandem.Credit: FlowBelow AeroThe system can also move with the trailer’s sliding suspension. In general, truck operators regularly adjust the position of trailer axles to distribute cargo weight and comply with road weight limits. Since the AeroSlider moves alongside the axles, its aerodynamic parts remain properly positioned without the need for additional adjustments.FlowBelow first unveiled the AeroSlider in 2017. The new version features a single, improved fairing, rather than a separate center and rear fairings. The redesigned system saves more fuel, weighs less, and costs less, and takes less time to install. It is also designed to fit almost any dry van or refrigerated trailer.Fuel savings confirmed in testsThe redesign involved computational fluid dynamics simulations, wind-tunnel experiments, and track testing. In June 2026, independent testing company MVT Solutions evaluated its performance using 2019 International LT tractors pulling loaded 53-foot dry van trailers.The initial configuration already included the trailer side skirts and wheel covers. Adding the redesigned rear fairings and flow-through mud flaps slashed fuel use by 1.77 gallons per 1,000 miles. At the same time, separate testing confirmed that the trailer wheel covers could save another 1.23 gallons over the same distance.The device comes amid high US diesel prices. Figures cited by the company show that the national average hit USD 6.179 per gallon on October 12. This translates to potential savings of USD 18.54 every 1,000 miles. For a trailer covering 100,000 miles annually, that could mean approximately USD 1,854 in yearly fuel savings.‘Our goal with the AeroSlider was to develop an aerodynamic system that could pay for itself in less than 18 months for a typical regional or long-haul fleet at USD 3.00 per gallon diesel,” Josh Butler, FlowBelow president and CTO, stressed in a press release. “At today’s fuel prices, payback can be less than 12 months, even for fleets whose trailers travel as little as 30,000 miles per year.”

title: Amazon backs plan for 12 nuclear reactors at former US coal site
content: Amazon is backing plans for a 960-megawatt nuclear power facility in Indiana that could house 12 small modular reactors (SMRs) at the site of a former coal-fired power plant.The company has signed an agreement with American Electric Power (AEP) and nuclear technology developer X-energy to assess the feasibility of the project. If built, the facility would supply electricity to the regional grid and Amazon’s data centers.The proposed plant would use 12 of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors, each designed to generate 80 MW of electricity. Amazon will help fund project development and plans to become the facility’s first electricity customer once it begins operating.The agreement comes as electricity demand rises across the United States, driven partly by expanding data centers, manufacturing and electrification. However, the project remains in the evaluation stage, with no confirmed construction schedule or operational date.Replacing coal with nuclearThe companies are considering the former Breed Generating Station site in Sullivan County, Indiana. The coal-fired facility’s location could allow the developers to reuse an existing power generation site rather than establish an entirely new one.The proposed nuclear plant would add up to 960 MW of electricity generation capacity in AEP’s Indiana service territory. According to Amazon, construction could create more than 1,000 jobs, while the completed facility could support over 100 permanent positions.X-energy’s Xe-100 is a high-temperature, gas-cooled reactor that uses helium instead of water to remove heat from its core. Each reactor is designed to generate 80 MW of electricity, allowing multiple units to be combined to meet larger power requirements.The design uses TRISO fuel, which contains uranium particles surrounded by several protective layers, including high-temperature ceramic materials. These layers are designed to retain radioactive materials even under extreme operating conditions.According to X-energy, the combination of helium cooling and TRISO fuel provides inherent safety characteristics intended to prevent core melting without relying on active cooling equipment or operator intervention.The reactor design also supports different cooling arrangements, including air-cooled, water-cooled, and hybrid systems. This could give operators more flexibility when selecting sites where water availability is limited.Amazon expands nuclear ambitionsThe Indiana proposal is the second project announced under Amazon and X-energy’s broader collaboration, which targets more than 5 gigawatts of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.Their first project, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington state, also aims to deploy X-energy’s reactor technology.Amazon’s involvement with X-energy dates to 2024, when it led a financing round that ultimately raised $700 million. The investment was intended to support reactor design, licensing, and development of a nuclear fuel manufacturing facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.Under the Indiana agreement, AEP would bring its electricity generation and utility experience, while Amazon would provide development funding and future electricity demand.The companies have not announced a final investment decision. Construction would depend on the outcome of feasibility assessments and subsequent project approvals.

title: OpenAI models hit 97.9% accuracy in tests to modernize old software
content: OpenAI has significantly improved its models’ ability to write software in older programming languages and migrate existing code. Its latest results include 97.9 percent accuracy on a test designed to measure the migration of legacy programs.The improvements could help businesses modernize software that remains essential to daily operations. Banks and financial institutions still rely on decades-old code, making replacement risky when developers must preserve established calculations and business rules.Tackling legacy codeCOBOL remains deeply embedded in financial infrastructure. IBM estimates that it supports more than 40 percent of online banking systems, 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions, and 95 percent of ATM transactions.Fortran also remains important in scientific computing, including weather forecasting and nuclear reactor safety analysis. Both languages have less training material available than popular alternatives such as Python and JavaScript.OpenAI said developers and enterprise customers had reported difficulties getting coding models to work reliably with these older languages. Documentation can be incomplete, and essential business rules may exist only in the original code.That creates problems during migration. A rewritten program might run without errors yet produce different results. COBOL, for example, can discard excess decimal digits unless a program explicitly requests rounding. Changing that behavior could affect financial calculations.Rewriting code accuratelyOpenAI’s COBOL migration evaluation tests whether models can translate existing programs into C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust without changing their behavior.GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 86.6 percent accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with 5.4 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI also reported a 39 percent reduction in API costs at that setting.Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic.These languages power software that banks, governments, and businesses depend on. Progress here means… pic.twitter.com/Mulo5P3iCO— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 19, 2026At higher reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Sol reached 97.9 percent accuracy. The evaluation requires translated programs to pass every hidden test, including checks that compare their observable outputs with the original programs.That figure reflects performance on OpenAI’s test suite, not a guarantee of error-free migrations. Developers must still verify rewritten applications against real workloads and undocumented dependencies.Building across languagesOpenAI also tested its models on MultiLangBench, which measures their ability to build a database engine compatible with SQLite across 20 programming languages.GPT-6 Astra achieved an average test pass rate of 87.4 percent, up from 26.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. Astra improved in every language tested.Its Fortran score climbed from 21.4 percent to 83.5 percent, while Visual Basic rose from 27.5 percent to 89.4 percent. COBOL remained the hardest language, although Astra raised its score from 10.9 percent to 72.1 percent.GPT-6 Luna delivered a lower average pass rate of 40.3 percent but cost approximately 78 percent less per sample than GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI estimated average API costs of $0.77 and $3.48, respectively.The findings point to stronger support for maintaining aging software. However, developers must still ensure that modernized systems preserve the behavior businesses depend on.The benchmarks also show where more work is needed. Astra’s results varied considerably across languages, and COBOL still posed the greatest challenge. Meanwhile, Luna’s lower costs could let engineering teams run more experiments without substantially increasing their budgets. The results offer encouraging evidence of progress, but teams will need to carefully validate production deployments before trusting migrated software with critical operations.

title: New Mercury 3 model claims 8-fold speed edge over GPT-6 rivals
content: California-based AI research and product company Inception has unveiled Mercury 3, its latest diffusion language model, claiming it outperforms speed-optimized rivals GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on a range of benchmarks while running four to eight times faster.The new model generates more than 1,000 tokens per second on widely available NVIDIA GPUs and supports a context window of 1 million tokens, allowing it to process substantially larger amounts of information in a single request.According to Inception, Mercury 3 is more than 40 times larger than its first-generation model, Mercury 1, while maintaining comparable processing speeds.The company says the results demonstrate that diffusion-based language models can become more capable without sacrificing the speed advantages of their underlying architecture.Scaling without sacrificing speedTraditional large language models generate text sequentially, predicting one token at a time. Diffusion language models take a different approach, generating and refining multiple tokens in parallel.This allows them to produce responses faster, potentially reducing delays in applications that require frequent interactions with a model.However, developers have traditionally faced a trade-off between model capability and response speed. Smaller models generally respond faster, while more capable systems often require additional processing time.Inception says Mercury 3 addresses this challenge by delivering performance comparable to or better than recently released OpenAI and Anthropic models across several standard benchmarks while maintaining inference speeds above 1,000 tokens per second.1/4 Today, we’re releasing Mercury 3. Mercury 3 is by far our most powerful model and the most intelligent diffusion LLM ever released. It outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality while running at 1000+ tok/sec. pic.twitter.com/TYevDl43Lm— Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon) October 19, 2026The release marks the company’s fourth model since introducing Mercury 1 in June 2025.Mercury 2 subsequently introduced reasoning capabilities, while Mercury 2.5 added adjustable reasoning and expanded the context window to 260,000 tokens.Mercury 3 increases that capacity to 1 million tokens, nearly quadrupling the amount of information the model can handle at once.“Since we launched Mercury 1, the question we’ve heard most is whether diffusion can scale. Mercury 3 is over 40 times larger, significantly more capable, and still runs at over 1,000 tokens per second,” said Stefano Ermon, co-founder of Inception.Ermon added that the company has already begun training its next model.Faster responses for developersThe company is targeting applications where response delays can affect usability, including interactive tutoring, live translation, writing assistants and automated software agents.In agent-based systems, models often perform multiple sequential tasks, such as searching websites, analyzing information or examining software logs. Delays at each stage can increase the time required to complete an operation.Inception says Mercury 3’s faster inference could help reduce these cumulative delays without requiring developers to switch to less capable models.Early-access customers are already testing the model in production workflows.Educational technology company RevisionDojo reported that Mercury 3 reduced response times for student feedback, including hints, definitions, and marked answers, to approximately one second.Mercury 3 is available through the Inception API, Baseten, OpenRouter, and Vercel.The model is compatible with the OpenAI API format, allowing developers to integrate it into existing applications without extensive code changes.

title: Japan launches Mars mission for world's first Martian moon samples
content: Japan has sent a spacecraft toward Mars on a mission that could answer a long-standing question about the planet’s two moons. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft lifted off aboard an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center on October 20, Japan time.Led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the $578 million mission will investigate Phobos and Deimos. Its primary objective is to collect material from Phobos and deliver it to Earth in 2031. No spacecraft has previously landed on either Martian moon and returned samples.JAXA later confirmed that MMX had successfully separated from the H3 F10 rocket’s upper stage. The separation placed the sample-return spacecraft on its interplanetary trajectory toward Mars and Phobos, marking a key milestone in the mission.Inside the missionThe mission begins with a journey lasting several months before MMX reaches Mars in 2027. The spacecraft will then spend roughly three years studying the moons before departing for Earth.JAXA developed the H3 launch vehicle alongside Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Standing 207 feet tall, the rocket uses two LE-9 engines on its first stage. They burn liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to generate approximately 331,000 pounds of combined thrust.Four solid rocket boosters provide additional power during liftoff. The vehicle sheds these boosters during ascent before discarding its protective payload fairings. After first-stage separation, the upper stage will perform the burns needed to send MMX toward Mars.The mission builds on Japan’s experience returning asteroid samples. Its earlier missions demonstrated the country’s ability to retrieve material from small celestial bodies. Phobos presents a different challenge because it orbits Mars and has an extremely weak gravitational pull.Phobos landing plansPhobos stretches about 14 miles across and has an irregular, potato-like shape. Its surface conditions could complicate the landing operations needed for sample collection.MMX will deploy IDEFIX, a French-German rover designed to examine the terrain. The four-wheeled vehicle may bounce across the surface before settling into place. Its design allows it to recover from an upside-down landing, although soft soil or obstructing rocks could leave it stranded.／ MMX、打ち上げ成功！！🚀＼長い年月をかけて完成させた探査機が宇宙へ飛び立っていく姿に、胸が熱くなりました🥹ここから始まる、約5年間にわたる壮大な旅。いってらっしゃい、MMX！👋三菱電機は、引き続き地球への帰還までの長い旅の運用をサポートしていきます！ pic.twitter.com/utFvV0d3HT— 三菱電機｜Mitsubishi Electric (@ME_JP_official) October 20, 2026IDEFIX will spend approximately 100 days surveying Phobos. Its findings will help mission controllers identify suitable landing locations for the main spacecraft.The Japanese lander will attempt two touchdowns during late 2028 or 2029. It will use a sampling mechanism to gather material before securing the collected material inside its return capsule. Each surface operation will require careful coordination because Phobos offers little gravity to hold the spacecraft down.The return journeyScientists want to determine whether Phobos formed from debris following an impact on Mars or represents a captured asteroid. Samples could help distinguish between these competing explanations.MMX will also investigate Deimos, the smaller of Mars’ two moons. Measuring approximately eight miles across, Deimos will receive several close flybys during the mission’s final months.The spacecraft plans to leave the Martian system in November 2030. Its return capsule should reach Australia in 2031, carrying material collected from Phobos.Laboratory analysis could reveal details about the moons’ composition and their place in the solar system’s history. The findings may also help researchers understand how other planetary moons formed.

title: Russia revives Tu-160 bomber production, upgrades 80% of its systems
content: More than a decade after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced plans to revive production of the Tu-160 strategic bomber, Russia says it has rebuilt the industrial base needed to manufacture the aircraft.Tupolev CEO Yuri Abrosimov confirmed the development in an October 15 interview, marking a significant step toward restarting production of the Soviet-era supersonic bomber, one of Russia’s most prominent strategic missile carriersThe head of Russia’s Aerospace and defense company said that under the new program, the bomber’s appearance and variable-geometry wing configuration will be retained. Its variable-sweep wings can be adjusted between 20 and 65 degrees, allowing the bomber to operate efficiently at lower speeds and during supersonic flight.Modernizing the Soviet-era bomberThe planned modifications are focused on modernizing 80 percent of the aircraft’s systems and equipment. Abrosimov said that the modernized version of the aircraft, the Tu-160M, is “built on an entirely new technological foundation, incorporating digital technologies, with 80 percent of its systems and equipment modernized.”This would be in contrast to the manufacturing of the original Tu-160 that was built using an older Soviet-era manufacturing system.He further noted that instead of a complete overhaul of the design, individual components, such as radar, navigation equipment, communications systems, or weapons-control computers, can be upgraded separately. These proposed changes will include a new NK-32-02 (NK-32 Series 02) engines, complete upgradation of avionics, aircraft- and weapons-control systems, navigation equipment, and onboard radio-electronic systems. The programme also introduced a shared digital environment linking aircraft design and manufacturing. Sukhoi, Mikoyan and Ilyushin design bureaux helped prepare digital documentation, while United Aircraft Corporation enterprises now operate within a common information system that enables engineering changes to be incorporated into production more quickly.Abrosimov said resuming serial production would strengthen Russia’s technological independence and support the long-term development of its Long-Range Aviation fleet and the airborne component of the country’s nuclear triad.Reviving Soviet-era bomber productionHe, however, noted that rebuilding the industrial and technological framework needed to manufacture the aircraft again was the major hurdle for the Russian Space and Defense company.The programme required restoring links with suppliers of raw materials and semi-finished products, rebuilding production chains for key aircraft assemblies, upgrading factory workshops and flight-test facilities, and installing specialised equipment for electron-beam welding and vacuum annealing of titanium components. He described the first flight of an all-new Tu-160M in January 2022 as the programme’s defining milestone and said the project paired younger engineers with experienced Soviet-era specialists to transfer manufacturing expertise.“It is a test of the strength of our entire engineering and manufacturing tradition, which we passed successfully,” Abrosimov said.The older model, Tu-160 was developed by the Soviet Union nearly five decades ago to counter the U.S. Strategic bombers. The aircraft entered service in 1987 and was nick-named, the ‘White Swan.’ To this day, it remains one of the world’s largest and fastest operational bomber, capable of carrying long-range conventional and nuclear cruise missiles over intercontinental distances.

title: China confirms third-generation nuclear sub missile launch tests
content: China has revealed for the first time the deployment of third-generation nuclear submarine tests in the Pacific, announcing its intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) missions to the world.In a statement issued Saturday by the state news agency, Xinhua said, “The Changzheng series of nuclear submarines have now reached the third generation and successfully organized the test launch of a submarine-launched strategic missile.”Stepping up its naval defense, the People’s Liberation Army of China for the first time conducted these ICBMs using the third generation of submarines.  ICBM tests in JulyPrior to Saturday’s announcement, Beijing demonstrated its sea-based nuclear capabilities in July this year, which drew sharp criticism from regional countries, including its neighbors, Japan and Australia.The latest statement was posted with pictures of the previous missile tests conducted in July, as reported in the Japan Times. Much like those tests, the latest mission is also notable because it used a nuclear-powered submarine, which can remain underwater for months without refueling. Unlike regular submarines, these use nuclear reactors, allowing them to travel farther and patrol for longer.Hidden underwater ballistic missile submarines are mainly designed for strategic nuclear deterrence. They are hard to detect and can be ready to respond if needed. No official confirmation regarding the type of subs and ballistic missile submarine deployment has been made by China so far. After the July trials, Chinese state media did not identify the submarine involved. Defense analysts believe a Type 094 ballistic missile submarine may have carried out the launch. China is believed to operate at least six of these boats, which can carry JL-2 missiles and potentially the newer JL-3 missile, a weapon with enough range to strike parts of the United States from waters near China. Beijing has also begun introducing the more advanced Type 095 submarine while continuing development of the next-generation Type 096.According to China’s state news agency Xinhua in July, the missile was launched at 12:01 p.m. local time during a routine military exercise. The report stated the test was not aimed at any country or specific target, and that relevant governments were informed ahead of time.China’s second vessel handling UUVsMeanwhile, China has expanded its nuclear submarine launch capacity by building a second vessel to support the handling of uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs).The new ship shares several design features with its counterpart, including a flight deck, a hangar behind the forward superstructure, and structures for handling underwater vehicles. It was constructed at Guangzhou Shipyard International and appears smaller than a similar vessel identified earlier in Shanghai. The vessel was spotted by satellite imagery earlier this month on October 2, as it emerged from a covered graving yard at the shipyard. Large uncrewed underwater vehicles can perform tasks such as seabed mapping, mine detection, and surveillance. They may also support operations involving submarines and surface ships. Some UUV designs can accommodate other payloads, including weapons, although no specific payload has been confirmed for these vessels.

title: NVIDIA runs largest-ever 104-qubit quantum simulation on JUPITER
content: NVIDIA has announced that JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer, has completed a record-breaking quantum computing simulation, allowing researchers to explore and validate magic state cultivation.The 104-qubit simulation, described by NVIDIA as the largest comprehensive simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computing system to date, ran on NVIDIA GH200 GPUs at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany.Magic states are essential for performing complex calculations on fault-tolerant quantum computers. However, producing them with sufficiently low error rates remains a major challenge.Traditional methods require substantial hardware resources, with some estimates suggesting that up to 95 percent of a quantum computer’s physical qubits could be dedicated to producing these states, leaving relatively few available for calculations.NVIDIA’s announcement comes days after Google reported that its Willow quantum processor achieved a 40-fold reduction in errors while preparing specialized quantum states.Unlike NVIDIA’s work, which uses classical supercomputing hardware to simulate quantum processes, Google’s experiment involved preparing magic states on an actual quantum processor. The two approaches address different challenges in developing fault-tolerant quantum computers, with simulations helping researchers evaluate designs before testing them on physical hardware.Simulating real-world quantum errorsLast year, JUPITER simulated a full 50-qubit universal quantum computer under ideal, noiseless conditions, surpassing the previous 48-qubit record established by Jülich researchers in 2019 on Japan’s K computer.The latest 104-qubit simulation, however, accounts for realistic hardware noise, allowing researchers to examine how errors affect magic state cultivation.Unlike ideal simulations, which assume quantum operations can be performed without errors, the new work models the disturbances that physical quantum processors encounter during calculations. This provides a more realistic way to assess whether proposed methods can operate reliably under practical conditions.Germany knows how to build, and now it’s bringing that expertise to industrial AI. 🇩🇪Tonight in Berlin, @JensenHuang and Chancellor @_FriedrichMerz discussed combining German engineering with NVIDIA AI to advance manufacturing and automotive.We’re also backing Germany’s… pic.twitter.com/9uwH0rYYLk— NVIDIA (@nvidia) October 19, 2026By simulating the process under these conditions, NVIDIA researchers validated an advanced magic state cultivation approach, providing a way to test future improvements. The results could also help identify weaknesses in proposed designs and guide researchers toward more efficient methods before committing resources to building quantum hardware.Scaling across 8,192 GPUsFor the new project, NVIDIA researchers first developed and tested their methods on a GB200 NVL72 system at the company’s Accelerated Quantum Research Center.They scaled testing from four GPUs to hundreds before moving to 8,192 GPUs on JUPITER. According to NVIDIA, the development work helped reduce simulation efforts from weeks to days.The team used NVIDIA’s cuQuantum software to optimize simulation performance and its CUDA-Q platform to model the fault-tolerant quantum circuit.The detailed simulation could allow researchers to predict how future quantum computing designs might perform before building physical hardware. This could reduce the need for repeated hardware testing and help accelerate the development of quantum applications in drug discovery, financial modeling and materials science.“Useful quantum computing will require fantastically complex, fault-tolerant systems — and understanding how they behave at scale is essential to building them,” said NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. “Our results from Jülich show how quantum processors and GPU supercomputers can work together to tackle research that would otherwise be out of reach, accelerating the discovery of transformative quantum applications.”

title: Humanoid robot covers 348 miles in a grueling 9-day treadmill test
content: Figure AI is putting its latest humanoid robot through an extended endurance test to uncover weaknesses that shorter demonstrations might miss. Figure 03 has covered 348 miles and logged 1.2 million steps during nine consecutive days on a treadmill, CEO Brett Adcock reported on X.Adcock said the experiment began as a side project designed to stress the robot and expose potential failures. The time-lapse shows Figure 03 walking on a treadmill inside a testing facility, with a power cable attached to the robot. The test follows several other attempts by Figure to push its humanoids beyond short demonstrations.Figure 03 targets longer operationIntroduced on Oct. 9, 2025, Figure 03 represents the company’s third-generation humanoid platform. Figure redesigned its hardware to support domestic tasks and commercial work, with manufacturing scale also a priority.F.03 just crossed 9 straight days walking on this treadmill: 348 miles and 1.2 million stepsStarted as a side project to stress the robot for any failures. Let's see how long it can go pic.twitter.com/mxsJcrO8jP— Brett Adcock (@adcock_brett) October 19, 2026The robot features updated cameras that deliver twice the frame rate and one-quarter the latency of its predecessor. Each camera also offers a 60% wider field of view, according to Figure. Its hands incorporate palm cameras and tactile sensors that detect forces as small as three grams.Figure also equipped the robot with wireless inductive charging. Coils inside its feet let it recharge by stepping onto a compatible stand, which delivers power at 2 kilowatts. The system could support extended deployments, although the treadmill post does not explain how charging factored into this particular test.Previous endurance testFigure has already tested its humanoids in a much longer operational demonstration. In May 2026, the company livestreamed Figure 03 robots sorting packages for approximately 200 hours. The run began as an eight-hour demonstration before extending into a nine-day event.The robots collectively processed 249,560 packages during the livestream, according to reports. However, multiple machines rotated through the task, allowing individual units to recharge between shifts. Each robot typically operated for three to four hours before another took over.The treadmill experiment differs because Adcock’s post focuses on accumulated walking distance and steps. It remains unclear whether one robot completed the entire run or how the team managed its power requirements. Those details will help establish what the latest milestone demonstrates about endurance.Figure 02 leaves the fleetFigure’s newer platform also arrives as the company retires its predecessor. On Sept. 30, Figure announced the decommissioning of its Figure 02 fleet as production of Figure 03 expands. View this post on Instagram Figure 02 marked several milestones, including the company’s first deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant in South Carolina. There, the robots handled sheet-metal components during vehicle production. Figure said the deployment contributed to manufacturing more than 30,000 BMW X3 vehicles.The company chose to retire the older machines partly because their custom-built components made dismantling them time-consuming. Figure instead trained robots to jump into molten steel at a foundry in Finland, melting most of the fleet.Figure 03 now faces a different challenge. Its latest treadmill run could reveal how well the platform withstands prolonged repetitive movement. The results may offer useful clues about the reliability required before humanoids can take on longer shifts in industrial settings.

title: Palladium-coated membrane destroys toxic ‘forever chemicals’ in water
content: Researchers at Arizona State University have developed a new technique to destroy per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), commonly known as “forever chemicals.”Forever chemicals are a family of synthetic substances that do not rot, rust, or break down in sunlight or soil, until now.In a study, an international coalition designed a catalytic “hunter-killer” membrane to annihilate these toxic molecules.“We all have PFAS in us. They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem,” said Bruce Rittmann, director of the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology. The chemistry that huntsConventional water treatment methods like activated carbon filters, ion-exchange resins, and reverse osmosis extract toxic PFAS from drinking water. However, these methods fail to destroy the chemicals and simply trap the contaminants. Also, these processes leave behind concentrated brines and hazardous waste filters. Facilities ultimately bury or incinerate this waste, which delays the problem rather than solving it.“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” added Rittmann. The reason behind this stubbornness is the carbon-fluorine bond. It is widely considered the single strongest bond in organic chemistry. Fluorine atoms shield the carbon backbone like interlocking armor plates. Microbes can’t digest it. Chemicals can’t pierce it.“There’s really no place to get a start to break it down,” Rittmann explained.To crack the uncrackable, Rittmann’s team worked alongside collaborators from Rice University, Tongji University, the National University of Singapore, and Nanjing University. And turned to a clever piece of molecular matchmaking.Researchers constructed a hollow fiber membrane lined on the outside with palladium nanoparticles rather than attacking PFAS in open water.The process works from the inside out. Pressurized hydrogen gas passes through the center of microscopic hollow fiber straws, diffusing outward until it meets a palladium catalyst. This catalyst splits paired hydrogen molecules into highly reactive individual hydrogen atoms. At the same time, PFAS molecules floating in the surrounding water attach to the palladium surface, bringing the reactive hydrogen and target pollutants together for destruction.When the target and the activated hydrogen meet on the surface, the catalyst forces a violent chemical reaction. The hydrogen strips away the protective fluorine guard, stripping the molecule of its “forever” superpower and reducing it to harmless components.More refinement of tech During a continuous 58-day trial, the system treated water containing a cocktail of six different regulatory-priority PFAS compounds.It removed over 90 percent of each compound and stripped away 83 percent of the total fluorine, the study reported.High PFAS concentrations riddle groundwater near military bases, municipal landfills, airports, and wastewater treatment plants worldwide. These toxins accumulate in crops, livestock, and human tissue, where exposure has been linked to kidney cancer, thyroid disease, immune dysfunction, and developmental delays.A universal mechanism to dismantle the full family of compounds could transform environmental remediation.Several challenges need to be addressed before this technology can be deployed in municipal water systems. For instance, there’s a need to minimize the required amount of palladium to reduce costs. The precious metal trades at roughly $50,000 per kilogram. Practical deployment will likely pair the reactor with existing filtration methods to concentrate contaminated water first. This allows the catalytic system to efficiently destroy the resulting waste stream.The arrival of hunter-killer chemistry suggests this persistent toxic legacy might finally be coming to an end.

title: Biopolymers help desert sand hold water up to 28 times longer
content: ​Scientists are inching closer to making desert soil more viable by boosting the water-holding capacity of sand exposed to constant wind erosion.Researchers at Empa and Khalifa University of Science and Technology in Abu Dhabi found that sand reinforced with microbial biopolymer networks could slow water drainage by nearly 28-fold.​Like plastics, biopolymers are natural long-chain molecules. These materials can be obtained from bacteria and plants.​By binding sand grains and slowing water movement, the microbial biopolymers could help microorganisms and plants establish themselves, potentially supporting the gradual transformation of degraded land into more resilient soil.Microbial fibers trap sand particles​In this study, scientists used microbial cells that produce cellulose, a naturally occurring biopolymer made of repeating glucose units. These extremely fine thread-like structures are produced by some bacteria and plants and enhance their structural strength. ​To test how well microbes could give sand more life, researchers used two approaches. For the first, they took sand samples collected from dunes near Al Ain in the UAE and standardized laboratory sand, then exposed the samples to microbes, including bacteria and fungi.​To ensure that no living matter remained in the tested samples, the researchers sterilized them before introducing microbes and fresh nutrient solutions. ​In their study, researchers used the cellulose-producing bacterium Komagataeibacter medellinensis and two strains of the fungus Schizophyllum commune. These microbes formed biopolymers that soaked the sand, creating a mesh that traps nearby particles.​”This creates a kind of natural composite material,” said Gustav Nyström, who heads Empa’s Cellulose and Wood Materials laboratory.​The complex fiber structures created by bacteria enhanced the soil strength and slowed water drainage to six times less than in pure sand samples.​In the comparative study, the researchers showed that soil samples mixed with bacteria were much more robust than pure sand and fungi-treated sand samples.​Researchers found that in strength tests conducted with soil samples treated with the microbes after a week, the sand column with bacteria was nearly six centimeters in length and had enough strength to be cast out from the mold and cut into pieces without getting fractured.​On the other hand, researchers noted that samples treated with fungi were less break-proof. Some of these sand columns broke as they were being removed from the molds or while cutting them into pieces after the drying procedure.​Cellulose sheets improve strength, reduce water lossThe researchers found much greater progress in both strength and water retention when they first grew cellulose sheets, also called biotextiles, separately before placing them between two layers of sand. This sandwiched layer acted as a reinforcing fabric and distributed the force applied to the material, making the samples significantly tougher. These samples also performed better in collapse tests using 10-kilogram loads.Researchers found that samples in which the cellulose sheets were allowed to grow for longer periods became even stronger. They also recorded the greatest reduction in water drainage in sand reinforced with the cellulose sheets.To measure water retention, the team poured water into tubes filled with the different sand samples and recorded how long each took to drain. Although this sheet-based method was more labor-intensive, it produced the best results for both structural stability and water retention.Sand reinforced with cellulose sheets reduced water permeability by nearly 28-fold compared with untreated sand, whereas fibers grown directly within the sand reduced water permeability by about sixfold.The findings suggest that microbial fibers could offer a biodegradable alternative to some synthetic materials used to stabilize soil.“This approach allows us to introduce organic matter and water into the sand and stabilize it somewhat,” said Nyström.By strengthening grain-to-grain connections, the biopolymer networks could also help reduce wind-driven soil erosion, they said.The researchers have filed a patent application for the technology. They cautioned, however, that the work was carried out entirely under controlled laboratory conditions, where both the microbes and nutrient supply were carefully regulated. The team has not yet conducted field trials involving crop growth or evaluated how well the reinforced material would withstand prolonged exposure to harsh desert conditions.The findings of the study were published in Carbohydrate Polymers.​

title: US superconducting smart chip analyzes fusion plasma at record speeds
content: Scientists in the state of New York have created a first-of-a-kind superconducting neural chip that can reportedly process about one million fusion plasma samples per second.The new Super Intelligence (SI) computer chip was designed by researchers at the US Department of Energy’s (DOE) Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). For the project, they partnered with the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the DIII-D National Fusion Facility, and Colorado-based tech company Great Sky.BNL noted that the chip relies on superconducting circuits to mimic human neural networks. It could eventually improve the way fusion reactors monitor and control hot plasma. Lab tests showed the chip could detect unusual plasma behavior and predict instabilities.“It’s incredible to see the team processing data from our tokamak with this first-of-a-kind chip,” Richard Buttery, PhD, DIII-D Director, said. The team believes the technology could support faster and more reliable fusion reactor control systems.Handling plasma dataFusion reactors use magnetic fields to keep hot plasma confined at temperatures between 180 and 270 million degrees Fahrenheit (100 and 150 degrees Celsius). This extreme temperature is roughly 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun. Still, plasma conditions can change rapidly, making real-time monitoring essential to keep it stable. This requires computers that can process huge amounts of data almost instantly. But conventional silicon-based computing systems struggle to process such large amounts of data quickly enough. The wafers in the first-of-a-kind chips mimic human brain networks.Credit: Great Sky Inc.However, the novel superconducting neural chip can process signals at extremely high speeds. It uses superconducting circuitry arranged to mimic the connections found in the human brain.To test it, the scientists collected data from the DIII-D tokamak, a fusion research facility run by General Atomics in California. Two of these tests assessed the chip’s ability to spot unusual plasma activity and predict disruptions.The data were collected at a rate of one million samples per second, and the chip successfully handled the pace. “This is a powerful new platform for implementing many of the SI algorithms our team at Brookhaven Lab is developing,” Shinjae Yoo, PhD, CDS AI department chair and the project’s principal investigator, said. Plasma instabilitiesIn addition, a third experiment conducted by the team, involved simulated plasma data generated by TORAX. The system is a differentiable tokamak core transport simulator developed by Google DeepMind’s fusion team.During the experiment, the chip analyzed signals to predict the onset of sawtooth instabilities, which involve rapid changes in plasma conditions. The results showed that superconducting neural networks could potentially support real-time plasma monitoring and stabilization.Steven Cowley, PPPL director, stressed the importance of creating faster control systems for fusion reactors. “We are building the fusion machines of the SI era,” he added. “This chip took data straight from a tokamak at millions of samples every second and kept up.”Great Sky stated that the device is its largest superconducting neural chip to date. Similar chips could reportedly find use in quantum computing, cybersecurity, and high-speed X-ray data analysis.At present, the team is developing a new chip with a neural network 10 times larger than the current design. They plan to present the hardware at BNL in early 2027, before it undergoes testing at the DIII-D tokamak during fusion experiments later that year.“This is just the beginning,” Jeff Shainline, Great Sky founder and CEO, concluded in a press release. “This approach to AI hardware has so much to offer with regard to fusion, as well as other applications at the forefront of technology.”
