title: Sofab Inks and SAKATA INX develop an inkjet ink for perovskite solar cell ETLs
content:
Sofab Inks and SAKATA INX develop an inkjet ink for perovskite solar cell ETLs
Sofab Inks
and SAKATA INX are developing an inkjet-printable ink for the electron transport layer (ETL) of perovskite solar cells. The ink pairs Sofab’s tin oxide (SnO₂)-based ETL materials with SAKATA INX’s nano-dispersion, ink formulation and thin-film formation expertise from its industrial inkjet ink business.
Inkjet printing requires stable jetting and uniform, ultrathin films, in addition to high-performing materials. The companies say the ink is being designed to limit damage to the underlying perovskite layer. They expect it to allow more precise deposition and less material waste, as well as better durability and more efficient production. It could be used in single-junction and tandem perovskite solar cells.
The companies will present the product under development at Sofab’s booth at
Perovskite Connect
, held in Berlin on October 21-22. They plan to continue to evaluate its potential to support more sustainable and scalable manufacturing of perovskite solar cells.
The collaboration was first mentioned in an
earlier post
on Sofab’s full-scale production line results, where the company said it was also developing an inkjet-compatible formulation of its materials with SAKATA INX.

title: Raontek and SN Display to test perovskite color conversion for AR/VR microdisplays
content:
Raontek and SN Display to test perovskite color conversion for AR/VR microdisplays
Raontek and
SN Display
have signed a memorandum of understanding to develop perovskite-based microdisplays for augmented and virtual reality. Raontek is a fabless microdisplay company with LCoS, micro-
microLED
products. SN Display develops perovskite nanocrystals and color-conversion technology.
The first step is early-stage research. The companies will combine SN Display’s perovskite color conversion with Raontek’s microLED and micro-OLED microdisplays. They aim to verify ultra-fine pixels and full-color output, including whether the technology works as a color-conversion material for microLED pixels of 4 micrometers or smaller.
Raontek said perovskites can reach high color purity and a wide color gamut even in very small pixels. It can convert color efficiently at thicknesses of 0.5 micrometers or less and can be patterned with semiconductor processes, which makes it an alternative to quantum dots.
Depending on the results of sample evaluations, the companies may develop microdisplay prototypes together or expand their cooperation to other AR and VR display solutions. SN Display is also behind the
Vision Foundry project
, which aims to make perovskite microdisplays by vacuum deposition using existing OLED equipment.

title: Key takeaways from Intersolar Summit Romania  - pv magazine Global
content:
In the opening speech of the inaugural Intersolar Summit Romania, Florian Wessendorf, managing director of Solar Promotion International, referred to Romania as “the new renewables champion of Europe.” The country certainly has a strong claim to the title, largely thanks to its rapidly growing solar market. After installing
around 2.2 GW
of solar last year, Romania is set to deploy even more this year. Cumulative solar capacity
exceeded 8.5 GW
largest planned project in the EU
, suggests growth is set to continue.
In the opening panel of the event, Irene Mihai, policy director of the Romanian Photovoltaic Industry Association (RPIA) and Mihaela Nyerges, managing partner at Nyerges & Partners, told attendees how Romania has transformed into one of Europe’s most dynamic solar markets. They cited strong market fundamentals and a regulatory framework that includes some of, if not the, quickest permitting times for new solar projects in the European Union as key growth enablers. Mihai rounded out the first session of the event with a call for Romania’s future energy system to be “boring”, led by the predictability and stability required for players to continue investing.
As Romania’s solar market continues to grow, new challenges are entering the frame. Among them are grid access and expansion constraints. The country is currently undergoing the start of an auction-based mechanism for grid connections. The new rules are intended to curb speculative grid connection applications, but Nyerges said the process may need further refinement to give investors the certainty they need to participate. With the
first round only just underway
, initial results may not emerge until spring 2027.
Storage and flexibility emerged as recurring themes, reflecting the changing economics of solar projects and the emergence of negative electricity prices in Romania. Several discussions gave particular attention to flexibility solutions, including hybrid assets, co-location strategies and evolving revenue models. Panellists advised developers of hybrid projects to think from a system perspective and to look at where storage creates the greatest value. RPIA executive director Andrei Manea explained Romania is working to hybridize its existing assets. Manea said Romania had faced challenges this year, such as high electricity costs and drought, which left water levels on the Danube exceptionally low and disrupted power generation. He argued that higher electricity production and greater system flexibility will improve the outlook in the medium- to long-term.
Romania’s storage market is also picking up pace, having
surpassed 1 GW of utility-scale battery storage capacity
earlier this year, while solar prosumers are leading the growth of the smaller-scale storage market. If Romania wants to learn from a leading storage market, it needs to look no further than its southern border to find one of Europe’s leaders, in Bulgaria, where storage capacity reached 5.7 GW last month. Mariyana Yaneva, chief operating officer of IPS, explained this rapid storage buildout has contributed to Bulgaria registering no negative price hours since June, an impressive feat when considering Bulgaria is another of Europe’s
gigawatt-sized solar markets
The second day of the summit also explored innovations in solar power plant design and operation, the growing impact of artificial intelligence, data centres and energy resilience in Eastern Europe. Few countries know the importance of energy resilience as much as Romania’s northern neighbour, Ukraine. Chairman of the Board of the Solar Energy Association of Ukraine, Vladyslav Sokolovskyi, shared with attendees the latest on
Ukraine’s work to rebuild its energy system
amid ongoing attacks from Russia, which centres around a focus on deploying small-scale, distributed solar-plus-storage systems. This closing discussion also covered grid-forming storage, power grids, cross-border interconnectivity and cybersecurity, underscoring the importance of resilient and secure energy systems across Romania and the wider region.

title: Taiwanese PV manufacturers create back-contact TOPCon alliance - pv magazine Global
content:
Taiwan’s
Industrial Technology Research Institute
(ITRI) has announced the establishment of a TBC Photovoltaic Technology Alliance, bringing together seven domestic solar companies to strengthen Taiwan’s photovoltaic supply chain and accelerate the commercialization of TOPCon solar cell technologies based on back-contact (BC) design.
The initiative aims to establish a domestic supply chain for TOPCon back contact (TBC) solar technology, combining research and development capabilities with expertise in materials, manufacturing equipment and solar cell production, ITRI said in a statement.
The TBC cells developed by the Taiwanese manufacturers have achieved a power conversion efficiency of around 25.5%, according to a report by local media outlet Formosa News. The report did not specify whether the efficiency figure was independently certified or measured under laboratory or production conditions.
ITRI has also developed a laser-assisted silver-coated copper electrode technology designed to reduce the consumption of silver in solar cell manufacturing. The technology could reportedly lower cell production costs by 8% and generate approximately TWD 200 million ($6.3 million) in annual production value.
The alliance brings together companies operating across different stages of Taiwan’s photovoltaic value chain, including solar materials suppliers, cell manufacturers and module producers. Participants identified by ITRI include TeraSolar,
Giga Solar
, Sustainable Sunrise,
United Renewable Energy
Lin Fu-ming, a representative of ITRI’s green energy laboratories, said the collaboration will combine the institute’s research and development platform with the equipment, materials and technical expertise of participating companies to support the development of next-generation photovoltaic technologies.
The initiative reflects Taiwan’s efforts to strengthen its domestic solar manufacturing capabilities and compete in higher-value photovoltaic market segments through improved conversion efficiency and advanced cell manufacturing processes.

title: GCL Technology moves to buy LFP cathode maker from founder’s group - pv magazine Global
content:
GCL Technology Holdings has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to acquire about 81.91% of Sichuan GCL Lithium Battery Technology, an LFP cathode material producer, from Golden Concord Group, the parent group controlled by GCL Technology’s chairman, Zhu Gongshan, and his family.
The preliminary price is about CNY 2.5 billion, according to the Hong Kong-listed company’s filing. About CNY 650 million would be paid in cash and about CNY 1.85 billion in new GCL Technology shares, issued at no less than HK$1.30 each, or up to about 1,671 million shares. The final price will be based on an independent valuation.
Because the seller is controlled by the chairman’s family trust, the deal would be a connected transaction under Hong Kong listing rules. GCL Technology said it expects to seek a specific mandate from independent shareholders to issue the new shares. It has 30 days for due diligence and three months of exclusivity to negotiate a formal agreement.
The seller has guaranteed combined adjusted net profit of at least CNY 620 million for the target in 2027 and 2028. It has also committed to developing a sixth-generation LFP cathode material with a compacted density above 2.8 g/cm³ by the end of 2028, and would pay compensation if either target is missed.
LFP capacity
Sichuan GCL Lithium, based in Meishan, Sichuan province, has annual LFP production capacity of 120,000 tons at its first-phase facility, which occupies about 355 mu of a planned 1,000-mu site. A June report published by GCL said the company began production in July 2023 and supplies Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL) and Haichen Energy Storage.
GCL Technology already makes LFP cathode material through its subsidiary Leshan Xinneng New Materials Technology. The first 200,000-ton phase began shipments in June at an average tax-inclusive price of CNY 60,320 per ton and has been profitable since operations began, the company said.
GCL Technology said the acquisition would help it “reduce its reliance on the pricing cycles of polysilicon and wafer products and enhance the stability of its earnings.” The company posted a net loss attributable to shareholders of CNY 2.08 billion in the first half of 2026, 17.2% wider than a year earlier. It said the polysilicon industry fell “into involution once again in the first half of 2026, with prices plummeting below the cash costs of most enterprises.” Its granular silicon sold for an average CNY 31.97/kg excluding tax, against a cash production cost of CNY 25.23/kg.
The company set out plans in May to
transform into a multi-product new energy materials platform
, built around silicon, lithium and carbon. It cited Chinese government data showing the country’s cumulative new-type energy storage capacity reached 153 GW/396 GWh at the end of June, up about 61% year on year.
The move follows a failed effort to tackle polysilicon overcapacity through consolidation. GCL Technology
raised funds last year
to support a government-backed plan in which China’s six largest polysilicon makers would raise about CNY 50 billion to acquire and idle roughly one-third of national capacity. China’s antitrust regulator later halted that plan, and rival Tongwei has since
moved to acquire polysilicon producer Qinghai Lihao

title: U.S. startup launches 200 kWh flywheel energy storage pilot - pv magazine Global
content:
Sacramento-based
has begun low-speed testing of its flywheel energy storage system at its technology center in Shanghai, China. The prototype unit, dubbed Pulsar, represents a continuation of the company’s mechanical storage architecture that is expected to have an initial capacity of 200 kWh and
expandable to 500 kWh
with the same platform, which would enable four-hour storage at a nominal discharge rate of 125 kW.
Flywheels store energy
in rapidly spinning rotors as kinetic motion. Surplus electricity is injected into the system, accelerating the rotor to high speeds. When power is needed, a generator converts kinetic energy back into electricity, slowing the rotor. Advocates for the technology say that flywheels could challenge battery-based energy storage systems (BESS) now dominant for renewables on the grid.
Qnetic reported in September that Pulsar had successfully completed its first 100 continuous charge-discharge cycles with zero faults or capacity degradation. Tested separately, the system’s motor produced 130 kW of power output at 97.3% efficiency with speeds exceeding 11,000 rpm.
Qnetic has established a factory and headquarters in Sacramento where it intends low-volume production of commercial Pulsar units. Pulsar will be evaluated in a pilot program by the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD) under the auspices of a risk-reduction initiative run by the Electric Power Research Institute. Qnetic aims to be able to start the pilot in the first half of 2027.
Michael Pratt, co-founder and CEO of Qnetic, told
pv magazine USA
that his company’s implementation of flywheel technology is intended to overcome many of the shortcomings of lithium-ion batteries, particularly in the areas of cycling rates and degradation over time.
“When we were formulating our concept about five years ago, grid-connected lithium-ion batteries in the form of large, containerized systems were just getting into the mainstream,” Pratt said. “It was pretty clear at the time that batteries were too expensive, but the main problem was the degradation issue.”
According to Pratt, the pressing need to integrate renewables on the grid argued for BESS, with its drawbacks, as the best solution then available. Since then, he notes, many billions have been spent trying to improve battery chemistry, but the fundamental issues remain: cycle life and calendar life.
“Lithium-ion batteries are typically doing one cycle per day, and they’re only going to last so many years,” Pratt said. “In addition, the whole time you’re using them, they are getting weaker and weaker. We knew that flywheels had the characteristics to cycle repeatedly on the grid and not lose capacity over time. We also saw that nobody was putting together all the pieces in the way needed for grid storage.”
Historically, flywheels have served as energy storage devices, rapidly delivering high power for short-duration applications measured in minutes or even seconds. Examples include backup power in telecommunications and data centers, or as bridging power until diesel generators come online. Precision control and high output power has also made them suitable for creating tokamaks in fusion energy experiments.
Qnetic’s goal is to produce flywheels suitable for long-duration energy storage on the grid. If four-hour performance is just this side of “long,” it still fulfills many utility requirements. Moreover, flywheel units may be grouped into banks that can be tapped over longer periods of time. Also, discharge rates can be varied to meet demands.
Deployed grid-scale units are buried in the ground with the control machinery accessible through an exposed dome, an arrangement that suggests eggs in a carton. Pratt positions flywheels as safer than lithium-ion batteries from a fire perspective, but the high speeds of the rotors still require consideration in case of “rapid unscheduled disassembly.” He adds that safety measures like making sure the motor stays short of imparting the rotor’s maximum rated speed will keep this from happening.
Competing flywheel maker Amber Kinetics has also developed a version of its 32-kW units for above ground deployment in steel shipping containers.
While Pratt makes arguments for how flywheels overcome some specific drawbacks of BESS – namely cycling and degradation issues – he acknowledges that the mechanical storage technology faces developmental hurdles of its own in order to reach higher capacities and economies of scale.
Some of these are addressed in Pulsar’s architecture. The unit features a carbon fiber rotor rotating in a vacuum on no-contact magnetic bearings, all but eliminating friction. The rotor is kept clear of the central shaft using technology similar to that which enables magnetic levitation trains to travel with no contact with the rails. The assembly is housed in a cylindrical steel container.
A key objective in Pulsar’s development is to increase the strength of the composite rotor, which is made with carbon fiber filaments. The stronger the rotor, the faster it can be made to rotate, and the more kinetic energy stored. With Pulsar’s current configuration, further iteration of the carbon fiber will enable the increase of its capacity to 500 kWh.
“As you build up, you get excellent economies of scale,” Pratt said. “If you double the physical size, you can get eight times the potential energy capacity in that envelope. The second thing you want to do is go fast. You want to make a really strong rotor so that you can spin quickly. So, a really good rotor and going quite large are the keys to getting a low-cost system.”
At the same time, Pratt says there are practical considerations about achieving higher capacity and thus cost-effectiveness through size. One is that the company is essentially breaking new ground with composite rotors. The improved rotor is made using a process called filament winding from carbon fiber, and Pratt says it is not common to manufacture these larger than about two-and-a-half meters in diameter.
“We’re going to cycle the hell out of it, see if anything breaks, and if it does, we’ll fix it,” he said. “Once we’ve gone through that proving process, then we do the first pilots.”
On the whole, Pratt says, all of the fundamental technologies leading to Pulsar are mature and in service. Other than perhaps fabricating a larger carbon fiber rotor, Qnetic is doing a lot of systems integration and control optimization work as opposed to original engineering and research and development. The goal is to achieve MW-scale flywheel units based on a subsequent generation.
If flywheels seem like an exotic energy storage solution, that’s largely because they have generally been relegated to niche applications. A spokesperson for Qnetic told
pv magazine USA
that grid-connected flywheel pioneer Beacon Power deployed 400 of its 100 kW (25 kWh) units at two utility sites in New York and Pennsylvania between 2011 and 2014 to provide fast-responding frequency regulation. Each location had 200 units with a nameplate capacity of 20 MW (5 MWh), and both are still providing frequency regulation service and generating revenue.
Pratt says flywheel technology has only gotten better and more reliable. He says an asset lifetime in excess of 30 years and the ability to cycle multiple times a day with rapid response and no degradation make flywheels a promising energy storage solution at all scales, including long-duration grid applications.

title: Elevated agrivoltaics for olive cultivation - pv magazine Global
content:
Acesur, a Seville-based olive oil producer, has started construction of a 3.65 MW agrivoltaic project in Vilches, in the Spanish province of Jaén. The project will integrate solar power generation into an existing, fully productive olive grove adjacent to the company’s packaging plant.
Granada-based renewable energy company Greening is developing the project, which will combine industrial self-consumption with agricultural production while preserving all existing olive trees and maintaining cultivation.
According to the company, following several phases of system performance validation, the aim is now to scale up the technology for industrial use. All electricity generated by the installation will be used to power Acesur’s packaging plant.
The technology was developed in several stages, beginning with theoretical bioclimatic simulations, followed by laboratory testing under controlled climatic and greenhouse conditions. A prototype was then installed in a traditional rain-fed olive grove.
According to a company representative, results from two consecutive harvests have demonstrated that solar power generation and olive cultivation can coexist successfully. The installation reportedly improved local microclimatic conditions by reducing soil temperatures, retaining moisture and enhancing crop yields.
The representative said the Vilches project will be the world’s first industrial-scale “olivovoltaic” installation.
The 3.65 MW installation will feature more than 5,150 solar modules mounted on metal structures standing more than 4 meters above the ground, supported by steel pillars anchored in concrete foundations. The elevated configuration will allow agricultural machinery to operate beneath the panels, enabling conventional farming activities, including olive harvesting, to continue.
The project will also include a 3 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) to optimize energy use and improve operational flexibility.
Spain’s Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE) has awarded the project a €2.8 million grant to support the integration of renewable energy technologies into industrial operations..

title: Poland eases connection rules for home batteries up to 2.2x PV power - pv magazine Global
content:
Poland has changed its grid-connection rules to make it easier for households to pair PV systems with larger batteries, through an amendment to its Renewable Energy Sources Act that also revises the energy law.
Under the previous rule, storage power was excluded only if it did not exceed the PV system’s power, effectively a 1:1 ratio. Above that, the battery’s power counted toward the microinstallation’s installed power.
The limit applies to rated power in kilowatts, not storage capacity in kilowatt-hours. A 10 kW PV system could therefore be paired with a battery of up to 22 kW, and the provision does not limit energy capacity. Owners will need export controls to keep feed-in below the PV system’s rating. If either condition is not met, the battery’s power counts toward installed capacity as before.
The amendment also requires electricity sellers to give prosumers more detailed monthly information, including grid imports and exports in kWh, the value of exported electricity and their prosumer deposit. It changes rules for energy cooperatives and introduces an auction system for biomethane plants above 1 MW. The act itself does not provide battery subsidies.
The Sejm passed the act on Sept. 4 by 380 votes to 2, with 53 abstentions, and the Senate approved it without amendments on Sept. 24.
In a government scenario in which 20% of new net-billing prosumers install batteries at up to the new limit, connected storage power would reach about 3.7 GW by the end of 2029.

in June that industry groups said would have restricted home and business battery storage. Separately, the Ministry of Climate and Environment has launched a PLN 1 billion ($256.9 million)
home storage subsidy
, with applications opening Oct. 20. It covers up to 30% of eligible battery costs, capped at PLN 800 per kWh, for batteries of at least 10 kWh. Storage already accounted for 60% of applications under the

title: New framework prioritizes fire protection measures for BIPV façades - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team led by the University of Science and Technology of China has developed a framework to assess the fire performance of building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) façades. The framework identifies key fire risk factors and prioritizes measures to prevent ignition and limit fire spread.
“Although previous studies have investigated the fire behavior of PV materials and modules, systematic fire risk assessment and resilience optimization for BIPV façades remain limited,” corresponding author Yu Wang told
pv magazine
. “In this work, data-driven sensitivity analysis and expert-judgment-based weighting methods were used to identify the dominant fire risk factors among 16 indicators covering electrical conditions, environmental factors, module materials, and installation conditions.”
Wang said the team also conducted a fire resilience optimization analysis based on the fire performance assessment to translate the most significant risk factors into practical mitigation measures.
“These measures cover ignition prevention, fire-spread suppression, monitoring, maintenance, and emergency response, extending the analysis from risk identification to engineering application,” he said.
The researchers began by establishing 16 fire risk indicators: temperature differences between shaded and unshaded areas; aging of PV modules and associated equipment; DC voltage and current levels; circuit contact resistance; wind load; dust accumulation; ambient temperature; natural disasters such as lightning; module glass thickness; glass type; encapsulation material fire performance; module light transmittance; installation spacing; installation configuration; installation angle; and shielding width.
Comparison of the fire risk indicators using data-driven (NVC) and expert-judgment-based weighting methods (AHP and TFN-AHP).
Drawing on previous and ongoing experiments and published studies, the researchers used normalized variance contribution (NVC) analysis to assess variations in the indicators’ normalized risk scores. Nine experts from Asia and Europe, including university researchers, fire service leaders, fire investigators, and senior engineers, also evaluated the indicators using the analytic hierarchy process (AHP). A fuzzy version of AHP accounted for uncertainty in expert judgments, while data perturbation tests assessed the stability of the NVC rankings.
The team linked the dominant risk factors to 15 safety measures: electroluminescence inspection; compliant equipment and wiring; rapid shutdown; encapsulant flammability ratings; module layout and spacing; module and surrounding fire loads; DC arc-fault detection; drone-based infrared inspection; machine learning-based detection; inspection and maintenance frequency; fault diagnosis and maintenance coverage; cleaning frequency; safe firefighting distances and electric shock prevention; extinguishing agent selection; and firefighting strategies and standards. The same experts ranked the measures using AHP.
“The most surprising finding was that the data-driven NVC analysis and expert-based AHP and triangular fuzzy number (TFN)-AHP assessments consistently identified five dominant risk factors despite differences in their overall rankings,” Wang said. “DC voltage and current magnitude ranked first in both the data-driven analysis and the expert-based assessments. Equipment aging, circuit contact resistance, module glass type, and encapsulation fire performance also consistently emerged as important factors. This highlights the need to consider electrical ignition hazards alongside the materials that influence fire development.”
Further uncertainty testing showed that the same six indicators – DC voltage and current magnitude, equipment aging, module glass type, circuit contact resistance, glass thickness, and encapsulation fire performance – remained the highest-ranked in the NVC analysis across all valid scenarios, with rank correlations exceeding 0.99.
The experts assigned a combined weight of 60.83% to ignition prevention and fire-spread suppression measures, with rapid shutdown ranking first among individual measures at 19.62%.
The researchers presented the framework in “
Framework for fire risk assessment and resilience optimization of building-integrated photovoltaic façades
,” published in
Applied Thermal Engineering
. The research team included scientists from the
University of Science and Technology of China
and Italy’s
University of Trieste

title: Norwegian, Danish funds invest in 500 MW Philippine solar project  - pv magazine Global
content:
Climate Investment Fund
, managed by Norway’s state-owned investment fund for developing countries
, and Danish development finance institution Impact Fund Denmark are investing in a 49% equity stake in the 500 MW Ixus Bugallon solar power project in the Philippines.
The project will be built in Bugallon within the coastal province of Pangasinan, northwestern Philippines, by Singapore-headquartered renewable energy company
Vena Energy
, which holds the remaining 51% stake.
The Ixus Bugallon project reached financial close in July 2026 after securing around $310 million in senior loans from a consortium of eight international banks.
The investment is the Climate Investment Fund’s first in the Philippines. Norway’s Minister of International Development, Åsmund Aukrust, said the investment is a “good example of mobilising private capital and preventing emissions through profitable investments in renewable energy.”
He added that an increase to the Climate Investment Fund is being proposed in Norway’s 2027 state budget.
The Ixus Bugallon project will be located next to Vena Energy’s existing
550 MW Bugallon solar power project
. Together, the two plants are one of the Philippines’ largest solar clusters.
The latest plant was awarded under the Philippines Department of Energy’s (DOE)
second green energy auction
. It is expected to generate enough electricity to power roughly 650,000 Philippine households annually once operational.
Earlier this year, DOE unveiled plans to hold four editions of its flagship green energy auction programme over the next two years as part of wider plans to auction
25 GW of renewables
The Philippines installed
of solar in 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), taking cumulative solar capacity to 3,892 MW.

title: German DSO cuts residential solar grid connection approval time to 5 minutes - pv magazine Global
content:
Grid operators across Germany are facing a growing number of connection requests for battery energy storage systems and rooftop solar installations. To manage the increasing workload, distribution system operators (DSOs), including Netze BW, are turning to digital solutions.
The southern German grid operator has unveiled an automated assessment process for PV systems with capacities of up to 15 kW. The system can reduce processing times from an average of 12 days to around five minutes in areas where sufficient grid capacity is available.
Netze BW launched the system in late July 2026, following a testing and rollout phase that began in November 2025. Since then, the company has received more than 16,000 grid connection requests for small-scale PV installations, according to Angelika Ruß, a Netze BW representative, speaking at a press briefing.
More than 5,000 applicants have already received automated responses within five minutes. Marc Schmidt, also of Netze BW, said these responses constitute binding grid connection approvals and specify the connection point for installations up to 15 kW.
Jörg Reichert, chairman of Netze BW’s management board, highlighted the company’s strong performance in a digitalization index published this summer by Germany’s Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur), the country’s energy regulator.
“The energy transition cannot be achieved with a single mouse click – but the right digital solutions can certainly speed things up significantly,” said Reichert. “Anyone wanting to connect a photovoltaic system should be able to reach their goal without paperwork, waiting on hold, or follow-up inquiries.”
In a recently published comparison of German DSOs, Netze BW recorded an average processing time of 12 days for manually assessed grid connection requests, compared with a median of 80 days across all operators. The automated system could further improve the company’s performance.
However, automated approvals are currently limited to installations in areas where grid capacity is not considered critical. In these locations, the entire process is handled through Netze BW’s online customer portal, which accepts and processes requests around the clock.
Schmidt said 99% of grid connection requests are now submitted through the portal.
The automated assessment relies on a digital grid model that maps power lines, substations and individual customer connections. The system calculates available grid capacity, checks technical constraints and accounts for previously approved connections.
Where the assessment identifies insufficient grid capacity, the application is referred for manual review. Netze BW staff then determine whether grid reinforcement is necessary or whether an alternative connection point is available. Such cases can take up to 12 days to process.
Applications for PV systems larger than 15 kW also continue to require manual assessment. Staff must review and verify the technical data before issuing a binding grid connection offer.
Netze BW plans to extend automation to additional connection processes while maintaining grid stability.

title: Dutch development bank finances 50 MW of solar in Ivory Coast - pv magazine Global
content:
Dutch development bank FMO is financing the 50 MW Kong solar project in the Ivory Coast. Its €55.5 million ($62.3 million) financing package represents the project’s entire long-term financing with a 20-year tenor.
Located near the town of Kong in northern Ivory Coast, the solar project is expected to supply electricity to approximately 240,000 people once completed.
Construction of the power plant is already underway, following a
groundbreaking ceremony in October 2025
. Commissioning is currently scheduled for 2028. A 25-year power purchase agreement is in place with CI-Energies, the country’s state-owned electric utility.
FMO entered into the financing agreement with project company Kong Solaire SAS.
Africa Via, an Ivorian developer of renewable energy projects, holds a 51% stake in Kong Solaire SAS, while project development and investment company InfraCo holds the remaining 49%. Pan-African conglomerate Axian holds a 55% stake in Africa Via alongside its founders, giving it an approximately 28% indirect stake in Kong Solaire.
Marnix Monsfort, Director of Energy at FMO, said the financing agreement is the bank’s second solar energy investment in the Ivory Coast and coincides with the opening of an office in the country.
“[This] reflects our confidence in the country and the significant potential we see for increased private investment,” Monsfort said.
Earlier this year, the Ivory Coast switched on its second utility-scale project with the inauguration of the
52 MW Ferké solar plant
in the northern Tchologo region. It followed the Boundiali solar project which came online in
April 2024
Several other large-scale solar sites are under development, including the
52 MW M’Bengue
solar facility and
50 MW Bondoukou
solar plant.
The Ivory Coast is working towards a target of increasing the share of renewables in its energy mix to 46.3% by 2035. The target includes increasing solar capacity to more than 1.3 GW by the same year.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has tracked 723.4 MW of operational solar in the Ivory Coast, according to figures available in its project database, the majority of which is listed as unidentified commercial and industrial projects. The database lists a further 144.1 MW of solar as under construction.

title: Saft opens solid-state battery production line in France - pv magazine Global
content:
French battery manufacturer Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies, has inaugurated its first solid-state battery production line at its Bordeaux facility in southwestern France. The company says it is the first French manufacturer with development and production capabilities for solid-electrolyte batteries combining sulfide and polymer technologies at room temperature.
Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, which use a liquid electrolyte, solid-state batteries rely on a solid electrolyte. The technology promises improved safety and energy density up to 50% higher than conventional lithium-ion batteries, according to Saft.
Solid-state batteries may also offer manufacturing and environmental benefits. Some processes, including dry coating, can reduce energy consumption, while eliminating solvents can lower the environmental impact of production. Saft says these manufacturing methods can cut carbon dioxide emissions by up to 40% during this stage of the process.
Saft intends to use the new line to support electrification and decarbonization in the aviation and space sectors, where battery safety, performance and energy density are critical. The company aims to address a range of requirements through several electrochemical technologies.
In aviation, Saft has already delivered semi-solid battery cells for evaluating future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. The company sees solid-state batteries as a potentially important technology for the gradual electrification of air transport. The space sector is also a potential market, given its requirements for high energy density and enhanced safety.
Solid-state batteries could also find applications in stationary energy storage, provided they meet the technical and economic requirements of that market.

title: Uruguay plans 99 MW solar tender with 20-year PPAs - pv magazine Global
content:
Uruguay’s state-owned power utility, Administración Nacional de Usinas y Trasmisiones Eléctricas (UTE), plans to tender for electricity from three solar plants with a combined grid injection capacity of 99 MW under 20-year power purchase agreements.
UTE presented the preliminary terms of public tender P104220 at a technical event in Montevideo involving the Ministry of Industry, Energy and Mining. Tender documents are scheduled for publication on Oct. 28, 2026, with bids due to be opened in the final week of January 2027.
The tender comprises three independent projects, each with 33 MW of active power injection capacity at its grid connection point. This refers to the power delivered to the grid rather than necessarily the peak capacity of the installed PV modules.
The projects will be located in three designated areas. In Tacuarembó, connection options include the Chamberlain, Cuchilla Peralta A and Cuchilla Peralta B substations, all at 150 kV.
In Florida, options include the Pintado A, Pintado B, Colonia Sánchez, Florida and Durazno substations, with connections at 150 kV or 30 kV, depending on the site. The eastern region of the country offers connection points at Carapé, San Carlos, La Plata and Rocha, also at 150 kV or 30 kV.
Each plant’s connection point must be within 5 km of its selected grid node. Connection infrastructure must be dedicated to each project and independent of the other installations.
Bidders may submit offers for one, two or all three projects, with a single price offer for each. UTE will evaluate bids based on price and award each project independently, allowing one company to secure all three contracts.
UTE will purchase all electricity generated, along with the contracted power and ancillary services. Bid prices must include grid connection works, ancillary services and other contractual requirements.
The remuneration structure has two periods. During the first 15 years, payments will be based on the successful bidder’s offer price. For the final five years, remuneration will be based on 40% of that price.
Prices will be denominated in dollars per megawatt-hour and adjusted annually in January. During the first 15 years, the indexation formula assigns a 60% weighting to a fixed component, 12% to the US producer price index, and 28% to Uruguay’s domestic producer price index and exchange-rate movements.
For the final five years, the formula will apply to 40% of the original bid price, with weightings of 30% for the US index and 70% for the Uruguayan indicator adjusted for exchange-rate movements.
The tender also provides for compensation at the contractual price for electricity that cannot be supplied because of grid operating restrictions.
Technical requirements include reactive power services, including Q at Night, which allows solar plants to contribute to grid voltage control at night when they are not generating electricity. UTE will permit only solar PV technology and prohibit battery energy storage systems (BESS).
The plants must be installed within two years. UTE will manage the easements, rights of way and other land requirements for grid connections, although generators will be responsible for the associated compensation payments.
The tender requires a bid maintenance deposit of $300,000 per project. The performance guarantee will be calculated as 1% of estimated annual potential revenue over half the supply period, using a capacity utilization factor of 0.26. The good execution guarantee will equal four times that amount, while the guarantee required under subcontracting legislation will match the performance guarantee.
The tender also sets domestic participation requirements. At least 80% of the workforce must be national, including Uruguayan citizens and residents. Half of that share must comprise women, people older than 50, or young people younger than 24.
The tender assigns 65 points to a domestic goods component, based on a list that includes goods and uniforms for construction personnel. UTE said the Ministry of Industry, Energy and Mining must approve the final methodology, which will be communicated through a circular.
The tender forms part of Uruguay’s plan to add around 500 MW of solar capacity during the current five-year period.
In August, UTE received 10 bids to build a 30 MW solar plant in Fray Bentos, in the Río Negro department. The project will use 48,300 PV modules and requires an estimated investment of $20 million.
UTE is also developing a 100 MW solar plant in Melo, in the Cerro Largo department. The project will use approximately 140,000 modules and requires an investment of more than $75 million, with operations scheduled to begin in 2028.
At the end of August, UTE also confirmed a new solar plant in Baygorria, in the Durazno department, after objections to the original site led the utility to relocate its initial 30 MW project to Fray Bentos. UTE has yet to disclose the new plant’s capacity or construction schedule.
Unlike these initiatives, in which UTE directly develops the plants, tender P104220 will procure electricity from solar projects developed by private companies under long-term supply contracts.
Final participation, construction, grid connection and remuneration requirements will be established in the tender documents and subsequent circulars published by UTE.

title: Solar module manufacturing in Europe: Ideal factory capacity ranges from 1 GW to 3 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Global solar supply chains are undergoing a profound transformation, driven by growing protectionism and industrial policies aimed at supporting domestic manufacturing. This is the key takeaway from an interview with
pv magazine
featuring Laura Sartore, CEO of Ecoprogetti, an Italian company specializing in machinery and production lines for solar module manufacturing.
According to Sartore, this trend is increasingly evident across major international markets. “All the world’s primary supply chains, with the exception of China’s, are shifting toward a form of protectionism and price floors,” she said, citing the United States as one of the most prominent examples.
pv magazine Session @ NetZero Milan Expo Summit 2026
The dynamics shaping global PV supply chains – including solar modules, inverters, and battery energy storage systems – will be discussed during the “
Decoding solar supply chains
” session at the NetZero event in Milan on Oct. 21.
The session will examine the forces reshaping clean energy supply chains, from manufacturing and sourcing strategies to shifting trade and regulatory requirements. It will also explore what these developments mean for companies procuring solar and energy storage equipment in an increasingly complex global market.
Join us in Milan to hear from industry experts and take part in the discussion on the future of solar supply chains.
The US market shows that introducing minimum price thresholds, even above the prices charged by Chinese manufacturers, does not necessarily slow demand. On the contrary, according to Sartore, the sector continues to grow despite rising component costs, supported by the development of a domestic supply chain.
In China, prices are also gradually rising across the supply chain following government efforts to curb overcapacity, a trend that was expected to continue into 2025. According to Sartore, this shift reflects a growing focus on the economic viability of manufacturing in a market where solar technology has already firmly established its competitiveness against other energy sources.
India: An industrial policy covering the entire supply chain
Among international markets, Sartore identifies India as one of the most compelling examples of industrial policy in the solar sector.
The Indian government is progressively expanding protectionist measures and domestic manufacturing requirements beyond modules to include cells, wafers and ingots, aiming to reduce dependence on Chinese imports and strengthen local production capacity.
“In my view, India has the most serious industrial policy. They have observed Europe’s mistakes, and they continue to monitor developments in the United States,” Sartore said, highlighting the clear industrial strategy pursued by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.
A key element of this strategy is industry consolidation. Production capacity exceeding domestic demand is not necessarily seen as a problem. Instead, it can encourage mergers and direct investment toward segments of the supply chain that remain underdeveloped.
“The days of small-scale factories with a capacity of 200–500 MW are over; we are now seeing multi-gigawatt-scale facilities. And that is how it had to be—that is the only way forward for a continent-sized nation like India,” Sartore said.
This consolidation is helping create larger, more financially robust manufacturers capable of investing not only in solar cell and module production but also in the materials and components needed for manufacturing, including glass, encapsulants, backsheets and junction boxes.
According to Sartore, India now has the most comprehensive solar manufacturing supply chain outside China. However, domestic polysilicon production, a technically complex industrial process, remains underdeveloped.
“It will certainly be more challenging, because, beyond the raw material extraction phase, polysilicon production requires specialized technological expertise, capital-intensive facilities, and competitive access to energy. These industrial capabilities are currently lacking and must be developed and solidified; yet, India possesses the potential to scale them up,” Sartore explained.
Beyond technical expertise and investment, the environmental impact of manufacturing presents another challenge. Sartore stressed that developing a domestic polysilicon supply chain must also account for emissions from industrial processes.
“As India develops its polysilicon production, it must aim for high environmental standards and low-emission processes from the very outset. It is not enough to simply replicate production capacity—as seen in China—without prioritizing emissions; the goal must be to build an industrial supply chain that is competitive in terms of both energy efficiency and environmental impact,” Sartore added, noting that these requirements could lengthen the timeline for developing India’s domestic supply chain.
Europe: The medium-sized manufacturing model should not be abandoned
While India and the United States are focusing on large-scale factories and highly integrated supply chains, Sartore advocates a different approach for Europe.
She argues that Europe’s industrial model cannot be assessed using the same criteria as those applied in the United States or Asia. The continent’s manufacturing sector has historically been built around small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), industrial clusters and networks of specialized manufacturers.
“In Europe, we lack the ‘gigafactory’ or ‘mega-factory’ structure seen in India or the United States. Historically, our industrial fabric has been composed of small and medium-sized enterprises, across all sectors and fields,” she said.
Sartore points to Italy and Germany, where numerous industries have achieved international leadership through networks of relatively small but highly competitive companies.
According to Sartore, Europe’s solar manufacturing sector should build on this strength rather than attempt to replicate production models dominated by a handful of large manufacturers.
“The European multi-factory, network-based model is one that should not be abandoned,” she said.
However, this does not mean that small module assembly lines can remain competitive regardless of their production capacity. Manufacturers need to achieve a minimum production scale and invest in adequate levels of technology and automation to justify Capex and maintain competitive costs.
“A scale of 800 MW to 1 GW is the minimum threshold—necessary to make an investment sustainable—otherwise, the Capex burden becomes too heavy, making it impossible to reach competitive module price points,” Sartore explained.
Optimal production scale
Factory size is a key factor in the future of European solar module manufacturing.
According to Sartore, a production capacity of 1 GW to 3 GW offers an optimal balance between economies of scale, financial viability and operational complexity.
“A capacity of 1 to 3 GW is manageable,” she said, explaining that facilities of this size typically correspond to companies with annual revenue of €100 million ($112.2 million) to €200 million and approximately 150 to 300 employees.
Such companies are large enough to support industrial-scale manufacturing while remaining compatible with Europe’s existing industrial structure.
The challenge goes beyond the initial capital investment required to build a factory. Once production begins, manufacturers face substantial operating costs, particularly for raw material procurement.
Although increasing production capacity initially reduces module production costs per unit, there is a point beyond which the financial burden of operating a larger facility can offset these savings.
“In the European context, the 1 GW to 3 GW range captures the benefits of economies of scale. Beyond 3 GW, additional management costs and financial charges come into play; these weigh on the bottom line and do not necessarily lead to lower raw material procurement costs,” Sartore said.
For a 5 GW factory, working capital requirements can become particularly significant. Procuring and managing large volumes of raw materials requires substantial credit lines, bank guarantees and careful financial planning. These costs must be weighed against potential economies of scale, as greater production capacity does not necessarily translate into lower unit costs. Larger facilities also face greater financial exposure if demand falls short of production capacity.
“In Europe, without supply chain integration, if I need to purchase 5 GW worth of raw materials, I require structured bank collateral. There are high costs for credit guarantees and interest on cash flow—all of which weigh on the purchase price of the raw materials and on the company itself—potentially making the resulting photovoltaic module no more cost-effective than one produced by a smaller-scale manufacturer,” she explained.
As a result, a larger factory does not necessarily have lower production costs than a medium-sized facility, particularly when financing expenses and operating overheads are taken into account.
For medium-sized European manufacturers, a more moderate production scale can help limit financial exposure and make working capital requirements easier to manage, particularly given the financing conditions in Europe’s banking sector.
Flexible production for the European market
Production capacity should also reflect the characteristics of market demand.
According to Sartore, Europe’s solar market has a more fragmented structure than other major international markets, with projects generally smaller than gigawatt-scale installations and manufacturers required to handle a wider range of order sizes.
European solar projects often range from a few megawatts to several tens of megawatts, while installations approaching or exceeding 1 GW remain relatively rare.
Sartore argues that this further supports the development of a network of manufacturers capable of adapting production to individual customer requirements.
“There won’t be many gigawatt-scale solar power plant projects in Europe,” Sartore said. “The European market is defined by diverse requirements and local conditions, making the development of numerous medium-to-large-scale plants more likely than the creation of a large number of mega-installations.”
Production flexibility therefore becomes a key competitive factor alongside manufacturing costs and supply chain capabilities.
According to Sartore, this model is better suited to Europe’s industrial structure and the specific characteristics of its solar market.

title: Italy allocates €770 million for 505 MW of agricultural rooftop solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Italy has allocated all available funding under the latest round of its Agrisolare scheme, awarding €770.4 million in grants to 7,409 projects for approximately 505 MW of rooftop solar capacity on agricultural, livestock and agro-industrial buildings.
The Gestore dei Servizi Energetici (GSE), Italy’s energy services manager, published the list of approved projects under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) measure, which implements a decree issued by the Ministry of Agriculture on Dec. 17, 2025.
Three additional lists published by GSE show that 1,863 eligible applications were not funded because the budget had been exhausted. These applications represent €187.3 million in requested grants and approximately 170 MW of solar capacity.
A further 7,610 applications were deemed ineligible, representing €775.4 million in requested grants. Another 37 applicants withdrew, accounting for €3.9 million.
In total, the scheme received 16,919 applications seeking approximately €1.74 billion in grants — more than twice the amount awarded. Around 45% of applications failed the eligibility checks, and the value of grants sought by ineligible applicants exceeded the amount allocated to successful projects.
In May, Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida told the Senate that approximately 16,000 businesses had applied, with around 8,000 expected to receive funding in an initial phase. He said the government hoped to find additional resources for the remaining applicants.
Lombardy received the largest allocation, with 884 projects awarded €145.2 million, representing 18.8% of the total funding, for 92 MW of solar capacity. Veneto followed with 735 projects and €99.5 million, while Emilia-Romagna received €84.6 million across 633 projects. Piedmont had 664 projects awarded €72.5 million.
Sicily was the leading region in southern Italy, with 617 projects and €58.3 million in grants, followed by Puglia with €55.1 million and Campania with €48.9 million.
The largest individual grant, at €1.54 million, went to Società agricola Dossi di Franguelli Eugenio & C. in Costa de’ Nobili, in the province of Pavia, for an 847 kW installation. A pig farm in Roncade, in the province of Treviso, received €1.38 million for a 764 kW system, while a poultry farm in Scandolara Ravara, in the province of Cremona, was awarded €1.24 million for a system of approximately 1 MW.
The average grant was approximately €1,500 per kW of solar capacity.
Applications were submitted through the GSE platform between March 10 and April 9, 2026. Successful applicants have 18 months from the grant award to complete construction, subject to justified extensions. Final reporting must be completed by Dec. 31, 2028.
The earlier version of the Agrisolare scheme approved approximately 23,000 projects representing 1.7 GW of solar capacity.

title: Dominican Republic to introduce grid usage fee for distributed PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Dominican Republic’s national utility Edesur has announced that it will introduce a new billing charge for certain customers with rooftop solar installations in the Dominican Republic from Nov. 1, 2026, under the country’s distributed generation regulations.
According to a notice sent by the utility to its self-generation customers, the measure will initially apply to those who joined the net metering program before October 2021 and are subject to the BTS-1 and BTS-2 low-voltage tariffs, which cover residential and commercial electricity consumers, respectively.
The change is based on Resolution SIE-007-2026-REG, issued by the Superintendency of Electricity (SIE) in January 2026. Article 19(1)(e) of the resolution establishes a distribution network usage charge for customers on single-part electricity tariffs.
The charge will be calculated by multiplying the electricity injected into the grid, measured in kWh, by 25% of the energy component of the customer’s applicable tariff. It therefore does not represent a 25% increase in the total electricity bill or a charge on all electricity generated by the PV installation. Instead, it applies only to electricity exported to the grid.
Affected customers will continue to pay their usual fixed charges and electricity consumption charges, with the new distribution network usage fee added to their bills.
The new charge follows earlier regulatory measures introduced in 2026. Under Resolution SIE-103-2026-TF, the SIE established distribution network usage charges for distributed generation customers served by Edesur, Edenorte and Edeeste for the April-to-September period.
However, the scope of Edesur’s announcement must also be considered in light of the transitional provisions established by the regulator.
When introducing the new regulations in January, the SIE stated that existing interconnection contracts would retain their terms until their expiration. It also indicated that the network usage charge would apply to new installations with demand below 10 kW and to existing installations once their contracts expire.
As a result, enrollment in the net metering program before October 2021 does not necessarily mean that all contracts in that category have expired. Edesur’s announcement does not specify how many customers will be affected or provide details of the contractual conditions determining their inclusion.
The new distributed generation regulations, introduced in February 2026, also reduce the maximum approval period for installations to 45 days and eliminate the previous 15% PV penetration limit per distribution circuit. They also introduce changes to the compensation mechanism for accumulated annual energy credits.
According to the SIE, the network usage charge is intended to account for the costs of maintaining electricity distribution infrastructure used by distributed generation customers and support the financial sustainability of the electricity system.

title: Non-destructive testing tracks polymer degradation in PV modules - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team in Germany has investigated whether compressive stress relaxation measurement (CSRM) can be used to monitor polymer degradation in aging photovoltaic modules. The technique is typically used in manufacturing quality control to assess the degree of encapsulant cross-linking after lamination.
“This publication uses the CSRM not only for lamination control, but also to monitor the mechanical response of the mini-modules’ rear side,” the researchers explained. “To achieve a higher resolution and sample throughput, the cross-linking density will be used to calibrate the CSRM. The influence of encapsulants and backsheet degradation on the CSRM during weathering is of interest. Therefore, the degradation of the encapsulant and the backsheet will be decoupled.”
CSRM is a non-destructive technique commonly used to assess encapsulant curing after PV module lamination. It involves pressing a tip into the rear surface of a module and measuring how the force decreases while the indentation depth remains constant. The response reflects the mechanical properties of both the encapsulant and the backsheet.
To evaluate CSRM as a method for monitoring aging, the researchers fabricated 200 mm × 200 mm mini-modules incorporating passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) solar cells, ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulants, and polyethylene/polyethylene terephthalate (PET) backsheets. They varied lamination times at 155 C to achieve different degrees of cross-linking.
For each CSRM measurement, they heated the test location to 89 C, pressed a 4 mm steel tip approximately 100 µm into the module’s rear surface, applied a force of less than 20 N, and recorded the decline in force while holding the tip in place.
The modules were subjected to damp heat (DH) testing at 85 C and 85% relative humidity for up to 3,500 hours, or combined heat and ultraviolet (UV) irradiation at 85 C, 60% relative humidity, and an irradiance of 227 W/m2 for up to 2,000 hours. At 250-hour intervals, the team used CSRM to monitor mechanical changes and measured the modules’ electrical performance. Additional solvent tests and thermal analyses helped distinguish changes in encapsulant cross-linking from backsheet degradation.
“After the first 250 h of the DH test, the encapsulants showed an increase in the degree of cross-linking but maintained differences between the samples throughout the test,” the researchers said. “As a result, the PV module power degradation correlated with the initial cross-linking state. By the end of the test, the encapsulant and the backsheet had degraded, resulting in a drop in the CSRM response.”
The results also showed that the encapsulant’s cross-linking density subsequently decreased, while the backsheet underwent post-crystallization and exhibited chain scission.
“The combined DH+UV weathering test caused post-cross-linking within the first 250 h, leading to leveling of the cross-linking states,” the researchers concluded. “The canceled chemical differences in the encapsulants became reflected in a similar module power degradation. Thus, overacceleration shall be avoided by all means to deliver realistic reliability predictions.”
The findings are presented in the study, “
Non-destructive monitoring of polymer degradation in PV modules by compressive stress relaxation measurement and implications for the PV module reliability
,” published in
Polymer Testing
. The research team included scientists from Germany’s
Anhalt University of Applied Sciences
Fraunhofer CSP

title: JinkoSolar unveils 510 W rooftop solar module with 25.5% efficiency, 40-year warranty - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese solar module manufacturer JinkoSolar has unveiled a 510 W all-black residential solar panel based on its newly introduced
TOPCon-based Amorphous-Si Passivating Cell (TAC) technology
, which combines TOPCon electron-selective contacts, amorphous silicon heterojunction passivation and a back-contact electrode architecture.
The JKM485–510T series targets premium residential applications, including villas and homes with limited rooftop space, where power density, aesthetics and long-term reliability are key considerations.
The company said the 48-cell Tiger Neo 5.0 module has a maximum power conversion efficiency of 25.52% and a monofacial, dual-glass design. It measures 1,762 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm, weighs 22 kg and offers a maximum power density of approximately 255 W/m².
JinkoSolar said it has integrated several technologies to increase module power density and improve aesthetics. Its Gapless Cell Array (GCA) technology eliminates conventional gaps between cells, while concealed interconnections and busbars reduce inactive areas. According to the company, the design increases the effective light-receiving area by approximately 2%, resulting in an additional 10 W of module output.
The module also features Uniform Matrix Interconnection (UMI) technology, which replaces conventional printed main busbars with distributed electrical connections. JinkoSolar said the architecture shortens current paths, reduces resistive losses and enables interconnection processes that place less mechanical stress on the cells.
For improved aesthetics, the manufacturer has incorporated its All Consistent Color (ACC) technology, which combines precise control of coating thickness and refractive index with AI-assisted cell sorting. The process is designed to minimize visible color variations between cells, encapsulation materials and the frame, resulting in a more uniform black appearance.
The panel also uses Full-Spectrum Light Trapping (FLT) technology, combining surface texturing, antireflective coatings and rear-side reflection to improve light utilization under oblique sunlight and low-irradiance conditions.
The module features a power temperature coefficient of -0.24%/C, compared with approximately -0.26%/C for JinkoSolar’s previous TOPCon products. The manufacturer also claims the new panel delivers around 30 W more power than conventional back-contact modules of comparable dimensions.
For reliability, JinkoSolar has integrated a Perimeter Moisture Barrier (PMB) featuring butyl-based edge sealing to reduce moisture ingress and the associated risk of corrosion. The module also incorporates an optimized current-shunting design intended to limit power losses and reduce hot-spot risks under partial shading.
JinkoSolar offers a 40-year product warranty and a 40-year linear power output warranty for the module, according to its technical documentation.
“Our vision for Tiger Neo 5.0 was to develop a panel tailored to premium residential rooftops,” said JinkoSolar CEO Charlie Cao.
The new residential panel expands JinkoSolar’s Tiger Neo 5.0 portfolio, which includes larger-format TOPCon modules introduced in June 2026, with power outputs exceeding 700 W and efficiencies of up to 25.91%.
JinkoSolar has identified Europe and Australia as target markets for residential applications. The company has not yet disclosed commercial availability, pricing or production volumes for the new TAC-based module.

title: China proposes stricter efficiency standards for solar manufacturers - pv magazine Global
content:
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has proposed stricter efficiency requirements for photovoltaic manufacturers, raising minimum average conversion efficiencies for solar cells and modules and introducing separate thresholds for TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and back-contact (BC) technologies.
The draft 2026 Photovoltaic Manufacturing Industry Specifications, released for public consultation on Oct. 16 alongside proposed revisions to the system for listing compliant manufacturers, would replace the 2024 rules. The consultation period runs until Nov. 15.
For new and expanded solar cell production lines, the proposed minimum average conversion efficiencies are 26.2% for n-type TOPCon, 26.0% for HJT and 26.6% for BC technologies. The 2024 rules set a uniform 26.0% threshold for new n-type cells. Existing production lines would need to achieve efficiencies of at least 25.3% for TOPCon and HJT and 25.6% for BC, compared with the previous 25.0% requirement for n-type cells.
For new and expanded module production, the proposed minimum efficiencies are 24.2% for TOPCon, 24.0% for HJT and 24.4% for BC, up from a uniform 23.1% threshold for n-type modules under the 2024 rules. Existing module production would face minimum efficiency requirements of 23.4% for TOPCon and HJT and 23.7% for BC. All thresholds refer to average conversion efficiency, with bifacial modules assessed on front-side performance.
The draft also removes separate performance categories for multicrystalline and p-type crystalline silicon products while introducing requirements for emerging photovoltaic technologies. New tandem solar modules would need to achieve at least 27% efficiency, compared with 25% for existing tandem modules. New perovskite modules would face a minimum efficiency threshold of 20%.
The proposed revisions would also tighten requirements for upstream manufacturing. New polysilicon projects using the trichlorosilane process would face a comprehensive electricity consumption limit of less than 37 kWh/kg, compared with the previous general polysilicon benchmark of 53 kWh/kg. The draft separately proposes a 15 kWh/kg ceiling for new silane fluidized-bed projects and limits water consumption at new polysilicon facilities to 30 cubic meters per metric ton.
Manufacturers would continue to be required to spend at least 3% of annual sales on research, development and process improvements, but the minimum absolute expenditure would double to CNY 20 million ($2.94 million), from CNY 10 million. The existing minimum equity-capital ratio of 30% for new and expanded projects would remain unchanged.
The proposal also introduces a maximum degradation limit of 8.6% under combined environmental stress testing for crystalline silicon modules. It would strengthen oversight of manufacturers included on MIIT’s published compliance list through regular reviews and the removal of companies that no longer meet the requirements. Industry self-regulation would also be considered when evaluating applications.
MIIT states that the specifications are guidance rather than mandatory conditions for administrative approval. Their impact on investment decisions and efforts to reduce excess manufacturing capacity would therefore depend partly on how local authorities, financial institutions and industry participants apply the compliance criteria.
The proposed manufacturing standards were released on the same day that China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to a catalogue of restricted or prohibited technology exports. Under the separate proposal, exports of certain advanced perovskite and tandem manufacturing technologies would be prohibited.
The proposed export-control revisions are also subject to public consultation, although a temporary pre-export registration requirement for the listed technologies has already taken effect. The measures target technology transfers and certain associated equipment rather than imposing a blanket ban on solar product exports.
Together, the proposals signal increased government scrutiny of domestic photovoltaic manufacturing standards and the overseas transfer of advanced production technologies. Whether the revised efficiency requirements accelerate the phaseout of excess manufacturing capacity will depend on their final wording and implementation.

title: Holosolis secures EU Innovation Fund support for 5 GW solar factory - pv magazine Global
content:
French solar manufacturer
Holosolis
has been selected for funding under the EU Innovation Fund for its Solar4EU project, which aims to establish an integrated 5 GW solar cell and module manufacturing facility in Hambach, France.
The company is advancing plans to begin production in 2027, with a gradual ramp-up to full capacity by 2030. The project has already secured more than €220 million in initial financing, including €200 million through France’s C3IV tax credit scheme. Holosolis has also brought in Chinese solar manufacturer Trina Solar as a strategic technology partner.
Solar4EU is among 12 clean-tech manufacturing projects selected under the latest Innovation Fund call. Together, the projects are requesting almost €895 million ($1.05 billion) in support for manufacturing facilities covering solar modules, heat pumps, electrolysers, electric-vehicle batteries and rare-earth permanent magnets.
Other solar-related projects include Belgium’s ReGAIN Pilot, which aims to establish a circular production line for reusable germanium substrates for solar panels.
Battery manufacturing projects selected for funding include PowerCo Spain, which plans to develop a gigafactory for prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for electric vehicles, and Poland’s ArisEU project, which aims to establish a 9 GWh LFP battery cell manufacturing facility.
The European Commission has selected 77 net-zero technology projects to receive €3.4 billion ($3.98 billion) under the Innovation Fund, financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS).
The selected projects span 23 European Economic Area countries and cover industrial decarbonisation, renewable energy, energy storage, clean-tech manufacturing, low-carbon mobility, critical raw materials and carbon management.
According to the Commission, the projects could avoid approximately 290 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent during their first 10 years of operation.
The selected projects will now enter grant agreement preparations with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). The Commission expects the process to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.
