title: The rapidly growing business of solar grazing - pv magazine Global
content:
The business of solar grazing, using animals to manage vegetation at solar sites, has taken off in along with the growth of solar in the U.S. According to Stacie Peterson, executive director of the American Solar Grazing Association (ASGA), solar grazing became a business in 2018. This was one year before the U.S. achieved two million solar installations.
United States Solar Grazing 2024 Census
was the first to attempt to capture the full scope and scale of U.S. solar grazing. Conducted by ASGA in conjunction with U.S. Department of Energy National Lab of the Rockies (NREL), the census found that over 113,000 sheep grazed through fields of solar panels on 129,000 acres of land. The 2025 census has not yet been released, but Peterson told
pv magazine USA
that she believes the numbers have greatly increased.
The ASGA Solar Grazing Map is a resource for solar grazers and solar site operators and developers to connect with each other and build partnerships. Credit: American Solar Grazing Association
What solar grazers bring to solar sites is expertise in agriculture, land stewardship, vegetation management, soil health knowledge and forage and weed knowledge, according to Peterson. Graziers provide additional benefits to solar developers or owners including their connections within the local community and their deep understanding of the land.
Having a regular physical presence at the site is another plus, which Rebekah Pierce, solar grazer and owner of New York-based J&R Pierce Family Farms said has great value to O&M teams. “It’s hard to quantify on paper what being on site means to the O&M team, but we’re there every other day. If we see an issue that needs to be addressed like a loose wire or a hole in a fence, we let them know and that issue is addressed.”
While most solar grazing is done with sheep, J&R Pierce Family Farm raises cows as well as sheep. Pierce proposed a cattle-grazing pilot to Nexamp, a solar developer that grazed livestock at 89 sites this past season across five states for a total of almost 2,000 acres, according to Keith Hevenor, communications manager.
“We began our grazing program in 2019 with just one site and have been expanding significantly each year since,” Hevenor said. “We are looking forward to even more progress next year and love that our grazing partners are able to continue an agricultural application on these solar farms while providing a necessary service for us in a safer and more sustainable way.”
The cow pilot began last summer on two of Nexamp’s solar sites in Fort Covington, New York. Five cattle, including one bull, grazed among the solar modules mounted on trackers, and it was a success with the cows showing “no unusual behavior,” according to Pierce. She said that sheep remain the most flexible option for solar sites, especially those that were not designed for grazing larger animals. Pierce noted, however, that grazing cattle is worth consideration, especially when looking at market potential and the fact that Americans consume far more beef than lamb.
J&R Pierce Family Farm grazed cattle on two of Nexamp’s solar projects in New York state. Credit: J&R Pierce Family Farm
The arrangement between the solar grazer and the developer are different depending on region and for different graziers, Peterson said. In addition to signing an agreement that works for both parties, Pierce stressed that communication is key, so it’s important to have a connection with the right person in the company, especially in light of the fact that solar projects are commonly acquired and new people take the helm.
Many times, enhancing communication requires dispelling misconceptions. Pierce said that in most cases, livestock are less risky than mechanical mowers and other farm equipment. She said sheep don’t chew on wires and damage things, they don’t kick up rocks, they’re not creating fire risk. These misconceptions, she said, just aren’t true and the benefits are many.
A main challenge for both parties is in educating one another about priorities and how they can work together successfully.
“The more corporate world of solar companies can be quite the dichotomy from the one of farmers/ranchers, and vice versa,” said Matt Kovarik of Maine-based Black Earth Grazing. “Once we both do a little work of educating each other on our systems, the partnership can serve both interests and work out quite successfully.”
ReVision Energy, a renewable energy contracting company based in New England, has partnered since 2024 with Black Earth Grazing on a dual-management solar grazing program. It’s been so successful that the farmers changed the name from Black Earth Forest Farm to Black Earth Grazing. They started with 40 ewes and now manage a flock of several hundred. They’re currently responsible for 11 of ReVision’s community solar sites, and the flock keeps growing as more solar sites become available.
The many benefits of solar grazing for solar companies include vegetation management that requires fewer fossil fuels than mechanical methods, a human presence on site and a connection to local graziers who provide products to the community pay taxes, support local services and more.
“We are there to provide vegetation management, but we are a bit more invested in the land and its productivity than a mowing crew would be, as we are deriving benefits from a healthy well-managed pasture that feeds our sheep,” said .
For the grazier, the benefits include the pay they receive for performing land stewardship and vegetation management and access to a greater land area that enables them to expand the size of their operations.
Solar grazing offers a cost-effective solution to land stewardship and vegetation management, with many other tangible benefits as a bonus. For solar developers interested in solar grazing, ASGA offers a
one-day workshop
for site operations and management teams, developers, asset managers and sustainability teams. Participants receive a Level 1 Solar Grazing Management Certification.
Register for
pv magazine USA week
to learn more about solar grazing October 22 in a keynote fireside chat with Silicon Ranch, one of the leading solar grazing installers in the U.S.

title: A 50-Year-Old Mystery: Scientists Discover What May Have Killed Brazil’s Frogs
content:
A wild clay robber frog (Haddadus binotatus) seen near the Boracéia Biological Station, São Paulo, Brazil. Credit: Jack Boyette, Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
Museum specimens are helping scientists trace a deadly fungus linked to mysterious frog disappearances in Brazil nearly half a century ago.
Frog species that escaped a wave of population declines in Brazil carried widespread infections with a deadly fungus. Yet museum specimens from the species that suffered the steepest losses showed no detectable infection.
These findings come from an investigation that points to amphibian chytridiomycosis, commonly called chytrid, as the likely cause of die-offs at Boracéia Biological Station between 1979 and 1982.
Caused by the microscopic fungus
Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
, the disease can have very different consequences for different species. Scientists at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU) reported their findings in
Molecular Ecology
The preserved amphibians came from collections made at Boracéia by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles, and held at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History. The researchers suspect that differences in susceptibility could explain why the species hit hardest left no detectable infections in the specimens available for testing.
“It’s important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia,” said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the study. “The species that didn’t decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them.”
The timing points to chytrid
Comparing collection dates revealed a different pattern. Tests detected no chytrid infection in specimens collected before 1979, whereas more than half of those collected during the 1980s tested positive. Evidence of the fungus therefore appeared around the period when amphibians were disappearing.
The comparison covered more than 370 museum specimens representing 17 species. Heyer had collected them during five field campaigns, two in the 1970s before the sudden declines and three in the 1980s afterward. That record allowed the NZCBI researchers to investigate both the pathogen’s arrival and changes in how commonly it infected amphibians.
Climate change and extreme weather had previously been proposed as explanations for Boracéia’s losses.
“While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances,” Boyette said.
The infection timeline, considered alongside the differences among species, suggests that the fungus spread rapidly through a community of amphibians that had not previously encountered it. Establishing such a history is difficult when the suspected pathogen was unknown at the time of the deaths.
Researchers began observing drastic amphibian declines across Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, a global hotspot of frog biodiversity, in the 1970s. Chytrid is believed to have originated in Asia and likely spread worldwide during the 1970s and 1980s, but scientists did not formally describe the fungus until 1999. By then, catastrophic population losses had pushed hundreds of amphibian species around the world to the brink of extinction or beyond.
“After almost 50 years, we still aren’t confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology,” Boyette said.
Signs of recovery despite persistent chytrid
To see how Boracéia’s amphibians were faring decades later, the team made six visits between 2022 and 2024, working with researchers from the University of São Paulo. They located 12 of the 17 species represented in Heyer’s collection. The other five remain unaccounted for. Their absence raises the possibility that they have disappeared locally, although their fate is still uncertain.
Most amphibian species at the station now appear to have recovered since the early 1980s, despite continued chytrid infections. The researchers interpret modern infection patterns as evidence that widespread tolerance has evolved among species that previously declined, likely helping them persist and recover. DNA collected from museum samples is now being used to investigate the genomic mechanisms that shaped these amphibians’ historical responses to the fungus.
Filling gaps in chytrid’s history
Boracéia provides evidence from one site, and the researchers caution against extending its findings to the Atlantic Forest as a whole. The approach nevertheless offers a model for investigating other historical outbreaks, particularly those that unfolded before scientists recognized the disease involved.
“Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery,” said Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who participated in the study.
Other ongoing projects aim to fill gaps in historical specimen records using ancient environmental DNA, genetic material preserved in the environment. Together with research on museum samples, these efforts seek to reconstruct chytrid’s emergence, spread, and effects over the past century, building a clearer picture of its toll on biodiversity.
Reconstructing past outbreaks may also help researchers anticipate the consequences of emerging fungal threats. Another pathogen,
B. salamandrivorans
, is already threatening salamanders in Europe and could pose a serious risk to salamander populations in North America.

title: Scientists Solve a 30-Year Biological Mystery and the Discovery Could Change How We Treat Inflammation
content:
Tiny, transparent, fast-growing — zebrafish are an ideal model organism for studying some biological processes. Credit: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Scientists have solved a decades-old biological mystery, revealing an unexpected dual role for a key inflammatory signaling pathway.
Scientists have uncovered a surprising function of a molecule that controls inflammation: It not only recruits immune cells to fight infections but also helps protect healthy tissue from damage. The discovery, published October 7 in
, solves a biological mystery that puzzled researchers for more than 30 years.
The findings from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma.
An Unexpected Cause of Inflammation
The molecule, called 5-oxoETE, summons white blood cells to infection sites, where they attack harmful microorganisms.
“They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria,” says MSK cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD. “But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control.”
When researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD, disabled hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1), which allows cells to detect 5-oxoETE, the fish unexpectedly developed intestinal inflammation without an infection.
“So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you’d expect less inflammation, not more,” Dr. Lengyel says.
“It made absolutely no sense,” he says. “I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced.”
A Hidden Cellular Defense
Further experiments revealed that 5-oxoETE activates a protective process involving NUDIX hydrolases, enzymes that remove damaged DNA building blocks. Without this protection, intestinal cells became vulnerable to chemical stress from normal gut bacteria, leading to cell death and inflammation.
“As it turns out, this signal isn’t just an alarm, it’s also a shield,” Dr. Niethammer says.
“This makes sense when you think about it,” he adds. “These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time.”
Left to right: Zaza Gelashvili, Dr. Miklos Lengyel, Dr. Philipp Niethammer, and Dr. Yanan Ma Credit: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Solving a 30-Year Mystery
In a separate investigation, Yanan Ma, PhD, identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme that generates 5-oxoETE. Scientists had observed this enzyme’s activity in 1992 but had never identified its genetic source.
“Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally,” Dr. Niethammer says. “But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that’s extremely important to note.”
Zebrafish were crucial because mice lack a known immune cell receptor for 5-oxoETE.
“Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research,” Dr. Ma says. “It makes sense, they’re mammals, and there’s about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours.”
“This means that you can’t study the pathway in mice,” she explains. “But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds.”
Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Disease
Mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 have been identified in certain cancers, while disrupted 5-oxoETE signaling has also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease and asthma.
“More research is needed, but there’s a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress, which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy,” Dr. Lengyel says.
The researchers also connected the pathway to physical injuries. Mechanical stress releases arachidonic acid, a molecule used to produce 5-oxoETE.
“There’s a mechanical component to the pathway that’s upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying,” explains doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS. “You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal.”
“What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress, mechanical and metabolic, and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response,” Dr. Niethammer says.

title: Scientists Discover Exercise Changes the Body in Ways We Never Fully Understood
content:
Exercise affects far more than muscle, but its molecular effects vary across the body. By mapping changes across 22 tissues in mice, scientists uncovered a complex network of responses that could offer new insights into training, recovery, and long-term health. Credit: Shutterstock
Salk Institute researchers have created a molecular map of how healthy mice respond to exercise, offering clues that could help improve performance and reduce injury risk.
Exercise can help the body resist disease and dysfunction and recover from illness. Studies have also linked it to more than 30 percent lower mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Explaining those benefits is harder, partly because studies in people generally rely on blood and muscle samples, leaving researchers with an incomplete picture of how exercise changes other organs.
Researchers at the Salk Institute turned to mice to follow those changes through more of the body. They compared young male and female mice that ran voluntarily on a wheel for eight weeks with mice that remained sedentary, creating a first-of-its-kind molecular atlas spanning 22 tissues. The study was published in
on October 15, 2026.
No single gene responded everywhere
Exercise altered the activity of nearly half the genes examined in at least one tissue, yet no single gene’s activity changed in all 22. Those comparisons came from bulk RNA sequencing, which measures gene activity across whole tissue samples. Rather than revealing one response shared everywhere, the analysis showed that tissues adapted in different ways.
The researchers also cataloged the small molecules that cells use and produce during metabolism in eight tissues and plasma, the liquid part of blood. Alongside this metabolomics analysis, they used proteomics to measure protein levels in four specific leg muscles, examining a hamstring muscle, two calf muscles, and the quadriceps.
Manoj Hariharan (left), Geraldine Maier (center), and Ramesh Ramasamy (right) debuted a molecular atlas of exercise-associated changes in mice, defining the healthy, exercised-trained state, which could help improve performance and prevent injury. Credit: Salk Institute
“Exercise doesn’t just change our muscles, it changes many of our organs and cells at different levels—some short-term, some long-term,” says co-first and co-corresponding author Geraldine Maier, PhD, a staff scientist at Salk. “Our experimental setup allows us to capture that detail across tissues, and sexes, and in muscle, down to the individual cell types.”
Training changes DNA marks in muscle
Skeletal muscle accounted for most of the changes in gene activity, and the strong responses in leg muscles prompted the researchers to examine three of them more closely. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, they could distinguish neighboring cell types and compare their gene activity instead of averaging their responses together. They also conducted the first single-cell analysis of DNA methylation in muscle after exercise.
In some muscle cell types, training changed chemical marks on DNA that help regulate gene activity, while other cell types showed no such changes. These marks are added through a process called DNA methylation. Changes in their pattern can be more persistent than shifts in RNA or protein levels, allowing this form of epigenetic regulation to have lasting effects on how particular cell types and whole tissues behave.
“Exercise impacts the whole body, not just your muscles, so an atlas like ours that looks more holistically at many tissues is key to understanding the true impact of exercise,” says co-first author Manoj Hariharan, PhD, a former senior staff scientist at Salk. “That’s also why single-cell studies are so important—there are so many cell type-specific changes that get lost in bulk sequencing. I hope our work highlights that and encourages more single-cell atlases, and especially multi-omic single-cell atlases, moving forward.”
Exercise responses vary by sex and time
Female mice showed broader changes in gene activity and distinct expression patterns compared with males. The epigenetic response to training also differed strongly by sex.
To capture variation across daily biological rhythms, the researchers collected tissues during both the active and resting phases of the mice’s circadian cycle. Most tissues showed greater exercise-related changes when sampled during the active phase, with the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung as exceptions.
“Our atlas provides a comprehensive resource for understanding the systemic molecular adaptations to endurance exercise,” says co-first author Ramesh Ramasamy, PhD, a former computational biologist at Salk. “Now that we have all this data, researchers can begin developing strategies that harness exercise—either alone or in combination with other interventions—to ensure we all live long, healthy lives.”
51 genes distinguish trained muscle
The researchers have already used the gene activity dataset to develop a 51-gene exercise signature, a pattern that distinguishes exercise-trained muscle from sedentary muscle in both mice and humans. It could help identify biomarkers, measurable indicators of a biological state, and support research into muscle disuse and dysfunction.
“Now that we have the data,” adds Maier, “labs can identify one gene or metabolic pathway they find interesting, then dissect that mechanism. Our atlas gives the field a shared foundation to build on.”
How long those molecular changes last remains unresolved. Researchers still need to determine how long training must continue before lasting changes develop and whether cells retain a memory of exercise for months or years.

title: Scientists Unlock the Secret of One of the World’s Smallest Flowering Plants
content:
Duckweed is one of the smallest flowering plants in the world, forming tiny green fronds that float on the surface of freshwater ponds and lakes. Credit: Shutterstock
Tiny aquatic plants are attracting scientific attention for their untapped potential as future food sources, including for space missions.
Some of the world’s smallest flowering plants have found a way to fit the basic architecture of much larger species into a body just a few millimeters (about 0.1 inch) across. Researchers at the University of Nottingham discovered that duckweed retains essential structures found in larger plant shoots, but these components are tightly compressed and fused rather than lost.
Using advanced microscopy and gene expression analysis, the scientists examined how duckweed organizes its remarkably compact body. Their findings, published in
Current Biology
, challenge the assumption that extreme miniaturization necessarily involves losing parts of a plant’s original structure.
Duckweed on end of pencil. Credit: University of Nottingham
How Duckweed Shrinks Without Losing Its Blueprint
Dr. Anthony Bishopp, who led the research, explained: “We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space. While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.”
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there. Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant. That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Tiny Plants With Potential for Future Food Production
Despite their miniature size, duckweeds belong to a group of flowering plants whose relatives include some of the largest herbaceous species. Scientists are increasingly investigating duckweed as a potential source of food and protein, both on Earth and during future space missions.
Unlike major agricultural crops, which have undergone thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, duckweed remains largely unexplored as a cultivated food source. Its unusual anatomy has also been poorly understood, making it difficult to fully explain how the plant grows and develops. The new findings provide a foundation for investigating these processes and identifying traits that could eventually be improved for cultivation.
Dr. Alex Ware, a co-author of the study, said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case. Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”
Reference: “Miniaturization of duckweeds occurred through compression of the angiosperm body plan” by Alexander Ware, Emily Chan, Rahul Bhosale and Anthony Bishopp, 7 October 2026,
Current Biology

title: Antarctica’s Sea Ice Has Gone From Record Highs to Near-Record Lows
content:
Antarctic sea ice reached its annual maximum extent on September 14, 2026—the third-lowest maximum in the satellite record. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
Antarctica’s sea ice has plunged from record highs to its third-lowest winter peak, revealing a dramatic reversal in the frozen continent’s recent history.
Antarctic sea ice reached one of its lowest winter peaks ever recorded in 2026, continuing a striking shift in ice coverage around the frozen continent. Its annual maximum was the third lowest since satellites began tracking sea ice in the late 1970s.
Antarctica and the Arctic have very different geographies. The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, while Antarctica is a massive continent encircled by ocean. This allows Antarctic sea ice to spread across a much larger area during winter. However, as the ice extends into warmer waters farther from the continent, it becomes more vulnerable to melting when summer arrives. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its greatest extent in September, near the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, before shrinking to its annual minimum in February.
NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) reported that Antarctic sea ice likely reached its annual maximum on September 14 (above). At its peak, the ice covered approximately 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles). That made 2026 the year with the third-lowest winter maximum in the satellite record.
Antarctic Sea Ice Shifts From Record Highs to Historic Lows
For decades, Antarctic sea ice appeared to be moving in the opposite direction of Arctic sea ice. Between 1979 and 2014, the total extent of Antarctic sea ice grew by approximately 1 percent per decade. However, scientists remain uncertain whether this increase reflected a significant underlying trend, since ice coverage around Antarctica can fluctuate substantially from one year to the next.
The growth was particularly notable between 2012 and 2014, when Antarctic winter sea ice set new records for three consecutive years. During the same period, Arctic sea ice was experiencing a steep decline.
That pattern changed dramatically after 2014. Antarctic sea ice stopped expanding in 2015, and substantial declines began appearing in 2016. Although ice coverage has occasionally recovered somewhat, it has generally remained below normal in the years since.
The most extreme conditions occurred in 2023, when Antarctica recorded both its lowest summer minimum and lowest winter maximum in the satellite record. Researchers are continuing to track these changes to determine whether the persistent decline represents a lasting transformation in Antarctic sea ice or could still be explained by statistical fluctuations.
How Satellites Monitor Antarctic Sea Ice Through Clouds
Scientists track the extent of Antarctic sea ice using satellites equipped with passive microwave sensors. These instruments detect microwave energy naturally released by Earth’s surface. Because frozen sea ice emits more microwave energy than open ocean water, researchers can distinguish between the two and calculate how much of the ocean is covered by ice.
One major advantage of this technology is its ability to detect sea ice through clouds. Unlike conventional optical imagery, microwave observations are not blocked by cloud cover, allowing scientists to monitor Antarctica’s frozen waters consistently even when weather conditions are poor.
The continuous satellite record began in late 1978 with measurements from NASA’s Nimbus-7. Observations later came from satellites operated under the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), beginning in 1987, and NASA’s Aqua satellite from 2002 through 2011.
In 2025, researchers began incorporating observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s GCOM-W satellite, helping maintain the long-running record of Antarctic sea ice changes.

title: The Amazon Is Burning Again, and NASA Warns the Worst Is Yet To Come
content:
A dangerous chain reaction of wildfires is unfolding across the tropics, and the Amazon rainforest is now caught in its path.
A dangerous El Niño-driven wildfire cascade has reached the Amazon, and NASA scientists warn that the worst may still be ahead as hidden fires spread beneath the rainforest canopy.
El Niño is fueling a chain reaction of wildfires across the tropics, with fires first emerging in equatorial Asia before spreading to the central and eastern Amazon rainforest.
While tornadoes and thunderstorms can cause widespread damage in a matter of minutes, El Niño influences weather conditions over the course of months. In 2026, the climate pattern has intensified drought across the Amazon, leaving vast areas of rainforest increasingly vulnerable to fire. Scientists warn that the region is only beginning what could become an unusually long and destructive fire season.
Satellite observations have revealed a dramatic increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon since September 2026. The surge is apparent in several monitoring systems, including NASA’s
Fire Information for Resource Management System
(FIRMS), the
Global Fire Emissions Database
(GFED), and
NASA Worldview
. The affected area extends from the forests surrounding Manaus and Santarém, two important commercial and transportation hubs, eastward toward the mouth of the Amazon River.
Thick Wildfire Smoke Blankets the Amazon
On October 12, 2026, NASA’s Aqua satellite captured an image showing enormous plumes of smoke rising from fires on both sides of the Amazon River. The image was recorded by MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), one of the satellite’s Earth-observing instruments.
That same day, Manaus, the capital of Brazil’s Amazonas state, was engulfed in dense smoke. City officials
reported
dangerously polluted air, with concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. That level placed air quality in the second-worst category of a regional
air quality index
The smoke brought significant disruptions to the city of more than 2 million residents. Schools shut down, public events were called off, and children’s sports leagues suspended activities as authorities issued warnings about unhealthy air conditions, according to
news reports
Scientists Warn of an El Niño Wildfire Cascade
According to Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, the fires around Manaus and Santarém are part of a much larger pattern. He describes it as a “cascade” of tropical wildfires driven by changes in rainfall associated with El Niño.
The sequence typically begins near the equator, where dry conditions contribute to
peat fires in Indonesia
. Increased burning then develops in the central and eastern Amazon. Morton and researchers from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland documented this connection in a
2017 study
examining the devastating wildfire season associated with the
2015–2016 El Niño
. A similar sequence occurred in 2023.
The wildfire activity unfolding in 2026 appears to be following that same progression. Since August, parts of Indonesia have experienced persistent drought, widespread fires, and heavy smoke. In October, wildfires
destroyed hundreds of homes
, while thick smoke
covered entire islands
on most days.
“Now, in the Amazon, we’re seeing the second domino in the cascade fall,” Morton said, referring to the growing number of fires in the Brazilian states of Pará and Amazonas.
More Amazon Wildfires Could Be Coming
Scientists expect the next phase of the wildfire cascade to develop farther north during November and December. Areas at risk include the Brazilian states of Roraima and Amapá, northern Pará, and parts of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.
The danger could then shift southward. Morton predicts that drought and wildfire risk will reach their highest levels in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay around August and September 2027.
“It’s so striking—and frustrating—that this is happening all over again,” said Morton.
One particularly troubling aspect is that many of the forests now burning were also damaged during the El Niño events of 2015 and 2023. Fire can be especially destructive in tropical rainforests because most native plants and animals have not evolved to withstand frequent burning.
Previous wildfires have also weakened parts of the forest, leaving behind damaged and partially charred trees. Morton explained that these changes make the remaining vegetation more vulnerable, potentially allowing some fires to burn with greater intensity than before.
For communities around Manaus and Santarém, relief may not arrive until seasonal rains return in December 2026 or January 2027. However, Morton emphasized that regions farther north and south still have an opportunity to reduce their risk.
“Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs,” Morton said.
Extreme Drought Turns Human-Started Fires Dangerous
Despite the enormous number of wildfires affecting the Amazon, lightning is responsible for very few of them. The Brazilian Amazon is normally so wet that lightning starts
less than 1 percent
of fires. According to Morton, human activity is responsible for the overwhelming majority of the fires currently burning there.
What makes 2026 especially dangerous is the severity of the drought, which has been intensified by El Niño. Brazil’s National Institute of Meteorology reported that rainfall in Manaus was 95 percent below normal in
and 60 percent below normal in
September
Many of the major fires began as controlled burns used to manage agricultural land, such as clearing unwanted vegetation from pastures or removing crop remnants from fields. But with the forest floor unusually dry, some of those fires escaped their intended boundaries and spread into the rainforest’s understory.
Shane Coffield, an assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland who works at NASA Goddard, said satellite analysis suggests that between 50 and 70 uncontrolled fires are currently burning in the Santarém area alone.
NASA Discovers Hidden Amazon Fires That Satellites Miss
The true extent of the burning may be even greater than official fire monitoring systems suggest.
Through a
NASA Earth Action project
, Coffield is examining observations from VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) to find fires that fall below the detection thresholds used for official FIRMS fire data.
These additional detections, referred to as “candidate fires,” could help researchers build a more complete picture of wildfire activity. Coffield intends to provide their locations to scientists at
MapBiomas
, a collaborative network of universities, nongovernmental organizations, and technology companies that tracks fires and changes in land use throughout the Amazon.
“For the area around Santarém, we’ve identified about 40 percent more fires than you’ll see in active fire counts from FIRMS,” said Coffield.
Detecting every fire from space is difficult, particularly in dense tropical forests. Heavy smoke, cloud cover, and thick tree canopies can interfere with satellite sensors by obscuring the infrared heat signals emitted by flames. Smaller, less intense fires moving through vegetation beneath the forest canopy are especially easy to overlook.
This means that some of the days with the thickest smoke can produce surprisingly few satellite fire detections, even when extensive burning is taking place.
“On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn’t right.”

title: OpenAI’s ‘Pacing 2.0’ Problem: How Smart Is Too Smart?
content: OpenAI is bound to get a reality check soon, if it hasn’t already, on how difficult it is to “pace” AI technology, let alone getting all the frontier AI developers to agree on how to do so together. CEO Sam Altman last week walked employees through three proposals the industry has discussed for how to safely develop AI, we reported yesterday. Those options included plans for developing an international organization akin to the International Atomic Energy Agency ; merging the frontier labs into a single entity that would develop, test and distribute models; or a scenario, however far-fetched, in which one lab races ahead of the others and literally crushes their GPUs, ending their ability to catch up. It goes without saying that each of those options has major issues. But we’ll say it anyway. An IAEA-esque organization would require international cooperation from countries developing state-of-the-art AI, including China, which likely is wary of slowing down development given the hostile feelings firms like Anthropic have expressed towards it. The second proposal, the “Demis plan,” named after DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis , would be similar to CERN , the physics lab jointly controlled by dozens of countries to pursue cutting edge research. But for now, joint efforts like that might be a tough sell, given that the leading AI developers are for-profit entities, each with different shareholders. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are currently pursuing a self-regulating body that, while much less ambitious than CERN, have already disagreed on important points, my colleague Leo and I reported last month. The third option, the Eliezer plan, named after LessWrong creator Eliezer Yudkowsky , is perhaps the most troubling, though people at OpenAI might jokingly say Anthropic is pursuing it. During Altman’s talk with his employees last week, he also said that OpenAI can’t afford to give up too much ground right now, but within the next year it will need to decide which long-term path to pursue. Altman refers to this decision as “pacing 2.0.” The current approach, “pacing 1.0,” refers to the continued release of frontier models that have passed certain safety tests, while still disclosing any safety concerns associated with the new models, the people who overheard his comments said. As part of pacing 2.0, OpenAI will also need to adopt a “speed limit” on recursive self improvement —AI that can perpetually improve itself—or some sort of criteria that will help it decide when it should stop developing or releasing ultra-advanced AI, Altman said. Developing such criteria would be extremely difficult and somewhat subjective, however. For instance, one might argue that an AI that’s 10 times better than a human scientist is tolerable because it can still be controlled and monitored by existing technology, but not an AI that’s 1,000 times or 10,000 times better than a scientist, which may be able to sidestep those guardrails. But it’s unclear how to even measure such levels of intelligence. It’s safe to say that the industry debates about safety have just begun, and OpenAI and its rivals have their work cut out for them. Here’s what else is going on… AI Deep Dive: Interpretability Could Train Models More Efficiently, Says World Mechanics CEO Earlier this year, a paper called “Interpreting Physics in Video World Models” tackled a key question about how AI models predict the physical world: do they learn separate representations for physical concepts such as velocity and gravity? Or are those concepts lumped together in the patterns the models learn? It turns out that these concepts tend to be “highly entangled” in video models, said Sonia Joseph , the lead author of that paper, and the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics , in the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive . Joseph argues that separating out these concepts to ensure the model learns a distinct representation for velocity and gravity and so on could help train models with less data and compute. For example, at some point while training an AI model, a researcher could look into the math underlying the model to tell whether it has learned object permanence, and if it has not, add in more training data focused specifically on that capability, she said. Alternatively, scaling up current world models without new approaches could work, she argued. “It'll just take 20 years and be highly inefficient and consume 20 nuclear reactors of compute.”— Rocket Drew Big Number Nscale and Anthropic are in talks for a second compute deal worth roughly $45 billion, on top of the $45 billion, six-year agreement the two companies struck in August for 460 megawatts of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips at Nscale's West Virginia campus. title: How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning
content: In early 2023, Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman gathered with Jas Khaira, the company’s lead AI investor, and other top executives at the finance giant’s Park Avenue headquarters in Manhattan for a debate: Should they give billions of dollars to a little-known data center developer—CoreWeave—that they had turned down just a few months earlier? CoreWeave had gotten Blackstone to return to the table after landing a multiyear, multibillion-dollar contract to sell cloud computing services to Microsoft. It needed $2.3 billion to buy Nvidia GPUs and secure a data center to house them. In Blackstone’s discussion of the deal, several executives in the room had deep misgivings, according to a person who attended the meeting. CoreWeave was still something of a mystery, a six-year-old, privately held firm that had generated only $16 million in revenue in the previous year. Schwarzman himself was personally worried his investment team could be making a mistake, the person said. Still, Schwarzman signed off, and Blackstone went ahead with the deal anyway. Its confidence in making the loan was rooted in the fact that the debt was structured largely on Microsoft’s ability to keep paying CoreWeave. Besides, Blackstone was eager to get in on the action of the AI boom. These days, CoreWeave is a publicly traded outfit worth $35 billion, holding cloud computing contracts with Microsoft, Meta Platforms, OpenAI and other customers that added up to $5.1 billion in revenue last year. But lately, many people have been asking themselves the same question the Blackstone suits pondered—whether investing in CoreWeave was actually a big fat mistake. With a business built on mounds of debt, CoreWeave stands today at a moment of reckoning that is reigniting concerns about the stability of the AI economy. Investors in the company have been heading for the exits. Those fears have seeped into other stocks, too, and have prompted anxious discussions across Silicon Valley and Wall Street about whether October 2026 could possibly end up resembling March 2000—the moment when the dot-com bubble burst. In the last week, the company’s stock has sharply declined—from nearly $80 a share last Tuesday to just over $61 on Monday—a roughly 20% drop that far outpaced the broader market’s decline of less than 1%. CoreWeave belongs to a group of young companies called neoclouds that offer cloud computing services competing with those of Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Shares of Nebius and IREN, two other publicly traded neoclouds, have respectively lost 15% and 17% in a week. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator acknowledged the whipsaw in a staff memo last week. “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally,” he wrote. “We are confident in our disciplined execution.” The plunge in CoreWeave shares seems to come from an array of factors. There wasn’t any single disastrous announcement by CoreWeave in the last few days that shook confidence. But benchmark U.S. bond yields have been increasing, which means CoreWeave will almost certainly need to pay more for the financing it needs to keep growing. And last Wednesday, the latest U.S. inflation data showed a spike in prices in September, increasing the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates, which would further increase borrowing costs. At the same time, the yields on CoreWeave’s existing debt have spiked, climbing to more than 15% last week, a signal that investors were growing increasingly nervous about the company’s ability to repay its debts. Meanwhile, its CEO has sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. While those sales were prescheduled, investors often see such transactions as signals that they, too, should sell. Trying to decipher what’s going on with CoreWeave—and what will happen next—has become a favorite water-cooler topic in Silicon Valley. Last week, for instance, Elon Musk retweeted a chart showing CoreWeave’s rising bond yields with a single word: “Yikes.” And when venture capitalist Ben Horowitz made a Thursday appearance on the “All-In” podcast, he described CoreWeave’s business as a “Rube Goldberg financial machine” and said his firm, Andreessen Horowitz, has largely stayed away from investing in companies like CoreWeave because of their debt-heavy strategies. (Andreessen Horowitz does own a stake in Volta, a newly created neocloud formed by former Brookfield infrastructure investors.) When asked to comment for this story, CoreWeave declined to make any executives available for interviews. Instead, a spokesperson sent a three-page document titled “Financing Overview October 2026” that outlined its debt maneuvers and how it plans to repay its obligations. The document ends with an attempt at succinct optimism: “CoreWeave is well-positioned to help shape [its] market as it grows and evolves.” With cloud computing and data centers at the heart of the AI era, CoreWeave’s ability to keep going is seen as an important bellwether for the entire AI industry, an outsize position for a firm that remains little known—and little understood—beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley insiders. Worries about whether CoreWeave may stumble amid rising borrowing costs then lead to broader concerns about what dominoes may fall next. Other storm clouds have gathered over the landscape. Last weekend, Microsoft said it would pull out of a compute deal with London-based Nscale over power issues that threaten to delay a 50-megawatt data center in rural Britain. And a week earlier, Firmus, an Australian data center operator backed by Nvidia and Blackstone, pulled its IPO. A day before Firmus yanked its public offering, one CoreWeave executive, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the company had not authorized him to speak publicly, argued that CoreWeave investors shouldn’t see that as a warning sign for CoreWeave. He sought to differentiate CoreWeave from Firmus by highlighting the former’s deeper stockpile of long-term contracts, which he says isn’t the same for Firmus. “They have some contracts—and some potential,” the executive said. Jerry Tang, CEO of AIB Data Centers, a small data center developer, has been biting his nails while watching CoreWeave’s declining stock price. “This is a classic liquidity crunch,” said Tang, whose firm just signed a contract with Nebius to provide 50 MW of data center capacity. “I am very concerned, because this affects everybody,” including his new partner, he added. Short of Compute CoreWeave got its start when a group of hedge fund commodities traders decided to get into crypto mining. They set up in a New Jersey office in 2017, starting with one and later expanding to many Nvidia GPUs, which are essential for running the computations involved in crypto mining. A crash in cryptocurrency prices the following year convinced them to use their pile of chips for something else. They pivoted toward high-performance cloud computing, renaming their company from Atlantic Crypto to CoreWeave along the way. As CoreWeave turned its attention to the cloud, it saw debt as a way to supercharge its growth. Then as now, one form of debt it favored allowed it to raise money for specific data center projects anchored by large customers—like Microsoft. Following ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch, Microsoft quickly found itself short of compute after promising OpenAI that it would provide the computing power for the company’s nascent models. In February 2023, CoreWeave signed its compute deal with Microsoft. Two months later, Nvidia joined a $221 million round of financing for CoreWeave, throwing its support behind a competitor to the traditional cloud giants—Amazon, Google and Microsoft—as part of a bid to diversify its reliance on the firms that buy its chips. By the time CoreWeave got the loan from Blackstone in August of that year, the two firms had come up with an innovative financial maneuver, backing the $2.3 billion with AI chips as collateral. That provided a template for CoreWeave’s future borrowing. For each data center project, CoreWeave secures a contract with a customer. It then uses that agreement to line up financing, structuring the loans to pay down the debt with the revenue earned from the contract. The company has said it should take two and a half years to repay such a loan as it continues collecting payouts through the entire life of the contract. In a staff memo last week, CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator acknowledged his company’s gyrating stock price:  “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” (Getty Images) To fund its operations, CoreWeave borrows additional debt that isn’t tied to its contracts and must be repaid out of the corporate coffers. It uses some of those funds, according to analysts, to pay for costs that aren’t covered by the project loans. That means the company is piling debt on top of debt. Armed with Blackstone’s money, CoreWeave continued working closely with Microsoft, adding other customers like Meta Platforms and OpenAI along the way. In March 2025, CoreWeave sold shares to the public at $40 a share, then the largest AI-related listing ever. The stock surged beyond $183 in the months after. In July, CoreWeave became the first company to deploy Nvidia’s most advanced server rack, and this January, the chipmaker invested another $2 billion in the company. As CoreWeave grew, it continued using the loan structure it designed with Blackstone to fund its expansion. As one of the few companies that actually trades in the public markets, CoreWeave has also become a proxy for the broader AI trade. Many investors who have long exposure to private tech companies such as the leading frontier labs have turned to CoreWeave as a way to hedge other investments, according to one adviser who speaks with numerous large investors. To hedge, they can short the stock. They can also buy credit default swaps, which offer a payout if the company defaults on its debt. “If you are taking a negative bet, what better place than in a liquid bet on [credit default swaps] for CoreWeave?” said John McPeake, an analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, who rates the stock a buy. McPeake said he attended CoreWeave’s customer conference several weeks ago in San Francisco, where the company said it would raise prices an additional 10%, on top of an increase it had already announced, on the main product it sells: GPUs by the hour. ‘We Can’t Figure It Out’ Despite all the recent commotion, CoreWeave still enjoys the support of the industry’s biggest players. In addition to having connections to Blackstone, the private equity firm with the most assets under management, the company also enjoys cozy ties to Nvidia. Last Thursday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had full confidence in CoreWeave. “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he said. “I’m optimistic.” The comments arrested the slide in the company’s stock price before it picked up again on Friday. And early backer Blackstone has more recently introduced the company to a new base of investors: insurance companies. CoreWeave finds insurers alluring because they have deep pockets and generally invest with long-term time horizons. Brannin McBee, a CoreWeave founder, acknowledged the importance of the insurance segment last week in an FT interview published just as the company’s bonds were plunging . Steve Schwarzman’s Blackstone has been a major partner for CoreWeave, most recently helping it win insurance giants as investors in its debt offerings. (Getty Images) Insurance companies, which like to invest in high-yielding investment-grade debt, bought more than $740 million of a project-specific loan CoreWeave had arranged for a Meta contract, according to data compiled by S&P Capital IQ. Blackstone manages investments for some of the largest insurers involved in the deal, including American General Life Insurance, Fidelity & Guaranty Life and Security Life of Denver. The next thing on the horizon for CoreWeave could be equity sales. Michael Haber, a desk credit strategist at Jefferies, said last week in an interview that he has had a lot of conversations with equity investors who have finally taken notice that higher interest rates and too much supply of AI-related debt are making the credit markets more expensive—and perhaps totally unavailable in the future—for some data center projects and chip purchases. They’re coming to the realization that neoclouds and other developers are going to need to raise money by selling stock. “A lot of equity investors were not paying attention and are now waking up and saying, ‘Why is the equity down so much?’” he said. “The AI story is moving from being a tech story to a financing story.” Selling that story to investors could be difficult if stock and bond prices continue to fluctuate without a clear reason why. Last week, even CoreWeave’s bankers at Goldman Sachs couldn’t explain the swoon in the company’s share price. When Christopher Miglino, CEO of compute provider Axe Compute, sat down with his bankers at Goldman Sachs, they acknowledged that there was no fundamental reason why CoreWeave should have been hammered so hard. Goldman was one of the company’s IPO underwriters. “I was having breakfast with Goldman Sachs yesterday, and I said, ‘What do you guys think?’” Miglino said. “They said, ‘We can’t figure it out. Fundamentally, there is no rhyme and reason for what’s going on.’” On Monday, Goldman’s research analysts upgraded CoreWeave’s stock to a buy rating. Such moves can often bring some relief to a battered stock. Even so, CoreWeave shares finished the day down 0.4%.

title: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph
content: Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models —and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability . Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin . Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. ( The full episode is available here .) “You need interpretability to have world models,” she said. “You need to be looking at their internal representations. You need to be using that to guide training for data efficiency, for performance, and also for reliability, and physical safety and security.” For example, if an AI model is guiding a surgeon through an operation, “how do I know that’s not a hallucination?” Joseph asked. Identifying the concepts that AI model has learned could help ensure that the AI is not basing its decision on “spurious cues, like the color of the surgeon’s mask, or does the surgeon have a ring on their finger, which current world models do.” We also discussed why Joseph does not think that language models automating AI research will work for the physical world, the ways in which she disagrees with her former colleague Yann LeCun, and how AI systems could be interpretable to blue collar workers rather than exclusively to academics. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Sonia Joseph. Sonia is the co-founder and CEO of World Mechanics, a startup that’s working on training interpretable world models. Meaning, we want the physical world to be understood by our AIs, and we also want those AIs to be understood by us. Before co-founding World Mechanics, Sonia was a researcher at Meta, where she led Meta’s forum on interpretability. Thanks for coming on the show, Sonia. Joseph: Thank you so much, Rocket. I’m so excited to be here. Drew: Me too. I’m really glad you’re here. I think we probably first met maybe three years ago or so at a dinner that Neel Nanda, an interpretability researcher at DeepMind, hosted, and it was over at a Nepalese restaurant in Berkeley. And this comes to mind because I think every time we talk, I start craving Nepalese food. Joseph: It’s a great association. I still think about the food. Drew: I’m totally conditioned. Yeah, it was a great conversation. But now I think I’m gonna have to get dumplings after this. Joseph: Oh, okay. You’re making me hungry now. Drew: I’m excited. Joseph: Me too. That’s great. Drew: Well, I’m really glad you’re on the show today, we’re going to talk about this intersection between interpretability and world models, which are two—I mean—fascinating topics in their own right. But we’re going to get into the intersection between them. I want to start with a post that you wrote, claiming that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. I think that’s kind of a provocative claim. I guess usually when I hear people talk about the importance of interpreting models, they’re talking about language models, talking about chatbots and language-based agents. And then when people talk about world models, they’re sort of talking about a whole nother universe. They’re talking about models that understand the physical world for manufacturing or for robotics. But often these two things are not in conversation with each other. So, can you explain why these are two sides of the same coin? Joseph: Okay, so world model has become a very slippery term, and there is an East Coast definition of world models that’s often used in New York and Montreal, where I was for the last five years. And then there’s a West Coast definition, which listeners here and people here are probably more familiar with. So, I’d say interpretability is baked into the East Coast definition. In the East Coast, which is full of neuroscientists, there’s also a lot of thought about internal representation. So, what is the neural net representing, and does it map one to one with the physical world? So this can be a proxy for true physical reasoning or physical understanding. And I sometimes use the term physical reasoning instead of world model to prevent confusion from the West Coast definition. And the West Coast definition often focuses on either one of two aspects. One is either generating very photorealistic worlds. This is a hard problem. It’s a cool problem, but it’s a different problem. And the second is putting the model inside a robot and having the robot being able to navigate the world. And these problems are closely related. I would argue that you need understanding to get a very effective version of the other two, but here on the West Coast, I actually see very little talk of internal representations and interpretability in the context of world models. As you said, it’s usually in the context of language, and I would argue that an agent that’s able to navigate the world, as with the second West Coast definition, or even the first, to generate a physically plausible world, that you need to have an understanding, you need to be looking at the internal representations, and I would even argue—this is an even stronger claim, and a lot of neuroscientists would disagree with me—but I would argue that the world model in the East Coast definition needs to be a functional homomorphism with the physical world. Drew: What does that mean? Joseph: A one-to-one mapping on the physical world in a functional way, in the sense where, for example, in the physical world, say I have to throw a ball in the air and catch it, there would be an internal representation inside the neural net tracking that in a way that’s interpretable and legible. And I’m gonna make a series of increasingly stronger claims, and I can imagine some of the more research oriented people might have reason to disagree, but I, based off evidence we’ve seen, this is the direction I think things are going, where if you’re to throw a ball in the air and catch it, inside the body of the world model itself, if the world model is highly accurate, performant, data efficient, there will be a very clean representation of the ball being thrown up in the air and caught. And this is why I think you need interpretability to have world models. You need to be looking at their internal representations. You need to be using that to guide training for data efficiency, for performance, and also for reliability and physical safety and security, which is a whole topic. And I would argue that no one’s really thinking about it this way. Drew: So, what is the strongest version of this claim that you subscribe to? Joseph: You need interpretability to have world models is the strongest claim, and I would argue you need interpretability to have accurate world models, data efficient world models, and reliable world models. Drew: I see, I see. So on the West Coast, when we talk about world models, often what we mean is it’s a video model. It’s generating videos, and maybe they are physically realistic or physically plausible. Or we mean we want to have some kind of generative model that can act as the brain of a robot, or can generate simulated environments to train a robot in. You’re saying the East Coast definition is more inflected by this history of neuroscience, almost. Joseph: Absolutely. Drew: What does a world model mean to someone on the East Coast then who is thinking about it from more of a neuroscience perspective? Joseph: Yeah, it would mean an agent, or you could think the brain, a foundation model that understands the world to the point its internal representations are disentangled and causal. So, for example, if there’s a ball being thrown into the air and it comes down, there’s an internal representation of the ball that is disentangled from other things inside the mind of that agent, that person, that foundation model, opposed to some conflationary set of heuristics or memorizations or shortcuts, which arguably most of our current world models still have. Drew: Do you think that sort of people’s minds have world models in this sense, where there are factorized representations or specific representations of these different physical concepts, or are we relying on this loose collection of heuristics that changes task to task? Joseph: It depends on the task. I’d say, for most physical tasks, yes. I would say humans are often very conflationary reasoners. When you get into the whole world of stereotypes and biases, this is actually not having disentangled and causal representations. This is having highly correlational heuristics. So a superhuman intelligence, I think, would have highly disentangled internal representations. Drew: So say I’m with you that in order to be a good world model, you would have these disentangled representations somewhere in the brain of that model. Why is it important that we be able to find them? Why do we have to do interpretability to make sure that they’re actually in there or that we’ve found them in the right place? Joseph: Yeah, so there are a variety of reasons. One to start with might be safety or reliability. If you could think of one of these robots in your home, we may want to test that this robot, its foundation model brain, has reliable representations of the physical world. So one example is object permanence, this water bottle. If I look away and look back, we want that representation of the water bottle to stay. We want to test that that foundation model or that agent has these understandings of physical plausibility. And with a white box analysis, you can probe inside the model to see if there are certain representations that correspond to physical plausibility. For example, there might be a manifold or some kind of feature that corresponds to object permanence, unlike various other properties of the physical world that would be harder to find with black box evaluation alone. So, combining white box evaluation to make sure that the information is there and doesn’t—sometimes it might appear and then in the middle of the net it might start disappearing to make sure yeah—to make sure that information is there is very necessary. So the example I gave was in robots in our homes, but there’s also surgical robotics as well. We want to make sure that these models are reliable and we want to be probing them for the qualities we care about at every part of the net. Drew: So when you say black box, you mean sort of strictly relying on inputs and outputs and looking at the outward behavior of the model. When you say white box, you’re talking about interpreting the internals, trying to understand the computation that’s going on under the hood that makes up these models. Is that right? Joseph: That’s exactly right. Drew: Okay, so evaluation is one reason it would be really great to have interpretability. Basically, we can evaluate and make sure that the model is understanding the right thing at the right time, and that means it’s not going to take some unwanted or unpredicted action. Are there other reasons interpretability is really important here? Joseph: Yeah, one is data efficiency. Currently, these models are extremely expensive to train, and one analogy I think of is imagine you’re in school and you have a huge test tomorrow and you’re cramming for that test and you just cram for six hours. When you actually go to take the test, you might perform okay, but the information in your mind might be kind of disorganized and you might make some errors and you might not truly understand what’s going on. And I would argue that the way we’re training a lot of these models now is kind of analogous to that. While in contrast, interpretability guided training is actually checking at various time points if the model has learned a certain behavior, for example, object permanence, and if it hasn’t, feeding in more data in a loop that encourages the learning of certain capabilities at certain times in a way that might consume orders of magnitude less data. Similarly, there’s this idea of influence functions given a capability, which data elicited that capability and where in the weights is it stored, and these are fundamentally interpretability questions. So maybe another analogy is you can imagine in a utopia or in a dystopia where we really care about the learning of children, maybe we can have some kind of fMRI as they’re learning from a textbook, and if their neural correlates are corresponding to patterns that map to understanding, this is good. And if they’re not, maybe we can intervene and be like, hey, this is clearly not working. Let’s give the kid a new textbook, or let’s do something a little bit different. And I’d say interpretability-informed training is very similar. Drew: Yeah, even without going that far as fMRI’s, or intervening— Joseph: Not to make it too sci-fi.
